stem: Jon Hamilton, a 19-year-old man comes to the ER because of right wrist pain and swelling 2 hours after falling on an outstretched hand while skateboarding trying to impress his Ram Ranch™ roommates Aaron and Devin. His right wrist is swollen and tender; range of motion is limited by pain. There is tenderness to palpation in the area between the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor pollicis longus muscle. His thumb can be opposed actively toward the other fingers. Muscle strength of the right hand is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Scaphoid fractures typically occur following a fall on an outstretched hand. If pain occurs in the anatomical snuffbox (area between the tendons of the abductor pollicis longus, extensor pollicis brevis, and extensor pollicis longus muscle) after trauma, the injury should be treated as a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise to prevent possible complications such as avascular necrosis and bone nonunion.

stem: While being arrested by London's finest for public indecency after a night at Jack’s. James Bunker's arms were handcuffed behind his back. What actions did his upper limb have to perform to get to this position? Write your answer here:
answer:
Shoulder aBduction, extension, Internal rotation, and Elbow flexion.

Break the position down joint by joint. The elbows are bent, so elbow flexion. The humerus swings behind the trunk, which is shoulder extension. The forearms turn inward so the hands meet at the small of the back, which is internal (medial) rotation. Bringing the two wrists together behind the body draws the arms toward the midline, which is adduction, not abduction. The muscle notes put this exact combination in one muscle: latissimus dorsi (from 02.1 - Anatomy of the Back & Neck) "extends, aDDucts and medially rotates the humerus". That is the hand-behind-the-back movement, and why the lats and teres major are what the cuffs load.

flags.title: The key looks wrong
flags.html: The key lists shoulder aBduction. Reaching behind the back to bring the hands together is adduction with extension and internal rotation, the actions the latissimus dorsi and teres major notes give. Extension, internal rotation and elbow flexion in the key are right; read the abduction as an error.

stem: A 76 year old female patient with osteoporosis presents to the ER in immense pain over her right hip around the region of the greater trochanter for the past 6hrs. She reports rolling off her couch when she was napping and landing on her hip. You order an xray and confirm a intrascapular femoral neck fracture. What is the next step in the management of this patient?

options.html: Recommend conservative management for this patient – non-weight bearing for 3-4 weeks
Urgent open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF) within 48hrs
Urgent hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty within 48hrs

answer: The correct answer is D. With hip fractures, surgery outcomes are best when surgery is performed within 24-48hrs of the fracture. For older patients (60+), the surgical method of choice is a hemiarthroplasty or total hip arthroplasty over ORIF.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has numbness of the thumb and index finger. Which finding most favours C6 radiculopathy over carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.html: Symptoms that wake her at night
Weakness of thumb abduction and opposition
Numbness extending up the lateral forearm

answer: The correct answer is E. In carpal tunnel syndrome, median nerve function proximal to the wrist is normal, so sensory change stays in the hand; symptoms are nocturnal and worse with wrist flexion or extension, with Tinel/Phalen positive and possible thumb (LOAF) weakness. C6 radiculopathy extends to the lateral forearm and weakens the wrist extensors. EMG/NCS distinguishes the two.

stem: An 84-year-old woman cannot get up after a fall at home and has groin pain. Which appearance of the affected leg is most typical of a hip fracture?
answer: The correct answer is A. Hip fracture (proximal femur): acute groin pain, worse with movement, unable to bear weight. On look the leg is shortened, externally rotated and abducted; feel for hip tenderness; move shows painful ROM (log roll). Check distal pulses and sciatic nerve function.

stem: A 65 year-old male presents to your clinic with a 2-year history of intermittent hip pain which localizes to the groin. He has not tried any specific therapy to date. After taking a careful history and doing a thorough physical examination, you determine the most likely diagnosis is osteoarthritis of the hip. The patient asks if he should have an MRI to confirm the diagnosis. What should you tell him?

options.html: Of course! MRI is the best test for arthritis!
Well… we should do an x-ray and CT scan instead, because they’re better at looking at bones!
Let’s start with an x-ray, it’s great at looking at bones and will help confirm my diagnosis!
Instead of an MRI, we should get an US! It’s faster to get so you won’t have to wait as long!

answer: The correct answer is C. "Let's start with an x-ray, it's great at looking at bones and will help confirm my diagnosis!" MRI is not required to confirm the diagnosis of arthritis; it comes with a lengthy waitlist and adds no benefit in confirming the diagnosis. X-ray and CT are better at looking at bones, but CT carries much more radiation, and arthritis can be confidently confirmed on X-ray. Ultrasound is a poor modality for assessing arthritis, especially in a deep joint like the hip.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. Hip osteoarthritis treatment starts with non-drug measures: education, exercise and physiotherapy, functional supports, weight management, tai chi and a cane. He has tried nothing yet, so this is where to begin; drugs, injections and replacement follow if he does not improve 05 - Clinical Approach to Hip Pain.

  • B: Image-guided intra-articular injection (steroid, hyaluronic acid or platelet-rich plasma) is a later step, not a first one for a man who has tried no therapy.
  • C: Hip replacement is the end of the treatment ladder, not the start.
  • D: Oral NSAIDs and duloxetine are on the drug list, which comes after the non-drug measures are in place.

stem: You are seeing a 71 year-old female with lateral hip pain. You can’t seem to decide whether the history is more in keeping with GTPS or hip OA. The patient then tells you she has absolutely no difficulties getting her socks on in the morning when she’s sitting down. Which one seems more likely now?
answer: The correct answer is A. GTPS (greater trochanteric pain syndrome). Putting socks on in a seated position needs hip flexion and external rotation (basically the FABER test), so it is commonly uncomfortable with hip osteoarthritis. People with GTPS normally have a relatively pain-free hip range of motion, so socks are not a problem, unless they are standing: a single-leg stance needs the hip abductors (gluteus medius and minimus) to stay upright, those usually have some tendinopathy in GTPS, and using them hurts.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. GTPS is a chronic tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus with flares of bursitis, and its treatment starts with physiotherapy that stretches the iliotibial band and strengthens the hip abductors, together with load management and weight management. NSAIDs, injections and possibly surgery come later 05 - Clinical Approach to Hip Pain.

  • A: Arthroscopic labral debridement or repair is the surgical option for a labral tear, which gives groin pain with clicking and locking.
  • B: Hip replacement treats hip osteoarthritis, and her easy seated sock-putting argues against OA.
  • D: Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection of piriformis treats piriformis syndrome, which causes buttock pain, not lateral hip pain.

stem: A 19-year-old soccer player plants her foot and pivots, feels a pop, and her knee swells markedly within a few hours. Which examination manoeuvre is most accurate for the likely injury?
answer: The correct answer is D. Non-contact pivoting during deceleration with a pop and rapid hemarthrosis is classic for an ACL tear (a vessel runs through the ligament). The Lachman test has the best sensitivity and specificity; anterior drawer is weaker and pivot shift is mostly done in the OR. X-ray rules out fracture; MRI if the exam is unclear.

stem: A 30-year-old driver hits his flexed knee on the dashboard in a collision. He has poorly defined knee pain and minimal swelling. With both knees flexed, the affected tibia sags posteriorly. Which structure is most likely injured?
answer: The correct answer is E. PCL injury follows a direct blow to the anterior tibia with the knee flexed (dashboard injury) or hyperextension. Pain is ill-defined with minimal swelling; posterior drawer, sag sign and reverse Lachman are positive. It usually involves other posterolateral structures; PT and bracing, with surgery for rotary instability or PLC injuries.

stem: A 42-year-old man twisted his knee with his foot planted. The knee swelled the next day, and it now catches and locks. There is medial joint line tenderness and a positive Thessaly test. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. Meniscal injury: rotation/twisting with the foot planted, joint line pain, delayed or intermittent swelling, and mechanical symptoms (locking, catching); McMurray and Thessaly tests. ACL tears swell within hours. Conservative management first for small or degenerative tears; MRI if that fails or a large tear is suspected.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 27 year old male football athlete pivots with his left knee as he changes direction to the right. He feels his knee "move" as it gives way. The athlete collapses to the ground and is unable to weight bear due to significant pain and swelling.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture follows the case with its "ACL Injury" section. The mechanism is the one the lecture gives for a non-contact ACL tear (60-80%): cutting or pivoting while decelerating. The knee "gives way" (the lecture's "instability" or "giving out"), and the swelling is significant at once - the lecture's immediate swelling / hemarthrosis, and in the traumatic knee pain section (Part Two) an ACL tear sits among the injuries that swell within 6 hours. An MCL sprain (A) comes from a valgus collision and swells minimally or not at all. A PCL tear (C) needs a blow to the front of the tibia with the knee flexed, or hyperextension, and gives minimal swelling. A meniscal tear (D) comes from twisting on a planted foot but swells late or on and off, not immediately.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 23 year old male ice hockey athlete falls awkwardly to the ice while his skate is caught up with another player. His knee rotates and he suffers immediate medial pain. There is no obvious initial swelling but develops a moderate amount of swelling later on that night.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture follows the case with "Meniscal Injuries". The mechanism is the lecture's for a meniscal tear: rotation or twisting with the foot planted (here the skate is caught). The pain is at the medial joint line, and the swelling is delayed - the lecture's "delayed or intermittent swelling/effusions", and in the traumatic knee pain section (Part Two) meniscal injuries swell after 6 hours. The medial meniscus is the one that tears more often, because it is fixed to the tibial collateral ligament. An ACL tear (A) swells immediately (hemarthrosis). An MCL sprain (B) also gives medial pain, but it is caused by a valgus collision and swells minimally or not at all. A PCL tear (C) needs a blow to the front of the flexed tibia, or hyperextension.

stem: A patient presents with a large swelling at the elbow. On the lateral elbow radiograph the osseous structures are normal, and there is a well-defined, low-density oval mass within the soft tissues, causing anterior displacement of the overlying soft tissues. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (stem assembled from the lecture, leaving out the caption and annotation that name the diagnosis; the lecture poses no question)
answer:
The correct answer is D. The module's own reveal (page 46): based on its low density and well-defined appearance, the mass was suspected to be a large lipoma, later confirmed with CT or MRI. Its lesson is that normal-looking bones do not exclude pathology, so the soft tissues must always be checked.

  • Joint effusion shows as the posterior fat pad sign (a visible posterior fat pad, always abnormal) inside the joint, not as a soft-tissue mass displacing tissue anteriorly.
  • Olecranon bursa swelling sits over the posterior olecranon (the bursa swells with inflammation or bleeding), not in the anterior soft tissues.
  • Giant cell tumour of bone is a lesion of the bone itself: an expanded bone with a large lytic lesion and thinned cortex (the module's example is in the distal radius). Here the bones are normal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 18 year old female presents with a three month history of worsening bilateral anterior knee pain. There was no injury but she recently started running. Her pain was initially only with exercise but now it is painful with prolonged sitting and stairs. There is no swelling and she describes the pain as a deep anterior aching pain.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The notes follow the case with "Patellofemoral Pain Syndrome (PFPS)": anterior knee pain during or after repetitive loading of the extensor mechanism, commonest in females and adolescents, of gradual onset (biomechanical overload - here a new running habit), an aching pain worse after activity and with prolonged sitting, and no joint swelling. Prepatellar bursitis (B) shows mild swelling and tenderness over the bursa, and she has no swelling. Iliotibial band friction syndrome (C) is an aching lateral knee during running. A popliteal cyst (D) is a swelling behind the knee.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 45-year-old man who works for a moving company felt a "pop" in his anterior elbow while lifting a refrigerator a day ago. The pain is severe, throbbing and deep, worse with any elbow movement and better with ice, and he has bruising over the front of the elbow. He smokes a pack a day and drinks 8 beers a week. There is a visible change in the contour of the arm; the bottom of the "lump" and the bruise are tender, and the antecubital fossa feels "empty". Active elbow flexion and supination are reduced, passive range is full, and full extension hurts a little. Pulses are normal and sensation is intact apart from around the bruise. Shoulder flexion 4/5, elbow flexion 4/5, supination 4/5, everything else 5/5. The biceps reflex is absent; brachioradialis and triceps reflexes are 2+.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Long head of biceps tendon rupture

answer:
The correct answer is C. The session concludes a complete distal biceps tendon rupture. Its differential sorts weakness or loss of active range without sensory changes into tendon, bone or joint, and nerve; with normal sensation the tendon heads the list. The "pop" on a heavy lift, the bruise, the change in muscle contour and an empty antecubital fossa place the tear at the elbow, and the biceps supinates and flexes the elbow, which are the movements he has lost.

  • A The musculocutaneous nerve would weaken the same muscles, but it also ends as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, and his sensation is intact.
  • B A proximal (long head) rupture gives anterior shoulder pain, is often degenerative in older patients, and usually leaves the arm functional.
  • D Passive range is full and nothing points to the bone; the session's X-ray is only to rule out an avulsion.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 45-year-old above has a complete distal biceps tendon rupture, yet he can still flex his elbow (4/5) and supinate.

stem: Which muscle does most of the work of his remaining elbow flexion?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The session asks which muscles compensate and answers with a labelled picture that does not survive as text, so this answer is reasoned from the lecture: brachialis, not biceps, is the primary flexor of the forearm. It runs from the distal anterior humerus to the coronoid process of the ulna, crosses only the elbow, and is untouched by a tear at the radial tuberosity.

  • B Coracobrachialis crosses the shoulder only: it flexes and adducts the shoulder, which is part of why his shoulder flexion is still 4/5.
  • C Anconeus is at the back of the elbow and helps extend it.
  • D Supinator is what keeps some of his supination; it does not flex the elbow.

lectureMeta: Source: the Week 9 synchronous upper extremity case review (uppere_1, OneNote PoM 2 / B3 MSK / Synch W9), 3 cases, Q93-102. Tests 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Arm. Case 1. Written for this bank 2026-11-02.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 45-year-old mover above, with a complete distal biceps tendon rupture confirmed on ultrasound, is otherwise well and uses his arm for heavy lifting at work.

stem: What is the most appropriate management?

options.html: A sling, then physiotherapy, and reassessment at six weeks
A corticosteroid injection at the anterior elbow
Rest, ice and pain control until the swelling settles
Early referral to orthopedics for surgical repair

answer:
The correct answer is D. The session: "This is a surgical problem unless there's a reason for it not to be" (a much older patient, comorbidities, not using the arm functionally), and the referral is a limited-time offer. The distal tendon retracts and scars to the surrounding tissue soon after it ruptures, so primary reattachment gets harder with every week and may come to need a graft. A distal rupture is rare but has consequences: poor supination and weak flexion.

  • A, C RICE and pain control are part of the plan, but only alongside the referral; waiting six weeks spends the repair window.
  • B Nothing in the plan injects a torn tendon.

Contrast the proximal rupture, which is usually still functional and typically managed without surgery.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 22-year-old student is seen in the ER hours after colliding with another player during a volleyball game, his arm extended for a spike. The pain is diffuse around the shoulder ("it just hurts"), worse with any movement, and he is holding the arm against his body. He is clearly very uncomfortable and very protective of the arm. The shoulder is sore all round, with a change in its contour. He will not let you move the shoulder; the elbow, wrist and hand move normally. He cannot tolerate special tests.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus

answer:
The correct answer is B. The session's films show an anterior dislocation, "which you already assumed, but you can never assume". Over 90% of shoulder dislocations are anterior, and a traumatic dislocation is anterior far more often than posterior; a change in contour and an arm held against the body fit a humeral head that has left the glenoid.

  • A A surgical neck fracture is the injury of a low-energy fall onto the hand in an older patient with osteoporosis.
  • C Posterior dislocation is the rare direction, and only the Y-view proves which one it is.
  • D An AC separation is graded by how far the joint is displaced; it is the glenohumeral joint whose contour changes when the humeral head leaves the glenoid.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 22-year-old student is seen in the ER hours after colliding with another player during a volleyball game, his arm extended for a spike . The pain is diffuse around the shoulder ("it just hurts"), worse with any movement, and he is holding the arm against his body . He is clearly very uncomfortable and very protective of the arm. The shoulder is sore all round, with a change in its contour . He will not let you move the shoulder ; the elbow, wrist and hand move normally. He cannot tolerate special tests. Later: an AP film shows the humeral head out of the glenoid, and the scapular Y view confirms an anterior glenohumeral dislocation.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. A traumatic dislocation is reduced first: safety first with monitors, analgesia, manipulation to correct the deformity, then re-examination of neurovascular status and a post-reduction X-ray. Surgery is often offered later to young or recurrent dislocators 05.2 - Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity.

  • B: Capsule-labral repair is for young or recurrent dislocators once the acute dislocation has been dealt with, not in place of reducing it.
  • C: Rehab first is the plan for atraumatic multidirectional (AMBRI) instability, not a dislocated shoulder after trauma.
  • D: Inferior capsular shift is the uncommon surgery for atraumatic (AMBRI) instability.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 22-year-old volleyball player above has an AP film of the shoulder that shows the humeral head out of the glenoid.

stem: Which view must also be taken before you can say which way it has dislocated?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The session's films are missing a view, and its point is that the scapular Y view is what shows the dislocation is anterior. The lecture: you need more than one view to tell the direction, and the Y-view tells anterior (humeral head under the coracoid) from posterior (farther from it).

  • A The Grashey view is part of the standard shoulder series, but the lecture gives the job of setting the direction to the Y-view.
  • B A second AP shows the same single plane again.
  • D The injury is at the glenohumeral joint; nothing points to the clavicle.

Tests 04 - Neurovascular Supply of the Proximal Upper Extremity, 05.2 - Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity. Case 2. Written for this bank 2026-11-02.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 22-year-old's shoulder is relocated in the ER under conscious sedation, and the post-reduction X-rays look good. On re-examination he has numbness over the deltoid, otherwise intact sensation, and shoulder abduction is 3/5; every other movement is 5/5.

stem: Which nerve has been injured?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The session: the axillary nerve is the most common nerve injury after a shoulder dislocation, giving the "sergeant's patch" of numbness and weak abduction. The axillary nerve (posterior cord, C5, C6) supplies the deltoid and teres minor and the skin over the deltoid, and a dislocation, usually anterior and inferior, puts it at risk. This is why the reduction is followed by re-examining neurovascular status before he goes home.

  • B The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus, which only starts abduction, and gives no patch of skin over the deltoid.
  • C The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the front of the arm (elbow flexion, supination) and the lateral forearm skin.
  • D The radial nerve would weaken elbow, wrist and finger extension, which are normal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 22-year-old volleyball player's anterior dislocation has been reduced and his axillary nerve injury documented.

stem: Which complication is he at particular risk of because of his age?
answer:
The correct answer is D. The session's list of complications: nerve injury (axillary most often), recurrent dislocation, "especially in the young!", fractures of the humerus or glenoid, and rotator cuff tear, "especially in older patients". The lecture's treatment of traumatic instability adds that young or recurrent dislocators often go on to surgery.

  • A A cuff tear is the complication of the older dislocator.
  • B, C Neither is on the session's list of complications of a dislocation.

lectureMeta: Source: the Week 9 synchronous upper extremity case review (uppere_1, OneNote PoM 2 / B3 MSK / Synch W9), 3 cases, Q93-102. Tests 01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2. Case 3. Written for this bank 2026-11-02.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 53-year-old right-handed man who works in an automotive parts factory has had 3 months of gradual pins and needles over the radial side of the hand, worse overnight and whenever he uses the hand, and the hand feels clumsy. He has chronic widespread pain in his neck, shoulders and both forearms, smokes a pack a day and drinks 7 drinks a week. There is nothing to see. Both the medial and lateral epicondyles are tender, and range of motion is full. Tinel's test over the wrist and Phalen's manoeuvre both bring on tingling in the fingers. Pulses are intact, pinprick is reduced over the lateral hand, strength is intact throughout the arm, and reflexes are intact.

stem: Which diagnosis best explains his numbness and tingling?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The session's reveal is carpal tunnel syndrome, with epicondylosis alongside it. Its differential starts from the fact that an objective loss of sensation points strongly to a nerve, where subjective tingling alone has a wide differential. The lecture's picture of CTS is numbness and tingling in the median territory, often predominantly at night, worse with the wrist bent, median function above the wrist normal, and perhaps Tinel's and Phalen's signs.

  • A C6 radiculopathy is the main differential; his symptoms are reproduced at the wrist, and strength and reflexes are intact. EMG and nerve conduction studies are what separate the two.
  • C Ulnar neuropathy gives tingling into the ring and little fingers and a Tinel sign at the elbow; his loss is on the radial side.
  • D Epicondylosis explains his tender epicondyles, but a tendon does not reduce pinprick.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 53-year-old factory worker above has tingling over the radial hand, worse at night, positive Tinel's and Phalen's signs at the wrist, reduced pinprick over the lateral hand, and tender medial and lateral epicondyles.

stem: Which investigation should be ordered?

options.html: MRI of the cervical spine now
Plain X-rays of the wrist and hand

answer:
The correct answer is D. The session's plan: EMG/NCS to confirm CTS (abnormalities only in the median territory), and no investigations required for the elbow. The lecture gives EMG and nerve conduction studies three jobs here: nerve versus muscle or bone, CTS versus C6, and how severe the nerve damage is.

  • A A cervical MRI chases C6, which the nerve studies are the way to exclude.
  • B Nothing in the history suggests a fracture or other bony cause.
  • C Epicondylosis is a clinical diagnosis; the session orders nothing for the elbow.

lectureMeta: Source: the Week 9 synchronous upper extremity case review (uppere_1, OneNote PoM 2 / B3 MSK / Synch W9), 3 cases, Q93-102. Tests 01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2. Case 3. Written for this bank 2026-11-02.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 53-year-old factory worker's nerve studies confirm carpal tunnel syndrome. His strength is intact.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial management of his carpal tunnel syndrome?

options.html: A rigid wrist splint worn overnight

answer:
The correct answer is C. The session's plan for CTS: education (a compressed nerve at the wrist, typically very treatable), relative rest (can he rotate tasks at work?) and overnight splinting. The lecture's order is the same: education → a rigid wrist-hand orthosis worn overnight only → corticosteroid injection → carpal tunnel release.

  • A Release is for CTS that is refractory to splinting or severe at the outset (weak, with a bad EMG/NCS); he is neither.
  • B The session lists no drug treatment for CTS; a topical anti-inflammatory is offered only for the epicondylosis.
  • D Injection is the next step after the orthosis, not the first.

The session's last word on the case: your patient is a person. His work is part of the problem and part of the plan.

Tests 02.2 - Clinical Approach to Mechanical Back & Neck Pain, 03.2 - Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain. Case continued, question 3. Written for this bank 2026-11-02.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
A 42-year-old customer service representative comes to the ER with 3 weeks of mid-thoracic back pain, progressively more severe and more frequent, that radiates to her right shoulder and around to her right upper abdomen. It comes in spasms of 30-40 minutes, sharp and lancinating, 10/10, with no trigger she can identify; between episodes she has the low back ache she has had for years. She has mild nausea and at times feels feverish, and denies trauma, weakness, numbness, rash and urinary symptoms. Acetaminophen and ibuprofen have not helped, and she has been to four emergency departments in 3 weeks; at the last one she was refused pain medication. History: spontaneous urticaria, and whiplash 15 years ago.

On examination: temperature 38.4, pulse 110, blood pressure 104/62, BMI 32. Lungs clear. The abdomen is obese and slightly distended, with significant epigastric and right upper quadrant tenderness, and rebound and guarding in the right upper quadrant. Neurological exam normal. The right shoulder has full active and passive range with no impingement, weakness or instability. Palpating the thoracic and lumbar spinous processes and paraspinal muscles, and percussing the thoracic vertebral bodies, reproduces no tenderness.

stem: Where is her pain most likely coming from?

options.html: Mechanical back pain from the thoracic paraspinal muscles
A rotator cuff problem referring pain into the back
Vertebral osteomyelitis of the mid-thoracic spine
An abdominal source referring pain to her back

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's first step for back pain is to exclude non-spinal causes, and its visceral red flag depends on the site: flank or writhing pain, GI or genitourinary symptoms. Her spine and shoulder are normal on exam, while her abdomen has right upper quadrant tenderness with rebound and guarding, and she has a fever and a pulse of 110. The pain is coming from the abdomen and being felt in the back and shoulder.

  • A Mechanical pain should be reproduced by palpating the spine and paraspinal muscles; nothing was.
  • B Her shoulder has full range, with no impingement, weakness or instability.
  • C Fever fits infection, but the lecture finds vertebral osteomyelitis by point tenderness on percussing the spine, and percussion was painless.

Which organ is the source is not in these notes; it is left open for the session. Her four ED visits, and the refusal of pain medication at the last one, are the case's other lesson: the label a patient arrives with is not a diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 72-year-old woman presents to the clinic two weeks after undergoing surgery for a total hip replacement. She is complaining of a &lsquo;limp’ while walking. You ask her to walk for you. While walking you notice that her right hip drops every time her right leg leaves the ground for the swing phase.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. This is a Trendelenburg sign: gluteus medius and minimus on the standing leg normally stop the pelvis tipping to the unsupported side. The pelvis drops on the unsupported (right) side, so the weak abductors are on the left, and they are supplied by the superior gluteal nerve, which a hip replacement can injure 04 - Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh.

  • A: A right-sided lesion would make the pelvis drop on the left when the left foot leaves the ground.
  • C: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus, which extends the hip and does not stabilize the pelvis in gait.
  • D: Wrong nerve and wrong side.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Conservative care with PRICE for 6 weeks

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. A popliteal aneurysm is the most common peripheral aneurysm and is at risk of embolization, thrombosis and rupture; a rupture not treated quickly can cost the foot and leg. These are high-risk aneurysms that are typically treated with surgery 04 - Anatomy of the Gluteal Region & Thigh.

  • A: Six weeks of PRICE is the conservative plan for a popliteal (Baker's) cyst, and only when there is no vascular compromise 07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 2.
  • B: An intra-articular steroid is an option for a Baker's cyst, not for a pulsatile mass.
  • D: NSAIDs and waiting 6 weeks is again the Baker's cyst plan and leaves a high-risk aneurysm untreated.

stem: You are the team physician covering the women’s basketball game. One of the athletes attempts a jump shot, but as she comes down an opponent lands on the outside of her knee, forcing the lower leg away from her body. She develops immediate onset medial knee pain with minimal swelling. What is the most likely injured ligament?
answer: The correct answer is B. MCL – the valgus force stretches the medial collateral ligament causing a strain. ACL can be affected in the unhappy triad (ACL, medial meniscus and MCL) however those typically produce significant swelling and higher intensity mechanism of injury. PCL is more often injured in hyperextension or dashboard injuries. LCL is more commonly injured in varus force injuries.

Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. The MCL is injured by a valgus force, swells little, and is treated with early range of motion and bracing 06.2 - Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 1.

  • A: Orthopedic referral for reconstruction is the plan for an ACL tear, which gives a pop and immediate swelling.
  • B: Surgical repair is taught for an LCL injury with other injuries or instability, not an isolated MCL injury.
  • C: Meniscal repair is for red or red-white zone and bucket-handle meniscal tears, and nothing here points to a meniscal tear.

weekLabel: Week 9 - Wrist & Hand, Hip & Knee
lecture: Clinical Approach to the Knee: Part Two
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (4 questions). Tests [[07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 2]].
stem: You are working in your local Emergency Department. The next patient is 23-year-old male soccer player with a LEFT KNEE injury. While pivoting to avoid a defender, he felt a ‘pop’ as his knee gave way. His coach helped him off the field and he did not return to play. He reported swelling but is unsure when it started, and he has been unable to weight bear on his left leg. He is otherwise healthy with no medications or allergies. Please select all potential diagnoses this patient could have:
answer: The correct answers are A, B, E, J, L, and M. Acute meniscal tear Acute meniscal tears typically occur during twisting injuries (i.e. a flexed knee is rotated with the corresponding foot planted). Chronic degenerative tears occur in older patients with minimal twisting or stress. Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury The ACL is the most commonly injured ligament of the knee. Approximately 70% of injuries occur with a noncontact mechanism (e.g. sudden deceleration, change in direction, or pivoting/landing with rotation and valgus collapse of the knee). Contact-related ACL injuries usually occur from a direct blow causing hyperextension or valgus deformation of the knee. Crystal arthropathy Crystal arthropathy is the accumulation of tiny crystals in one or more joints. The knee is most commonly involved in pseudogout (calcium pyrophosphate dihydrate crystal deposition). Gout (monosodium urate crystal deposition) can also occur in the knee. Attacks are characterized by severe pain, redness, swelling and disability. Inflammatory arthropathy Inflammatory arthropathy refers to an influx of inflammatory cells into the synovial membrane or fluid. This causes pain, swelling, reduced mobility and functional impairment in one or more joints. This is usually associated with another systemic condition (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, spondyloarthropathy, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, preceding extraarticular infection, etc.) Knee (tibiofemoral) dislocation with multi-ligament injury Knee dislocations are infrequent but potentially limb-threatening. They are caused by high energy trauma (e.g. motor vehicle collision) and are associated with multiple knee ligament injuries. This is a surgical emergency that requires immediate reduction followed by careful neurovascular assessment. These can be missed if the knee spontaneously reduces, as x-rays may appear normal. Lateral collateral ligament (LCL) sprain Isolated injuries of the LCL are among the least common of knee injuries. They occur when the joint is struck from the inside (varus stress). More commonly, LCL injuries occur in combination with posterolateral corner and multi-ligament injuries. Medial collateral ligament (MCL) sprain The MCL is commonly injured in contact and collision sports, or those that require twisting and torque of the lower extremity. They occur via direct valgus stress from a blow to the lateral aspect, or via indirect stress through abduction or rotation of the lower leg (e.g. shoe catches on playing surface). Femoral shaft fracture Fractures of the femoral shaft in young adults result from high energy forces (e.g. motor vehicle collision). They can cause extensive hemorrhage and shock may develop. There is a well-documented correlation between femur fractures and soft tissue injuries of the ipsilateral knee (partial of complete anterior or posterior cruciate ligament tears or meniscal injuries in 20-50% of cases). Osteoarthritis Osteoarthritis is common in the middle-aged or older person. It is typically characterized by joint pain, stiffness and reduced mobility. It starts with a predictable, sharp pain that eventually limits high-impact activities. As the disease progresses, pain becomes more constant with episodic stiffness or swelling that affects daily activities. Patellar dislocation Lateral patellar dislocations are most common, although medial or superior are described. They occur when the foot is planted, and a rotatory force is applied to the flexed knee in valgus (e.g. twirling in dance or swing a baseball bat). Direct trauma to the medial knee may also result in lateral patellar dislocation. Patellar tendon rupture Patellar tendon ruptures occur after sudden, strong contraction of the quadriceps muscles (e.g. landing from a high jump, changing direction at high speed). Conditions that weaken collagen put the tendon at risk, such as systemic illness (e.g. lupus, rheumatoid, diabetes), local degenerative change (e.g. tendinopathy or prior injury), or iatrogenic (e.g. corticosteroid injection, fluroquinolones, etc.). Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) tear Most PCL injuries occur in association with multi-ligament injuries after high energy trauma. The typical mechanism is a posteriorly directed force applied to a flexed knee (e.g. the classic ‘dashboard injury’). In athletes, PCL injuries can occur from a fall onto a flexed knee while the foot is plantarflexed or a direct blow to the anterior knee. Tibial plateau fracture Closed tibial fractures are common long-bone fractures. They can occur from significant direct trauma (e.g. motor vehicle collisions), knee hyperextension (e.g. collision during contact sport causing hyperextension) and twisting motions in the elderly or osteoporotic individuals. Tibial fracture is the most common injury associated with acute compartment syndrome of an extremity.

lecture: Clinical Approach to the Knee: Part Two
lectureMeta: Follow-up written for this bank on 2026-11-19; the source case does not ask it.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are working in your local Emergency Department. The next patient is 23-year-old male soccer player with a LEFT KNEE injury. While pivoting to avoid a defender, he felt a &lsquo;pop’ as his knee gave way. His coach helped him off the field and he did not return to play. He reported swelling but is unsure when it started, and he has been unable to weight bear on his left leg. He is otherwise healthy with no medications or allergies.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Plain X-rays of the left knee
MRI of the left knee first
Stress X-rays of the left knee

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. A pivot with a pop and giving way puts an ACL tear first, but his differential includes fractures (tibial plateau) and dislocations, and he cannot bear weight. The lecture's first imaging after an ACL-type injury is X-rays to rule out a fracture, with MRI kept for when the examination cannot decide 06.2 - Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 1.

  • B: MRI comes after X-rays, when the diagnosis cannot be made on examination.
  • C: Ultrasound confirms a popliteal (Baker's) cyst, which is not on his differential 07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Knee - PART 2.
  • D: Stress X-rays grade a PCL injury and are not the first film after an acute injury with possible fracture.

answer: The correct answer is D. The anterior talofibular ligament — injured during hyper-inversion of the ankle, which is the common mechanism. See ankle sprain.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: Which of these patients requires further assessment and an x-ray?

options.html: An 18-year-old female trips over a soccer ball while playing pick-up in a park. She is unable to weight bear on her left leg following the injury and is partially carried and driven to UH to see you. In the emergency department she still cannot weight bear to let you see her gait.
A 26-year-old male comes in limping from a construction site. He can slightly weight bear during his limping. On examination you note tenderness in the last 4 cm of lateral malleolus.
A 45-year-female comes in after tripping while getting out of the shower. On examination she has marked tenderness over the base of the 5th metatarsal.
All of the patients above need an ankle or foot X-ray series

answer:
The correct answer is D. Apply the Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules:

  • Ankle series if unable to weight bear immediately post-trauma AND in the emergency room → patient A
  • Ankle series if pain over the bottom 6 cm of the medial OR lateral malleolus → patient B (4 cm falls inside 6 cm)
  • Foot series if pain over the base of the 5th metatarsal or the navicular bone → patient C

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: A patient comes to you after rolling her ankle. You note that she is not able to weight bear and so you send her for an x-ray. Which of the following are incorrect management?

options.html: You should image the ankle properly with an AP, lateral and mortise view
You find that the patient has an ankle with an approximate displacement of her medial malleolus by 1 mm, with the mortise undisplaced. You decide to manage her with conservative treatment

You find that the patient has an ankle with bi-malleolar fracture, but the mortise is not displaced, and the medial malleolus displaced under 2 mm. This patient should be considered for surgical management.
Ankle fractures classified as B and C are regarded as 'unstable'
All of the above are true

answer:
The correct answer is E — all of the above are true.

  • A — AP, lateral and mortise are the normal ankle series.
  • B — the findings meet the criteria for non-operative treatment: (i) single malleolus involvement, (ii) mortise undisplaced, (iii) <2 mm of malleolar displacement.
  • C — correctly escalates, because it involves a bimalleolar fracture (failing criterion i).
  • D — Weber categories: A = fracture below the syndesmosis, B = fracture at the syndesmosis, C = fracture above the malleolus. With fractures below the syndesmosis and only 1 malleolus involved, the ankle is relatively stable and can likely be managed conservatively — so B and C are the unstable ones.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Ankle & foot injuries and the imaging rules
lectureMeta: Workbook Q39, Q46-Q48. Tests [[01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot]], [[02 - Lower Extremity Radiology]].
stem: A patient comes to you following a long run in the woods. They complain of having stepped into a pot hole and having their right foot forcefully pushed up toward their shin (dorsiflexed) and hearing a 'pop'. Following she had a great deal of pain. On examination you note a swollen painful ankle with a concentration of swelling on the back of the ankle and heel. On examination you find she has 5- strength in dorsiflexion, eversion and inversion, and a 1 in plantar flexion. What statement is correct?

options.html: The patient appears to have sustained a L4-5 injury, and is likely to display what is called a 'drop foot'.
The patient likely has a likely ankle sprain. The side whether talofibular ligaments or deltoid ligaments have not yet been determined by this examination.
Patient seems to be suffering from a common runner's injury called 'plantar fasciitis'
This patient would be expected to have a positive Thompson test, and may have a history of gout and seronegative arthropathies.

answer:
The correct answer is D. This is an Achilles tendon rupture — suspected from the isolated loss of plantar flexor strength (grade 1), the characteristic swelling at the back of the heel, and the history of forceful dorsiflexion. A positive Thompson test confirms it. There is also an association with chronic tendonitis seen in patients with gout and seronegative arthropathies, though that history is not required.

  • B is possible with this mechanism, but the specific loss of plantar flexor tone, the location of swelling, and no pain over the medial or lateral ankle argue against a simple ankle sprain.
  • C — plantar fasciitis was possibly present in a runner, but would not produce this swelling or loss of plantar flexor strength.

See Achilles tendinopathy.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Neuropathic pain is:

options.html: Pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease
Pain caused from stretching of visceral tissues resulting in poorly localized cramping pain
Pain resulting from local tissue damage that is well localized but with variable descriptions

answer:
The correct answer is A. Neuropathic pain is pain caused by abnormal neural activity occurring in the absence of disease.

The distractors are the two nociceptive subtypes:

  • B → visceral nociceptive pain (stretching of visceral tissue; poorly localized, cramping)
  • C → somatic nociceptive pain (local tissue damage; well localized, variable descriptors)

See 05 - Neuropathic Pain and Q65 for the symptom list.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Wallerian degeneration is the process of _____ nerve tract degeneration _____ to the site of injury.
answer: The correct answer is D. Wallerian degeneration is the breakdown of nerve tissue that occurs when a nerve is transected through traumatic injury. Degeneration starts at the site of injury and progresses distally (anterograde), obliterating the nerve segment distal to the injury. See Q66 for where this fits among neuropraxia/axonotmesis/neurotmesis.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Nerves repair at a rate of:
answer: The correct answer is A. 1 mm/day ≈ 1 inch/month. Both halves of that equivalence are worth carrying, since exam options are written in either unit.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Localize the following physical exam findings: The patient is stepping with their affected foot in a plantar flexed position during swing phase of normal gait and makes contact with their forefoot. The patient has MRC grade 3 strength in dorsiflexion and 4+ in plantar flexion.

options.html: Lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh

answer: The correct answer is B. The patient has a foot drop on gait analysis with profound weakness of the dorsiflexors (grade 3) and relatively preserved plantar flexion (4+). This lesion localizes to the common fibular/peroneal nerve — or the deep fibular/peroneal nerve for the anterior compartment specifically. See common peroneal neuropathy.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q11, Q16-Q17, Q24, Q66. Tests [[03 - Nerve Injury]].
stem: Which of the following correctly describes neuropraxia?

options.html: Damage to a neuron's outer sheath progressing to Wallerian degeneration, often resulting from severe crush injuries
Complete severance of both the nerve and its sheath
Temporary loss of sensory and motor function from transient neural ischemia & edema. Patients usually make a full recovery

answer:
The correct answer is C. The three-tier classification, with all three options accounted for:

GradeDefinitionOption
NeuropraxiaTemporary loss of sensory and motor function from transient neural ischemia & edema; usually full recoveryC
AxonotmesisDamage to the outer sheath, progressing to Wallerian degeneration; severe crush injuriesA
NeurotmesisComplete severance of both nerve and sheathB

See Q16 for Wallerian degeneration and Q17 for the recovery rate.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A comminuted fracture is a:

options.html: Fracture involving the flare of a long bone
Fracture involving more than two fragments

answer:
The correct answer is D. Comminuted = more than two fragments. The distractors are the other descriptors:

  • A → diaphyseal fracture
  • B → metaphyseal fracture ("the flare")
  • C → intra-articular fracture

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: Complete the following statement: A _____ fracture does not involve external environmental contamination and has _____ outcomes whereas a _____ fracture involves contamination of soft tissues and has _____ outcomes.
answer:
The correct answer is B. Closed → better; open → poorer.

From Fracture Management and Fracture Radiology. An open (compound) fracture exposes the bone or fracture hematoma to the external environment through a break in the skin, so it is contaminated by definition. The lecture lists its cost: ↑ infection, non-union, delayed union and incomplete recovery, worst after high-energy trauma. That is why management aims to convert an unstable, contaminated wound into a stable, clean one - early antibiotics and tetanus, debridement and irrigation, early closure. A closed fracture keeps the soft-tissue envelope intact and does better.

  • A gets the outcomes backwards.
  • C, D swap the definitions: it is the open fracture that is contaminated.

Any wound near a fracture, even a distant one, counts as open until proven otherwise.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A greenstick fracture is a:

options.html: Fracture involving the epiphysis and intra-articular surface
Pediatric fracture involving the growth plates and results in poorer bone development
Pediatric fracture that occurs because young bone is softer and less brittle

answer: The correct answer is D. A greenstick fracture is a pediatric fracture occurring because young bone is softer and less brittle — it bends and cracks on one side rather than snapping through. See Q82, where the radiographic appearance is the question.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A unique complication of fractures involving growth plates is:
answer: The correct answer is C. Growth arrest. Note the word unique in the stem: infection and non-union (A, B) are common complications of any fracture, so neither is unique to physeal injury. Excess ossification (D) is not a fracture complication. See Salter-Harris fractures.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: Which of the following is a typical reason why casting may fail to maintain reduction?

options.html: padding doesn't affect success of reduction

answer: The correct answer is A. Excess padding interferes with proper reduction — the limb can move inside the cast, so the cast no longer holds the alignment.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: You are counselling Mr. M about potential complications following surgical treatment of his fractured tibia. Which of the following are potential complications that you should discuss with him?

options.html: Non-union: failure of a fracture to heal after adequate realignment often due to poor blood supply
Avascular necrosis: degeneration of a piece of bone due to inadequate blood supply
Arthritis: can result from malunion or joint space narrowing resulting in degeneration of articular surfaces.

answer: The correct answer is E. Non-union, avascular necrosis and arthritis are all possible complications after fracture of a bone — and each definition as given in the options is correct.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q22, Q32, Q50, Q67. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: What are the six stages of fracture healing in their appropriate order?

options.html: Inflammatory stage, hard callus stage, remodelling stage, hematoma stage, granulation stage, soft callus stage
Hematoma stage, inflammatory stage, granulation stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, remodelling stage
Inflammatory stage, hematoma stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, granulation stage, remodelling stage
Hematoma stage, inflammatory stage, granulation stage, remodelling stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage
Remodeling stage, soft callus stage, hard callus stage, inflammatory stage, hematoma stage, granulation stage

answer: The correct answer is B. Hematoma → inflammatory → granulation → soft callus → hard callus → remodelling.

flags.title: No explanation in the workbook
flags.html: The key gives the letter only. The two ordering rules that eliminate every distractor: hematoma comes first (bleeding precedes the inflammatory response) and remodelling comes last.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the emergency department after falling off his skateboard onto his outstretched right hand. He reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move his hand. On physical exam, there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomical snuffbox and decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. FOOSH injuries are a common cause of wrist fractures, with the scaphoid the most commonly fractured bone in the wrist. The anatomical snuffbox is on the radial side of the wrist and contains the scaphoid; snuffbox tenderness is the classic finding, and patients may also have decreased sensation over the radial aspect of the hand from injury to the superficial radial nerve.

The distractors, each with its own signature:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius with dorsal displacement, typically older patients with osteoporosis (see Q84)
  • Radial head fracture — at the elbow; adults who FOOSH with an extended elbow
  • Distal radius fracture — common, but does not involve the anatomical snuffbox

See scaphoid fracture.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on her outstretched hand. She reports immediate pain and swelling in the wrist and is unable to move her hand. X-rays are negative for fracture, but there is tenderness to palpation over the anatomic snuffbox and the patient is unable to grip objects. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.html: Place the wrist in a cast for 6 weeks
Perform a CT scan of the wrist
Order an MRI of the wrist

answer:
The correct answer is D. A negative x-ray does not rule out a scaphoid fracture — scaphoid fractures may not be visible on initial films. With high clinical suspicion, order an MRI, which is the imaging modality of choice for diagnosing them.

Why the rest fail: A — casting for 6 weeks without proper diagnosis may lead to further complications. B — a repeat x-ray in 1 week may still not show the fracture. C — CT shows better detail than plain film, but MRI is the modality of choice.

Why this matters: a scaphoid fracture is a serious injury and can lead to avascular necrosis of the bone if left untreated — the same blood-supply logic as Q13.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 7-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off his bike and injuring his forearm. X-rays reveal an incomplete fracture of the radius with evidence of cortical thickening on the convex side of the bone, and no significant displacement or angulation. Which of the following types of fractures is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Incomplete fracture with cortical thickening on the convex side is characteristic of a greenstick fracture. These are common in children because of the pliability of their bones, and typically occur in long bones when a bending force is applied.

The distractors:

  • Colles fracture — distal radius fracture in older adults who FOOSH
  • Monteggia fracture — fracture of the proximal ulna with dislocation of the radial head
  • Buckle fracture — an incomplete fracture with bulging of the cortex on one side due to compression
  • Torus fracture — another term for a buckle fracture, which is why C and D cannot both be the single best answer

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 28-year-old male presents to the emergency department with a history of falling onto his outstretched arm during a football game. He complains of severe pain in his left shoulder and inability to move it. On examination, his left arm is held in adduction and internal rotation. X-ray reveals a dislocated humeral head posterior to the glenoid. What is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Trauma is the most common cause of posterior shoulder dislocations, accounting for approximately 75-90% of cases.

Seizures and electric shock can also cause posterior dislocations — they are the classically taught associations — but they are much less common, which is the trap this question sets. A rotator cuff tear is not a cause of posterior dislocation.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lectureMeta: Workbook Q78-Q79, Q82-Q84. Tests [[04 - Fracture Radiology]], [[05 - Fracture Management]].
stem: A 55-year-old female presents to the emergency department after falling on her outstretched hand. She complains of wrist pain and deformity. On examination, her wrist is swollen and tender, and there is an obvious dorsal angulation of the distal radius. X-ray reveals a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement. What is the name of this fracture?
answer:
The answer is D — Colles fracture.

From Colles fracture and Smith's fracture. Two discriminators settle every distal-forearm eponym: the mechanism and the direction of the distal fragment. A Colles fracture is the FOOSH (fall onto outstretched hand) injury with dorsal angulation of the distal radius - exactly this stem, in the older patient the workbook's own Q78 describes.

  • A fails: Smith's fracture is the reverse - volar displacement, from a fall on a flexed wrist or a blow to the dorsum.
  • B fails: Monteggia is a proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation - the elbow, not the wrist (Q82).
  • C fails: Barton is an intra-articular rim fracture of the distal radius with carpal subluxation; nothing here says intra-articular.

flags.title: No answer in the workbook
flags.html:
The key stops at Q83; there is no entry for Q84. The answer above is reasoned, but it is well supported by the workbook's own text elsewhere: Q78's explanation defines a Colles fracture as "a fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement of the wrist... typically seen in older patients with osteoporosis" — exactly this stem.

The distractors: Smith fracture is the reverse (distal radius with volar/palmar displacement); Monteggia is proximal ulna + radial head dislocation (per Q82); Barton is an intra-articular distal radius fracture with carpal subluxation.

lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Exaggerated lateral curvature of the spine is:
answer:
The correct answer is C. Scoliosis is the lateral curvature.

  • Lordosis — increased anterior curvature; either excessive lumbar curvature or reduced cervical curvature
  • Kyphosis — increased posterior curvature, normally used of exaggerated thoracic curvature
  • "Lateral curveosis" is not a real term.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: What are the Red Flags of abnormal gait in a child? (Select all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are B, C, D, E. A and F are wrong because they are the reassuring versions of two red flags — it is asymmetry and a suspected related condition that are the red flags, not symmetry and the absence of one.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following are involved in the 'Ponsetti treatment'?

options.html: Weekly manipulations with casting to correct varus foot deformities
Achilles tendon lengthening to correct equinus ankle positioning
This is treatment for cases of talipes equinovarus

answer: The correct answer is E. Options A-C describe the steps of the Ponseti treatment, and D correctly names the condition — talipes equinovarus (clubfoot).

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following about the natural history and etiology of club foot is correct?

options.html: The natural history includes progressive worsening of deformity and stiffness with gradual loss of ambulation
The etiology like calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus is related to intrauterine positioning rather than genetics
This condition appears to be more prevalent among females
All of the above are correct

answer:
The correct answer is A. That is the correct description of the natural history of congenital talipes equinovarus.

B is the substantive error: there are many etiological theories for clubfoot — arrested embryologic development, neurologic causes, muscular fibrosis — and there is some relationship with polygenic multifactorial inheritance, so it cannot be attributed to intrauterine positioning alone the way calcaneovarus and metatarsus adductus can.

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: In the analysis and description of curvature in a scoliosis patient requires the following except:

options.html: Ruling out any anatomical abnormalities (i.e. from trauma or tumours)
All of the above are required

answer:
The correct answer is F — all of the above are required. What each term means when describing a scoliosis curve:

  • Location — whether the vertex of the curve is cervical, thoracic or lumbar
  • Spinal level — the actual levels the curvature spans
  • Direction — whether the concavity points right or left
  • Magnitude — the number of degrees
  • Abnormalities — is there a fracture cause or tumour driving the curvature that could be addressed

weekLabel: Week 10 - Ankle & Foot, Nerve Injury, Fractures, Chronic Pain & Pediatric Orthopedics
lecture: Pediatric orthopedics: hip, limp, clubfoot & scoliosis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q3, Q10, Q51-Q55, Q80-Q81. Tests [[08 - Pediatric Orthopedics]], [[09 - Child with a Limp]].
stem: Which of the following are not a risk factor for further progression of scoliosis.

options.html: Onset at an older physiologic age
Thoracic are at greater risk than lumbar
Larger curves are at greater risk than smaller curves

answer: The correct answer is A. Patients who are physiologically older have less skeletal bone growth remaining, and therefore less potential for progression of scoliosis through asymmetric bone growth. Progression risk tracks remaining growth — so younger onset is the risk, not older.

stem: A 16-year-old patient comes to you with complaints of a rib hump that was noticed during a physiotherapy session for a shoulder injury she had. You complete a neurological examination which is normal as well as characterize her spinal curvature. You note a Right Thoracic curve from level T7-T12 with a 34-degree curve. The most appropriate treatment would be:

options.html: Follow the person with annual radiologic examination to assess progression

answer: The correct answer is C. Bracing. Patients with 30-40 degrees of curve are recommended to have bracing treatment, with the main goal of preventing further progression (not of correcting the existing curve). Her 34° falls squarely in that band. See scoliosis.

stem: A 13-year-old boy presents to the emergency department with hip pain and an abnormal gait. Imaging reveals a femoral head displacement, which was not initially evident on plain radiographs. The patient has a BMI of 35, and is undergoing hormonal therapy for a pre-existing medical condition. Which of the following management options is most appropriate for this patient?

options.html: Observation and follow-up imaging in 4 weeks
Non-weight bearing with crutches and physical therapy
Surgical reduction and internal fixation of the hip
Encourage weight loss and activity modification

answer:
The correct answer is C. This is SCFE, and the stem's two risk factors — high BMI and hormonal therapy — are what flag it.

Surgical reduction and internal fixation is typically required for moderate to severe cases, to prevent further displacement and degenerative arthritis. B may be appropriate for some cases, and A for mild ones — but the pain and abnormal gait here suggest a moderate to severe case. D is beneficial for overall health and future prevention but is not sufficient treatment for an acute SCFE.

stem: A 4-year-old girl presents to the clinic with a history of frequent falls and difficulty with balance. She also complains of leg pain at night that is relieved by rubbing. On physical exam, she has a waddling gait and is unable to stand on one leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease (LCPD) is a non-traumatic condition of the hip joint in children, occurring when blood flow to the femoral head is interrupted, leading to bone death and subsequent deformation.

Symptoms: hip or groin pain, limping, difficulty with mobility. Nighttime pain relieved by rubbing is a classic feature. Children may have a waddling gait and be unable to stand on one leg.

DDH, JIA, osteogenesis imperfecta and SCFE can present similarly — the history and exam here are what favour LCPD. Note the age contrast with Q80: LCPD in a 4-year-old, SCFE in a 13-year-old.

stem: Why is it important to have multiple Xray views when assessing a fracture? (select all that apply)

options.html: To pick up microfractures that may only be seen in one view
To differentiate between a transverse and linear fracture
To assess whether an oblique fracture is actually a spiral fracture
To check whether tendons are involved in an avulsion fracture

answer: The correct answer is A, C, E. some microfractures may only be seen in one view. A transverse and linear fracture are very different, and can be differentiated from a single view. A spiral fracture may look like an oblique fracture in one view, so it is important to obtain another view to differentiate the two. Tendons cannot be seen well on Xrays. Rotational fractures usually need two views to look at joints proximally and distally to interpret the degree and type of rotation.

stem: Which of the following is true for fracture healing?

options.html: Primary healing is healing that comes spontaneously and seen more commonly
Bony callus forms at fracture site, then revascularization occurs
Distal humerus takes longer to heal than proximal humerus
Malunion refers to no healing in 6-9 months
Healing takes longer if the fracture is extraarticular since there is no synovial fluid involved

answer: The correct answer is C. A is wrong because this describes secondary healing, primary healing is the contact healing after closed reduction or ORIF. B is wrong because revascularization occurs first, then formation of bony callus occurs after. C is correct. D describes nonunion. E is wrong because intraarticular fractures take a longer time to heal.

stem: Patient presents with an open tibial fracture with a skin defect measuring 5cm. Which of the following are true? (select all that apply)

options.html: There is an increased chance of nonunion and infection
Obtain tetanus status and administer tetanus prophylaxis
Take a swab and wait for culture results before administering antibiotics
Contact plastic surgery to perform flap surgery

answer: The correct answer is A, B. there is an increased chance of complications (infection, nonunion, time to union) for open fractures. It is important to get tetanus status and prophylaxis for all open fractures. Do not wait for culture to administer antibiotics. Since this is a grade 2 open fracture, there is no need for flap surgery.

stem: You are in the emergency room assessing Rachel Green, a 31 year old female. Rachel was driving her friend’s Porsche at high speed on the 401 when the car in front of her braked suddenly. Rachel collided into the car in front of her. On your exam, you notice Rachel has some mild knee pain, minimal swelling of her right knee and decreased range of motion. Given the mechanism of injury, what knee ligament did Rachel most likely injure?
answer: The correct answer is D. This is a classic dashboard injury causing the tibia to move posteriorly relative to the femur when the knee is flexed. Patients typically present with poorly defined pain and minimal swelling.

stem: Tobiloba is a 19 year old woman coming to see you in the family medicine clinic with gradually worsening bilateral anterior knee pain. She describes the pain as deep and aching. She first noticed the pain when she increased her hurdles training volume, and initially the pain was brought on by exercise. However, the pain is now brought on when she climbs stairs and stands up after prolonged periods of sitting. Based on the most likely diagnosis, what would you offer Tobiloba? Choose all that are correct.
answer: The correct answer is A, C, D, E. Given the presentation and the demographics of this case, Tobiloba most likely has patellofemoral pain syndrome (PFPS). Because PFPS is related to increased Q angle, physiotherapy may focus on quadriceps strengthening (especially vastus medialis) to prevent lateral translation of the patella during knee flexion. Knee surgery is not indicated. Activity modifications are indicated, and bracing and taping may also help prevent lateral patellar translation.

stem: You are a family medicine resident seeing Kavi, 58 years old, who complains to you about pain in their legs. They have aching pain in both legs that sometimes feels itchy. Kavi works in customer service and finds the pain to be worse after a long shift standing. On physical exam, you see dilated, tortuous veins on both legs. Which of the following is not recommended for Kavi?
answer: The correct answer is A, B, D, E. Kavi has varicose veins. Exercise, compression stockings, and daily elevation of the legs can help return the blood towards the heart. Laser therapy damages the varicose veins, causing formation of scar tissue and eventual disappearance of the vein. Daily hot water soaks are NOT recommended as they can further vasodilation and venous stasis.

stem: How does physical activity affect the cardiovascular system? Check all that are correct.
answer:
The correct answer is A, D.

From 10 - Physical Activity Prescription. The lecture lists the cardiovascular benefits of regular activity: ↑ oxygen uptake, ↑ oxygen utilization, ↑ endothelial function, ↑ plasma volume and ↓ blood viscosity, with ↑ stroke volume, ↓ resting heart rate and ↓ blood pressure on the heart side.

  • A, D are on that list verbatim.
  • B fails on the word during: the ↓ BP is a chronic training effect. Acutely, blood pressure rises with exertion, which is why the notes require BP under 180/100 before starting and warn that strenuous resistance work can push LV pressure over 300 mmHg.
  • C is the reverse of the lecture: viscosity falls.

stem: Akbar is a 56 year old patient interested in adding physical activity to his lifestyle. He comes to you for advice because he is fairly sedentary and has a history of hypertension, with average readings of 185/100. Which of the following would you NOT recommend?

options.html: At least one rest day per week

answer: The correct answer is A. ACE inhibitor or calcium channel blocker will help control Akbar’s hypertension to make exercise safe. Including a warmup of 15minutes and a cool-down of 10minutes is an important consideration for patients with hypertension. One rest day per week will help Akbar avoid injury. Isometric exercises, overhead exercises and supine exercises are not recommended for patients with hypertension.

stem: Match the common presentation to the pediatric condition.
answer:
The pairings:

PresentationPediatric condition
A child (between 3-10 y.o) who was sick with a URTI about a week ago now has sudden unilateral hip pain and their hip is held in slight FABER positionTransient synovitis
An adolescent athlete (8-14 y.o female, 10-15 y.o male) has a painful bump over their tibial tuberosity and xray shows a teardrop sign.Osgood-Schlatter
An obese adolescent (~ 12 y.o female, 14 y.o male) has gradual left hip pain that refers to the knee, antalgic gait, and can’t weight bearSlipped capital femoral epiphysis
A child (between 4-8 y.o) who has a low body weight and protein S/C deficiency has gradual vague hip pain and stiffness and limb-length discrepancyLegg-Calve-Perthes

From 09 - Child with a Limp and 08 - Pediatric Orthopedics. Age plus one hallmark sorts each:

  • Transient synovitis: ages 3-10, a viral URTI 7-10 days earlier, sudden unilateral hip pain, the hip held flexed, abducted and externally rotated, afebrile.
  • Osgood-Schlatter: traction apophysitis at the tibial tuberosity in active 8-14 (F) / 10-15 (M) year olds; x-ray shows the "teardrop" sign.
  • SCFE: adolescent, gradual hip pain referred to the knee, left more often than right, painful weight-bearing.
  • Legg-Calve-Perthes: ages 4-8, low birth weight, gradual vague hip pain, stiffness and limb-length discrepancy from femoral-head osteonecrosis.

The stem's protein S/C deficiency is not in the note; its risk factors are family history, low birth weight and second-hand smoke.

stem: A 50-year-old woman has heel pain that is worst with her first steps in the morning and after sitting. She is tender at the medial calcaneal tuberosity and passive dorsiflexion of the toes reproduces the pain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C.
