stem: A 23-year-old basketball player lands on another player's foot, rolling the ankle into inversion with the foot plantarflexed. Which ligament is most likely injured?
answer: The correct answer is D. Most ankle sprains are lateral: inversion with plantarflexion (the least stable position) injures the ATFL most often, then the CFL, then the PTFL. The anterior drawer test assesses the ATFL. Medial sprains involve the deltoid ligament.

stem: A 25-year-old man wakes with a wrist drop after falling asleep with his arm hooked over a chair. The nerve was compressed but not cut. Which type of injury is this and what is the expected course?
answer: The correct answer is A. Compression that damages myelin with the axon intact is neurapraxia: slowed conduction, temporary, typically resolving in 6-12 weeks (radial nerve "Saturday night" palsy). Axonotmesis (crush/stretch) loses the axon, which regrows about 1 inch per month. Neurotmesis (cut) disrupts the epineurium and cannot recover without surgery.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Consider case of "numb thumb". Pt c/o frequent tingles. Exam shows diminished sensation over thumb.

stem: Two items in the DDx should include: (stem copied from the lecture, which answers it straight after; options written for this bank)

options.html: Carpal tunnel syndrome and C8 radiculopathy
Carpal tunnel syndrome and C6 radiculopathy

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture lists them: 1. Carpal tunnel syndrome (peripheral nerve: the median nerve) and 2. C6 radiculopathy (nerve root). The lecture shows why both fit: the median nerve sensory territory and the C6 dermatome overlap over the thumb. "Your job is to figure out which Dx fits best": a mononeuropathy gives a sharp-bordered patch and weakness only in that nerve's muscles (motor to abductor pollicis brevis for the median nerve), a radiculopathy gives a fuzzy-bordered dermatome, neck pain radiating down the arm and myotome weakness (motor to biceps for C6). On the sensory maps in the lecture note, C8 (A) and the ulnar nerve (B) cover the little-finger side, not the thumb, and C7 the middle finger; the radial nerve (D) covers the back of the hand.

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. The median nerve territory and the C6 dermatome overlap at the thumb, so the question is root versus named nerve. The notes name electromyography and nerve conduction studies as the test that separates carpal tunnel syndrome from C6 radiculopathy and grades how severe the nerve damage is 01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand - PART 2. Electrodiagnostic studies answer where along the peripheral nervous system the problem is 03 - Nerve Injury.

  • A: MRI images only the neck, so it cannot test the carpal tunnel half of the differential, and the notes keep it for neurological signs or pain past 4 weeks of conservative care 03.2 - Clinical Approach to Non-Mechanical Back & Neck Pain.
  • B: X-ray is not indicated for degenerative neck or arm pain; degenerative changes start in early middle age and are usually unrelated to symptoms.
  • D: CT of the spine is used only if MRI is contraindicated, and it also cannot look at the median nerve.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Onset with horseback riding trauma yesterday: ran into fence with R knee, thrown over and landed on low back; pain. Inability to dorsiflex, extend toes, evert. Plantarflexion, knee flexion weak & painful. Loss of sensation dorsum of foot. On examination: reduced pinprick sensation over the dorsum of the foot, clear borders; hip flexion, knee extension, hip adduction and abduction, plantarflexion and tibialis posterior 4+/5; dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and eversion 0/5; patellar and plantar reflexes intact. Sent for EMG studies. Needle EMG is abnormal in peroneus longus, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis only; gluteus medius, the tibial-innervated muscles and the paraspinals are normal.

stem: Where does weakness come from? (the case assembled from the lecture and its EMG table, leaving out the part that names the diagnosis)

options.html: Sciatic nerve in the posterior thigh
Tibial nerve in the popliteal fossa

answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture names it: common peroneal neuropathy at the fibular head. Only the peroneal muscles (superficial: peroneus longus; deep: tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum brevis) are abnormal, the sensory loss has clear borders, and the reflexes are intact, which is a mononeuropathy: weakness of the muscles that nerve takes care of but not of other muscles from the same root that another nerve manages. An L5 radiculopathy (A) also catches gluteus medius, tibialis posterior and the paraspinals (the lecture's alternate ending). A sciatic lesion (C) would add the hamstrings, including biceps femoris short head, which is normal here. A tibial lesion (D) weakens plantarflexion and spares dorsiflexion.

answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture: "This is an AXONAL INJURY. Can't say yet if axonotmetic or neurotmetic (would need to wait and see if it recovers spontaneously)." Dx: common peroneal axonopathy at the fibular head. Spontaneous activity at rest is denervation, which a myelin-only injury (A) does not produce (denervated muscle does not behave normally at rest). Neurotmesis (B) and axonotmesis (C) both cut the axon; what separates them is whether the epineurium is intact, and the studies cannot see that yet, only time can.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Onset with horseback riding trauma yesterday: ran into fence with R knee, thrown over and landed on low back; pain. Inability to dorsiflex, extend toes, evert. Plantarflexion, knee flexion weak & painful. Loss of sensation dorsum of foot. On examination: reduced pinprick sensation over the dorsum of the foot, clear borders; hip flexion, knee extension, hip adduction and abduction, plantarflexion and tibialis posterior 4+/5; dorsiflexion, extensor hallucis longus and eversion 0/5; patellar and plantar reflexes intact. Sent for EMG studies. This time needle EMG is abnormal in gluteus medius, peroneus longus, tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum brevis, semimembranosus, tibialis posterior and the lumbar paraspinals.

stem: Where does weakness come from? (the lecture's "Case: Alternate Ending"; stem copied from the lecture, leaving out the box that names the diagnosis)

options.html: Sciatic nerve in the posterior thigh
Superior gluteal nerve at the hip

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture names it: L5 radiculopathy. The abnormal muscles cross several named nerves (superior gluteal, common peroneal, tibial, and the sciatic branch to semimembranosus) but share one root, and the paraspinals, supplied by the posterior primary rami, are abnormal too: a myotome, not a nerve. A common peroneal lesion (B) would leave gluteus medius, tibialis posterior and the paraspinals normal. A sciatic lesion (C) cannot explain gluteus medius or the paraspinals. A superior gluteal lesion (D) would not weaken the leg muscles.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 14 y.o. male. Acute onset right hip pain while participating in 100m dash at school track meet. Antalgic limp, anterior hip pain. Hip radiographs are taken.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The reveal follows the case: "Avulsion Fractures - can occur at any apophysis; bones growing fast, muscle/tendon under tension - quick burst of activity/contraction pulls it off! Common: pelvis, 5th MT, medial epicondyle; treatment is often non-surgical." A sudden burst (a sprint) giving acute anterior hip pain in a growing teenager is that mechanism, at the pelvis. Overuse apophysitis (A) is the gradual-onset traction injury the notes turn to next (Osgood-Schlatter, Sinding-Larsen, Sever's), not an acute event. Osteochondritis dissecans (C) is a repetitive-movement loss of blood flow under the articular cartilage, not a sudden injury at a tendon attachment. Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (D) is listed among the hip causes of a limp, and is not what this case is teaching.

Closed reduction under sedation and a cast
Stop weight-bearing and pin it in situ urgently

preamble.html: Case - 15 mos with LLD. Pelvic radiographs are shown.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (stem is slide 55; the deck poses no question, and the diagnosis comes from the section the case sits in, slides 49-56)

options.html: Growth arrest after a Salter-Harris V injury

answer: The correct answer is C. The case sits inside the developmental dysplasia of the hip section, between the Ortolani test and "DDH Management". A leg length discrepancy is one of the exam findings the lecture lists for it (Galeazzi test), and at 15 months the Barlow and Ortolani tests are no longer reliable ("unreliable > 3-6 months old"), so the hip was not caught by them. At this age the management is no longer the Pavlik harness (up to 6 months) but closed reduction and spica cast, or open reduction ± osteotomies. Physiologic genu varum (A) is normal from birth to 2 years and is symmetric; asymmetry is one of its warning signs. Growth arrest after a Salter-Harris V injury (B) can cause a leg length discrepancy, but there is no injury here. Plastic deformation (D) is a bowing fracture after trauma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1. 33 year old ♂ with back/flank mass. History: noticed 6 years ago; "big"; not quite doubled in size; uncomfortable; multiple other lumps; has an uncle with lumps. Physical exam: obvious mass; skin over intact, normal; "big"; in subcutaneous tissues; easily mobile; other lesions, obvious lipomas.

stem: What Do You Do Next?

options.html: Excisional biopsy with minimal surrounding tissue
Imaging (MRI preferred) or a surgical expert
Reassure as a lipoma, no further workup

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture answers with its guideline: a mass > 5 cm goes to imaging (MRI preferred, CT, rarely ultrasound) or a surgical expert, then biopsy, whatever its other features. "Big" here is 17 × 16 × 5 cm on the ultrasound that follows: "probable lipoma, cannot rule out sarcoma, recommend MRI... or referral to surgeon familiar with soft-tissue tumors." Excision (A) is only for a mass < 5 cm with no suspicious features, and an excisional biopsy is "not ideal if sarcoma". Fine needle aspiration (B) is not widely used for primary diagnosis: poor cell yield, hard to tell tumour types apart. Reassuring (D) is the "whoops" the lecture warns about: a lump assumed benign that turns out to be a sarcoma.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Case 1, continued. The mass is excised. On pathology there are fat cells with spindle and multinucleated cells. Immunohistochemistry is MDM2 negative and CD34 positive.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (follow-up assembled from the case notes, which pose no question here)
answer: The correct answer is B. The notes give the differential for fat with spindle and multinucleated cells: benign spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma (observe) versus malignant well-differentiated liposarcoma (atypical lipomatous tumour), and resolves it with immunohistochemistry: "MDM2 negative and CD34 positive -> lipoma" (the result is labelled spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma). Well-differentiated liposarcoma (A) is the alternative that MDM2 negativity rules out. Dedifferentiated liposarcoma (C) is case 4's diagnosis, shown with MDM2 staining. Myxoid liposarcoma (D) shows lipoblasts, uniform oval cells, branching capillaries and a myxoid stroma.

Radiation therapy to the tumour bed
Staging CT chest, then tumour board

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. MDM2 negative and CD34 positive settles the pathology as a lipoma, and the notes list spindle cell/pleomorphic lipoma as benign, to be observed 11 - MSK Oncology. A benign tumour has limited growth and does not metastasise, so it needs no further treatment once excised.

preamble.html: Case 2. 18 year old ♂ brought in by his mother with right hip mass. History: noticed 18 mos ago? no change?; no trauma; asymptomatic; no other lumps; no family history. stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Marginal excision, sparing the normal tissue around it
Wide local excision, plus or minus radiation
Fine needle aspiration, then observation only

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. The tumour board's plan for this case in the notes is wide local excision with or without post-operative radiation, a chest x-ray, then follow-up at 6 months and a yearly chest x-ray 11 - MSK Oncology. Wide resection with a cuff of normal tissue is the preferred sarcoma operation, and radiation added to surgery cuts local recurrence from 30% to 10%.

  • A: A marginal resection is the "whoops" operation that the notes warn against.
  • B: Adjuvant chemotherapy is not a standard of care for soft tissue sarcoma; it gives no significant survival benefit.
  • D: Fine needle aspiration is not used for primary diagnosis, and a tethered mass that has been biopsied and taken to tumour board is not simply observed.

History: noticed past year; now a football, more than doubled in size; dull ache last 2-3 months, takes voltaren, continues to work; neurofibromatosis. stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? (the lecture asks "What Next?" and answers it with its guideline; this asks for the diagnosis it gives instead, leaving it out of the stem)
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "Sarcoma arising in the setting of neurofibromatosis, consistent with malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour." Neurofibromatosis is a genetic predisposition to sarcoma (neurofibromin mutation), and the mass has every suspicious feature on the lecture's guideline: > 5 cm, more than doubled in a year, painful, deep (in muscle) and tethered. Neurofibroma (C) is the benign peripheral nerve tumour in the nomenclature table, and benign tumours have limited growth. A well-differentiated liposarcoma (B) is a fatty tumour (case 1's malignant alternative), not one arising from nerve in neurofibromatosis. Rhabdomyosarcoma (D) is the malignant skeletal muscle tumour, one of the pediatric sarcomas.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Let's Review a Case! Open fracture. Distal 1/3 tibial diaphysis. Spiral. Mild displacement: shortened, posterior translation, apex lateral angulation.

stem: What to do??

options.html: IV cefazolin, tetanus prophylaxis, early debridement, irrigation and an intramedullary nail
Closed reduction and a cast, then antibiotics and tetanus only if a wound infection develops
Splint and elevate, then delayed surgery and wound closure once the swelling has settled
Irrigate the wound in the emergency room, close it, and treat the fracture as a closed one

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture works the case: early antibiotics (2 g IV cefazolin); tetanus prophylaxis, given in the emergency room; early surgery, removing all devitalized tissue including bone fragments, gently irrigating with sterile saline, and stabilizing with an intramedullary nail; and early closure of the soft tissue envelope where possible (minimal contamination plus minimal debridement = direct closure during the open reduction and internal fixation). The goal is to convert an unstable contaminated wound into a stable clean environment. B waits for infection instead of giving early antibiotics, and a cast is not the definitive stabilization here. C delays the surgery and the closure that the lecture wants early. D treats an open fracture as closed, when any fracture with a wound is open until proven otherwise and needs operative debridement.

lectureMeta: Source: Fracture Management and Complications Part 1.pdf slides 12-14 and Part 3.pdf slide 9 (2 cases). Tests 05 - Fracture Management. Part 3 slide 9.
stem: Sooo...tibial fracture with increasing narcotic requirements, terrible pain, pain increases with dorsiflexion or plantar flexion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. This is the lecture's compartment syndrome picture: a clinical diagnosis of pain out of proportion to the injury and pain with passive stretch of the muscle involved in the compartment, then paresthesia (midterm), paralysis (very late) and pulselessness (not typical). The lower leg is the most common site, and a tibial fracture bleeds and swells inside fixed fascial borders. It is an urgent call to orthopedics: remove casts and dressings, elevate, cool, monitor, and definitive fasciotomy. Deep vein thrombosis (A) is a thromboembolic complication from Virchow's triad, not pain on moving the foot. Heterotopic ossification (B) is ectopic bone around a joint, presenting as stiffness. Avascular necrosis (C) occurs in bones with a retrograde blood supply: femoral head, talus, scaphoid, not the tibia.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Lateral sprains make up to 85% of ankle sprains; the mechanism is a plantarflexed, inverted foot such as landing from a jump, and the anterior talofibular ligament is injured first 01.2 - Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot.   • D: A base of 5th metatarsal injury would give bone tenderness there, and she has no other focal tenderness.

stem: Jerry has had chronic long-standing back pain longer than you have been in practice. He had injured his back in a workplace incident over 20 years ago. You took him on from his now-retired previous family physician, who had always told Jerry to avoid bending his back to avoid aggravating the pain and injury further. Jerry considers himself a good patient and has always followed his doctor’s orders exactly as instructed, but is frustrated as he feels he has limited a significant portion of his life due to his injury. Which of the following statements should you NOT say to Jerry?

options.html: “I am truly sorry for all of the years you have suffered with your pain, and I am here to help”
“Exercising and stretching your back may help you reduce your pain”
“Your pain indicates that there is some ongoing tissue damage”
“Your pain may actually be due to dysfunction in your brain’s perception of pain”

answer: The correct answer is C. It is likely that Jerry’s back injury healed long ago. His pain does not indicate ongoing tissue damage. It is instead likely due to dysfunction in his pain signal modulation. Exercising and flexibility training may improve his pain. Acknowledging his pain and what he has gone through is a decent thing to do. Many with chronic pain suffer from depression and anxiety and these should not be missed.

stem: Which of the following definitions regarding chronic pain is incorrect?

options.html: In conversion disorder, there is incompatibility between the patient’s symptoms and their neurological condition

A diagnosis of somatic symptom disorder requires one or more somatic symptoms that are distressing or disruptive; thoughts, feelings, or behaviours related to the somatic symptoms; and chronicity of 6 months or greater
Medically unexplained symptoms are most common in neurology
If a patient presents themselves as injured but does not appear to have any obvious reason or reward for doing so, this is known as malingering
An adjustment disorder is described as emotional or behavioural symptoms that develop in response to a stressor, accompanied by out-of-proportion distress and/or impairment in function

answer: The correct answer is D. Malingering is when a patient is consciously acting to falsify their symptoms for external gain. The situation in D is more descriptive of a factitious disorder, where the patient is conscious of their behaviour but has no reward for doing so.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A twenty-something medical student fell asleep learning to draw the brachial plexus in order to complete a set of small group questions. Upon awakening, the student was aware of a prickly-tingly feeling in the pinky finger and pressure under the medial elbow.

stem: Where is the most likely nerve lesion, and how could the student confirm this on self-exam?

options.html: Median nerve in the carpal tunnel; hold the wrist flexed for Phalen's sign
Ulnar nerve behind the medial epicondyle; tap there for a Tinel sign
C8 nerve root in the neck; look for a reduced triceps reflex on that side
Ulnar nerve in Guyon's canal; tap over the wrist for a Tinel sign there

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's ulnar neuropathy at the elbow is numbness and tingling into the ring and little fingers, pain at the medial elbow, and a positive Tinel sign at the elbow, and one of its causes is sustained elbow flexion in sleep. Tinel's sign is light tapping over the nerve at the entrapment site sending tingling into its distribution.

  • A The median nerve supplies the radial digits, not the little finger.
  • C C8 is the main differential for an ulnar lesion, but pressure under the medial elbow after sleeping on a bent arm points to the nerve at the elbow, and the triceps reflex is not the C8 check.
  • D Guyon's canal is the ulnar nerve's other site; the pressure here is at the elbow, and the lecture's cause at the wrist is handlebar compression.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The medical student above woke with a prickly-tingly little finger and pressure under the medial elbow after falling asleep on a bent arm.

stem: List the Seddon grades/types of nerve injury. What grade of nerve injury has likely occurred, and how can this be confirmed?

options.html: Axonotmesis; it is confirmed by recovery at about 1 mm per day
Neurotmesis; it is confirmed by finding no recovery over months
Axonotmesis; it is confirmed by surgical exploration of the nerve
Neurapraxia; confirmed by recovery once the pressure is off

answer:
The correct answer is D. The Seddon grades are neurapraxia (myelin only), axonotmesis (axon, with the epineurium intact) and neurotmesis (the epineurium cut, the nerve discontinuous). Compression is the lecture's cause of neurapraxia (the Saturday night palsy), and it is temporary, resolving once the cause is addressed. Nerve conduction studies can show it too: timing and speed reflect the myelin.

  • A Axonotmesis is a crush or stretch, and its slow regrowth is the sign of an axon that was cut.
  • B Neurotmesis is a cut nerve with no spontaneous recovery; a night on a bent elbow does not cut a nerve.
  • C Nothing about a compression after sleep calls for exploring the nerve.

A rigid wrist-hand orthosis worn every night

Non-drug care is to avoid external pressure (no leaning on the elbow) and avoid elbow hyperflexion with a towel splint or elbow pad overnight 07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity. A neurapraxia from compression resolves once the cause is removed 03 - Nerve Injury.

  • C: A rigid wrist-hand orthosis worn overnight is the splint for carpal tunnel syndrome, not the ulnar nerve at the elbow.
  • D: Going to EMG and nerve conduction studies early is for significant or progressive weakness; a transient compression palsy needs education first.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
A 43 year-old right handed painter comes to see you about her neck and shoulder pain. This has been bothering her for some time, and your quick review of her chart indicates that she first started describing these symptoms about 8 years ago. She is otherwise healthy.

  • Pain worse with neck extension. Occasionally the pain radiates across the shoulder or into her mid-back. Sometimes headaches accompany the neck pain.
  • No fasciculations or atrophy. Her upper extremity reflexes are 2+ on the left and on the right. Strength testing is 5/5 and equal bilaterally in all myotomes. Normal sensory exam. Range of motion of the neck is limited by pain, especially in extension and rotation to the right. Spurling's maneuver is negative. The patient has tenderness to palpation over the paraspinal muscles and over the facet joints, worse on the right side.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis and what is your management plan?

options.html: Facet joint neck pain; education, staying active and physiotherapy
Cervical radiculopathy; an MRI of the neck and a referral to spine surgery
Cervical myelopathy; an urgent MRI and the same-day spine surgery opinion
Rotator cuff tendinopathy; a subacromial injection and shoulder rest

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: facet joint pain is worse with EXTENSION (and eased by flexion), and the facets are one of the possible pain generators of mechanical pain, which is axial and worse with movement. She is tender over the facets, her neuro exam is normal and Spurling's is negative. With no red flags, mechanical pain is treated conservatively, without imaging.

  • B Radiculopathy needs a root sign: radiating arm symptoms, a reflex, weakness or a sensory change. She has none.
  • C Myelopathy is the centre-squeezed nerve, with long tract signs; her neuro exam is normal.
  • D Her pain is in the neck and worse with neck extension, and she is tender over the facets, not the shoulder.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
Several months later, the 43-year-old painter reports pain in the lower neck on the right side rated 9 of 10, with pain that radiates across the shoulder and into her hand. It's worse than usual, and she feels that this changed about 4 weeks ago, after she started assembling scaffolding and frequently doing overhead work. She is experiencing pins and needles down her arm and into her hand, and her arm feels heavy and weak. Occasionally she has tingles into the hand that wake her at night.

You repeat the physical exam today: no fasciculations or atrophy. Her reflexes are 2+ on the left; on the right, the triceps reflex is 2+ but the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes are absent. Strength testing on the right shows mild weakness of wrist extension, and elbow flexion. Range of motion of the neck is limited by pain. Spurling's maneuver is positive to the right.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis given this patient's presentation?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The root table: C6 = lateral forearm and digits I and II, elbow flexion and wrist extension, the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. Her weak wrist extension and elbow flexion with absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes, pain radiating into the hand, and a positive Spurling's on the right fit the right C6 root.

  • A C7 would take the triceps reflex, which is 2+.
  • B C5 shares the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes and elbow flexion, but its movement is shoulder abduction; wrist extension is C6.
  • D Carpal tunnel syndrome leaves median function above the wrist normal; it does not take a reflex or weaken the elbow.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The painter above has a right C6 radiculopathy: 4 weeks of worse neck pain radiating into the hand after overhead work, weak wrist extension and elbow flexion, and absent biceps and brachioradialis reflexes. She has no red flags.

stem: What management would you recommend for this patient?

options.html: Urgent decompression surgery, since there is weakness and a reflex lost
An epidural steroid injection first, before any physiotherapy is tried
A soft cervical collar and bed rest until the arm symptoms have settled
Education, activity, physiotherapy, analgesics or neuropathic agents

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture: without red flags, start the same conservative care as for mechanical pain (education, keep moving, physiotherapy, then acetaminophen, NSAIDs and neuropathic pain agents), and it applies to radiculopathy too.

  • A Surgery is for symptoms refractory to an adequate conservative trial, a progressive or severe deficit, or certain red flags; mild weakness at 4 weeks is none of these.
  • B The epidural steroid injection is the lecture's next step for radiculopathy that does not improve with conservative treatment, not the first one.
  • C Rest is the opposite of the advice: keep moving.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The painter above has a right C6 radiculopathy with mild weakness and no red flags, and is starting conservative management.

stem: What is the prognosis for this patient? Will this patient require surgery? What are the indications for surgery?

options.html: Poor without surgery; any radiculopathy with weakness needs decompression
Likely to improve; surgery only if refractory, progressive or severe
Good only after an MRI shows the disc; surgery if a herniation is seen there
Fixed for life; surgery cannot change a reflex that has already been lost

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture sends radiculopathy to decompression surgery only for refractory symptoms despite an adequate conservative trial, a progressive or severe neurological deficit, or certain red flag conditions. Her arm symptoms did improve with conservative care (Part III says so).

  • A Weakness alone is not the indication; a severe or progressing deficit is.
  • C Imaging cannot separate symptomatic from asymptomatic changes, so a disc on MRI is not the indication.
  • D Most radiculopathies improve; the notes do not give her a fixed deficit.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
The now 45-year-old right-handed painter comes back two years later. Her arm symptoms gradually improved with conservative management. She now has gradual onset right base of neck and shoulder pain, which began about two months ago, with discomfort reaching for the doorknob and lifting objects; the pain wakes her at night. It is sharp/stabbing rather than tingling and does not radiate down to her hand. It was preceded by an unusually heavy workload.

  • Normal bulk, tone, and power both proximally and distally in the arm. Sensation is intact.
  • Pain is increased by resisted external rotation and abduction of the right shoulder. There are tender points just anterior and distal to the tip of the acromion. The right trapezius is also tender.
  • There is restricted active range of movement, with internal rotation limited to 45° and abduction limited in active range to 90° with a painful arc present. Passive ROM is reasonably full with slight limitation related to pain.

stem: Based on the physical exam findings, what is the most likely diagnosis? What is the significance of the restricted range of motion?

options.html: Adhesive capsulitis; passive range is lost just as much as active range
Glenohumeral osteoarthritis; passive range is lost with crepitus on movement
Rotator cuff tendinopathy; active range is lost while passive range is kept
C5 radiculopathy; the restriction is weakness from the compressed nerve root

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: in rotator cuff disease active motion << passive motion, with impingement signs (Neer, Hawkins, painful arc), whereas in frozen shoulder and noninflammatory arthritis passive motion is lost too. Pain on resisted external rotation and abduction loads the cuff (infraspinatus, supraspinatus), and overuse precedes it.

  • A Adhesive capsulitis loses passive range too; hers is reasonably full.
  • B Arthritis also loses passive range.
  • D Her bulk, tone, power and sensation are normal.

Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. The first treatment for every stage of rotator cuff disease is education, activity modification, pain management with NSAIDs, physiotherapy for muscle reconditioning and injections, and most are treated without surgery 02.2 - Clinical Approach to the Muscles of the Shoulder. preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 38-year-old male construction worker injured his back while moving a piece of heavy machinery. He was flexed and rotated at the time of the injury eight days ago. He reports unremitting midline low back pain with mild radiation to the buttocks despite limiting his activity only to bed and couch for the past week. Tenderness is present quite diffusely over the low back. Pain is worse on lumbar extension. Neurological examination is normal.

stem: What is the significance of back pain that is worse with extension?

options.html: It points to the intervertebral disc as the pain generator
It points to a compressed nerve root as the pain generator
It points to the sacroiliac joint as the pain generator
It points to the facet joints as the pain generator

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's disc versus facet table: disc pain is worse with FLEXION (bending forward squeezes the disc); facet joint pain is worse with EXTENSION (bending back squeezes the facets) and is eased by flexion.

  • A Disc pain is the flexion pattern.
  • B A root gives radicular pain with a neurological finding; his neuro exam is normal and the radiation stops at the buttocks.
  • C The sacroiliac joint is a possible generator, but extension pain is the lecture's facet sign.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 38-year-old construction worker above has had midline low back pain for eight days after a lifting injury. His neurological examination is normal and he has no red flags.

stem: What are the indications for imaging in his case?

options.html: None, with no red flags and under 6 weeks
An X-ray now, since the injury happened at work
An MRI now, since a week of rest has not helped
A CT now, to look for a fracture of a facet joint

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: most low back pain needs no imaging, and with no red flags and under 6 weeks, NO imaging. Imaging can't separate symptomatic from asymptomatic changes and rarely changes management; it is required to look for red flags, which he does not have.

  • B A workplace injury is not a red flag.
  • C Failure of rest is not an indication, and bed rest is not the treatment.
  • D Nothing suggests a fracture: no high-energy trauma, osteoporosis or neurological finding.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 38-year-old construction worker above, with eight days of mechanical low back pain and no red flags, has spent the week in bed and on the couch.

stem: How long should you recommend he stay off work?

options.html: Two more weeks of bed rest before he tries any work at all
Off work until the pain has gone completely, however long
As little as possible; stay active on modified duties
Off work for six weeks, until imaging can be justified

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture's management of mechanical pain is to keep moving, with no bed rest, and relative rest only from what aggravates it. The notes do not give a number of days off work; the point they make is that resting in bed, which he has been doing, is the wrong advice.

  • A Bed rest is the opposite of the advice.
  • B Waiting for no pain at all keeps him inactive.
  • D Six weeks is the imaging threshold, not a time off work.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
A 57-year-old woman presents with pain in the left thigh and lateral hip area. The pain has been coming on gradually and although she had a fall two years earlier, she did not notice this pain until six months ago. It is worse walking and climbing stairs, and worse at first when she rises from rest. She is unable to sleep on her left side and frequently awakens with this pain.

On examination she is healthy-appearing. The pain is reproduced by resisted abduction. Local tenderness is present over the greater trochanter of the left hip. There is decreased passive hip internal rotation on the left. There is a slightly antalgic gait, and a slight Trendelenberg gait. The lumbar spine is slightly restricted and painful especially with extension. There is no other wasting or weakness. Neurological exam is normal.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis for this patient? List 3 other diagnoses you should consider.

options.html: Hip osteoarthritis of the left hip
L5 radiculopathy from the lumbar spine

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture: lateral = the greater trochanter. Greater trochanter bursitis is a clinical diagnosis: pain over the greater trochanter with point tenderness (highly sensitive), worse with weight bearing, and she can't lie on that side. The others to consider are the remaining options: her decreased internal rotation and the painful lumbar extension mean hip OA and a referred lumbar source belong on the list.

  • A Hip OA is groin pain with internal rotation reduced first; her pain is lateral, with point tenderness at the trochanter.
  • C Piriformis is buttock pain, tender over piriformis.
  • D Her neurological exam is normal.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Referral for a total hip replacement

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Greater trochanteric pain syndrome is treated with physiotherapy (stretch the iliotibial band, strengthen the hip abductors), load management and weight management, with NSAIDs and injections as further options 05 - Clinical Approach to Hip Pain.

  • A: Hip replacement is the end-stage treatment for hip osteoarthritis, not a tendinopathy at the trochanter.
  • C: Arthroscopic labral debridement or repair is the treatment of a labral tear, which gives groin pain with clicking or locking.
  • D: Ultrasound-guided corticosteroid injection of piriformis treats piriformis syndrome, which gives buttock pain.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 57-year-old woman above has lateral hip pain, tenderness over the greater trochanter, pain on resisted abduction, and a slight Trendelenburg gait.

stem: What is the cause of her presentation?

options.html: A bursa inflamed by the fall she had two years before the pain began
A tear of the labrum inside the hip joint, felt laterally
Compression of the sciatic nerve as it passes the piriformis
Tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus at the trochanter

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture: in greater trochanteric pain syndrome bursitis is only half the story; it is overuse and chronic tendinopathy of gluteus medius and minimus, which insert on the greater trochanter. These are the hip abductors, which is why resisted abduction hurts and her gait is Trendelenburg.

  • A Bursitis is half of it, from chronic friction of the iliotibial band; the fall came long before the pain.
  • B A labral tear is inside the joint, and inside-the-joint pain is groin pain.
  • C Her neurological exam is normal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 17-year-old high school student fractured his left humerus during a rugby practice one week ago. The fracture has been successfully reduced; however, he shows you that he has a wrist drop and cannot straighten his fingers. Examination reveals paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors and hypoaesthesia over the dorsum of the thumb.

stem: What is your diagnosis and mechanism of injury?

options.html: Axillary nerve injury at the surgical neck, from the rugby fall itself
C7 radiculopathy, from the neck being stretched during the tackle
Radial nerve injury in the radial groove from the shaft fracture
Median nerve injury at the elbow, from the reduction of the fracture

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: shaft fracture → radial nerve, which lies in the radial groove. The radial nerve supplies the wrist and finger extensors and the skin over the dorsum of the thumb, which is exactly what he has lost. A stretch or crush gives neurapraxia or axonotmesis; nerve studies, and time, tell which.

  • A A surgical neck fracture threatens the axillary nerve, which supplies deltoid and the skin over the shoulder.
  • B A C7 root would take the triceps reflex and spare the thumb's dorsum, and nothing here is a neck injury.
  • D The median nerve flexes the wrist and fingers and supplies the palm side.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 17-year-old high school student fractured his left humerus during a rugby practice one week ago. The fracture has been successfully reduced; however, he shows you that he has a wrist drop and cannot straighten his fingers . Examination reveals paralysis of the wrist and finger extensors and hypoaesthesia over the dorsum of the thumb . Later: this is a radial nerve injury in the radial groove from the shaft fracture.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Ultrasound of the wrist extensor tendons

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. Electrodiagnostic studies (nerve conduction studies plus EMG) confirm that there is a nerve problem, show where it is, and show how severe it is: myelin or axon, and whether the nerve is in continuity. That sets the expected timeline for recovery, which may need repeat studies, as taught in 03 - Nerve Injury.

  • A: Cervical imaging chases a radiculopathy, which gives neck pain radiating down the arm and a fuzzy dermatomal map. Here the loss is confined to one nerve's territory after a shaft fracture, a mononeuropathy pattern.
  • B: Weakness alone can be a tendon problem, but true sensory loss is always neurogenic, and he has hypoaesthesia over the dorsum of the thumb.
  • D: A bone scan is taught for early heterotopic ossification, not for grading a nerve injury.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
A 16-year-old female presents with gradual onset (over a three-month period) of pain in the right knee, which is increased by activity, particularly by climbing stairs. She gives no history of the knee locking and has not injured it in any known way. Playing volleyball, she gets pain and "cracking" when she squats, and when she sits for a while and then stands, it often causes pain.

On examination she is healthy-appearing, with local tenderness along the medial and lateral borders of the patella. Patella grinding is present (positive patella grind test) and pain is elicited by resisted leg extension from a fully flexed position. The Q angle measures 15 degrees bilaterally. Other aspects of examination of the knee are normal.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: anterior knee pain worse after activity and prolonged sitting, with no swelling, in a young woman = patellofemoral pain syndrome, a clinical diagnosis. Her pain is at the borders of the patella, the grind test is positive, and the rest of the knee is normal.

  • B A meniscal injury is a medial or lateral pain, often with locking, which she denies, and usually an injury.
  • C Patellar tendinopathy is on the same list of anterior pains, but her tenderness is at the patellar borders and the grind test is positive.
  • D Bursitis gives swelling over the patella; her knee is otherwise normal.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

Standing knee X-rays with a skyline view

answer:

  • C: X-rays are likewise kept for the patient who is not responding to treatment.
  • D: Aspiration is for an acutely inflamed, red joint; she has no joint swelling at all.

stem: Outline the principles of management.

options.html: Arthroscopy to smooth the back of the patella and then release it

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
A 23 year-old student was involved in a snowmobiling accident three days ago. Since then he has very severe pain in his neck, clavicle, and left lateral arm, with features of allodynia, but with hypoalgesia over his shoulder, lateral forearm, and thumb. There is extensive bruising around his shoulder and down the arm.

  • Muscle strength testing: 0/5 rhomboids, deltoid, biceps, brachioradialis; 1/5 shoulder external rotation; 3/5 elbow extension; 2/5 wrist extension; 3/5 wrist flexion; 5/5 intrinsic hand function.
  • Reflexes are absent at the biceps and brachioradialis, diminished on the left triceps compared to the right.
  • Decreased light touch sensation along the lateral forearm and thumb.

stem: Give a differential diagnosis for the clinical presentation. (the case asks for a differential; banked as the lesion that heads it)

options.html: An injury of the lower brachial plexus or the C8 and T1 roots
An isolated axillary nerve injury from the shoulder trauma
A radial nerve injury from a fracture of the humeral shaft
An injury of the upper brachial plexus or the C5 and C6 roots

answer:
The correct answer is D. His losses map to C5 and C6: deltoid, biceps and brachioradialis at 0/5, the biceps and brachioradialis reflexes absent, and sensation lost over the shoulder, lateral forearm and thumb, with intrinsic hand function 5/5. The lecture's superior trunk is C5 + C6, and many named nerves are involved at once, which is a plexopathy or root lesion rather than one nerve. Whether the roots themselves are torn (his rhomboids are 0/5) is beyond these notes and is left open for the session.

  • A C8 and T1 run the intrinsic hand muscles, which are 5/5.
  • B The axillary nerve would not take biceps, brachioradialis or the forearm skin.
  • C The radial nerve would not take deltoid or biceps, and nothing says the humerus is broken.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 23-year-old above has an upper brachial plexus (C5-C6) injury after a snowmobiling accident three days ago.

stem: What investigations can assist with a diagnosis? Why is knowing the type of nerve injury important?

options.html: EMG/NCS; the type of injury decides if, and how fast, it recovers
A plain X-ray alone; the type of injury changes nothing about care
Blood work for nerve damage; the type decides which pain drug to use
An MRI alone; the type only matters for the medicolegal record

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: electrodiagnostic studies (NCS + EMG) separate a myelin injury from an axonal one, and the Seddon type is the prognosis: neurapraxia recovers in weeks, axonotmesis regrows on its own at about 1 mm a day, neurotmesis cannot recover spontaneously. In the lecture's foot drop case the studies showed an axonal injury, and whether it was axonotmetic or neurotmetic could only be told by waiting to see if it recovered.

  • B The type of injury is the prognosis.
  • C The notes give no blood test for nerve injury.
  • D Imaging has its place, but the notes give the type of injury to electrodiagnostics.

stem: As part of the evaluation of a 9-year-old boy for right knee pain, you ask him to walk up and down the hall. You note that he shifts his weight over his right hip while walking. He has normal stride length and stance phase timing. This pattern is characteristic of:
answer:
The correct answer is E. Leaning the trunk over the hip while walking is the compensated Trendelenburg gait: the trunk lurches over the weak side so the pelvis stays level, and the weak muscle is gluteus medius on the standing (right) side. Knee pain in a child is often referred from the hip, which is why the hip is the joint to look at.

  • B An antalgic gait shortens stance time on the painful side. Normal stance phase timing rules it out.
  • A, C, D Nothing in the stem points to a wide unsteady base, stiff scissoring legs or walking on the toes.

stem: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off a dirt bike about 6 hours ago. His complaints include increasing pain, swelling, and a loss of feeling in his leg. He was walking immediately after the accident but can no longer do so. Your presumptive diagnosis is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Hours after trauma, pain that keeps rising, swelling and new loss of sensation is compartment syndrome: the lecture's pain out of proportion and paresthesia (the midterm sign), with the lower leg the commonest site. It is a clinical diagnosis and an emergency: remove anything constricting, call orthopedics, fasciotomy.

  • B Perthes is a painless limp over months in a 4-8 year old, not an acute injury.
  • C Osteomyelitis takes days and brings fever, not six hours.
  • D No wound is described, and a puncture would not take sensation.
  • E SCFE fits the age and can follow a fall, but it is a hip problem without a sensory deficit.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 15-year-old boy presents to the emergency department after falling off a dirt bike about 6 hours ago. His complaints include increasing pain, swelling, and a loss of feeling in his leg. He was walking immediately after the accident but can no longer do so. Later: your presumptive diagnosis is compartment syndrome.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Elevate, give analgesia and reassess in 6 hours
X-ray the leg and arrange fracture clinic review
Call orthopedics now for an urgent fasciotomy

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. Compartment syndrome is an orthopedic emergency and a clinical diagnosis: call orthopedics immediately, remove any compressive dressings or casts, elevate, cool and monitor, and the definitive treatment is fasciotomy. His loss of feeling is paresthesia, a midterm finding, so there is no time to lose, as taught in 05 - Fracture Management.

  • A: Muscle and nerve are injured within 2 hours of ischemia; waiting lets the cycle of cell death and swelling run on.
  • B: No test is needed when the clinical picture is there. Pressure measurement is for a patient who cannot communicate (uncooperative, sedated, a young child), and this boy can.
  • C: Outpatient review does nothing for the rising compartment pressure and delays the fasciotomy.

stem:
A 2-year-old girl presents with increasing irritability over the past 6 hours. She had a presumptive upper respiratory tract infection last week. On the examination table, she lays with her left hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. She is very resistant to examination. Of the following, the data set that best supports a diagnosis of septic arthritis is:

TemperatureWhite cell countESRAmbulatoryCRP
A104°F (40.0°C)15,000/µL (15 × 10⁹/L)45 mm/hWalking4 mg/L (38.10 nmol/L)
B100°F (37.8°C)11,000/µL (11 × 10⁹/L)30 mm/hNot walking2 mg/L (19.05 nmol/L)
C100°F (37.8°C)14,000/µL (14 × 10⁹/L)45 mm/hWalking4 mg/L (38.10 nmol/L)
D104°F (40.0°C)22,000/µL (22 × 10⁹/L)65 mm/hNot walking5 mg/L (47.62 nmol/L)
E104°F (40.0°C)15,000/µL (15 × 10⁹/L)30 mm/hNot walking2 mg/L (19.05 nmol/L)
answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's Kocher criteria separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis of the hip: temperature over 38.5 °C, white cell count over 12 × 10⁹/L, ESR over 40 mm/h, cannot walk on it, with CRP added later. D is the only set that meets every one, and it has the highest CRP.

  • A Meets fever, white count and ESR, but she is walking.
  • B Meets only non-weight-bearing.
  • C Meets white count and ESR only; no real fever, and walking.
  • E Meets fever, white count and non-weight-bearing, but the ESR is under 40.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 2-year-old girl presents with increasing irritability over the past 6 hours. She had a presumptive upper respiratory tract infection last week. On the examination table, she lays with her left hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. She is very resistant to examination. Later: septic arthritis of the hip is suspected.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: MRI of the pelvis and both hips
Hip aspiration for cell count and culture
Bone scan of the pelvis and both hips first
Repeat blood count and CRP in 24 hours

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Suspected septic arthritis is worked up by aspirating the joint and sending the 3 C's (cell count, culture and sensitivity with Gram stain, crystals), along with blood cultures and blood work. The Gram stain and culture are what find the infection, as taught in 08 - Acute Monoarthritis and 01 - MSK Infections.

  • A: Imaging is only a "±" in the septic arthritis workup and cannot identify the organism.
  • C: A bone scan is taught for Perthes disease and early heterotopic ossification, not to confirm a septic joint.
  • D: Septic arthritis is a medical emergency; waiting a day risks fulminant joint damage.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 2-year-old girl presents with increasing irritability over the past 6 hours. She had a presumptive upper respiratory tract infection last week. On the examination table, she lays with her left hip flexed, abducted, and externally rotated. She is very resistant to examination. Later: septic arthritis of the hip is suspected.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Urgent incision and drainage with IV antibiotics
NSAID, reassurance and review in 7-10 days
Oral antibiotics and review in the clinic in 2 days

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. Septic arthritis is treated by admission, urgent incision and drainage of the joint (a closed space), repeated until it is clean, plus empiric IV antibiotics. In children the usual organisms are S. aureus and streptococci, as taught in 08 - Acute Monoarthritis and 01 - MSK Infections.

  • B: NSAID and reassurance, settling in 7-10 days, is the plan for transient synovitis, which is what septic arthritis must be told apart from (09 - Child with a Limp).
  • C: Oral outpatient treatment leaves the pus in the joint; this is an emergency that needs drainage and IV antibiotics.
  • D: Never inject a steroid before infection is excluded.

stem: A 4-year-old child presents to the clinic with a painless limp. His parents report that the limp has become more obvious over the past 6 months. He has no history of fever. Physical examination reveals limited abduction of the right hip. When he walks, he seems to "hop over" his left leg. The most likely cause for his limp is:
answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's line for Perthes: age 4-8, a painless limp that comes on gradually, with less abduction and internal rotation of the hip as the femoral head dies.

  • A DDH also limits abduction, but a limp from it starts when the child starts walking, not newly over the last six months at age 4.
  • C Septic arthritis is acute, painful and febrile.
  • D SCFE is the overweight adolescent, not a 4-year-old.
  • E Toxic (transient) synovitis is acute after a virus and settles in 7-10 days.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 4-year-old child presents to the clinic with a painless limp. His parents report that the limp has become more obvious over the past 6 months. He has no history of fever. Physical examination reveals limited abduction of the right hip. When he walks, he seems to "hop over" his left leg. Later: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is the most likely cause.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Hip aspiration for cell count and culture
Ultrasound of both hips for an effusion
Blood count, ESR and CRP only
X-ray, AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is avascular necrosis of the femoral head, and the test is an X-ray, AP pelvis and frog-leg lateral, looking for flattening and fragmentation of the head. Bone scan and MRI are the further tests, as taught in 09 - Child with a Limp.

  • A: Aspiration is for a suspected septic joint; this child has a painless limp over 6 months and no fever.
  • B: Ultrasound is among the tests done in transient synovitis to rule out septic arthritis, not the test that shows a necrotic femoral head.
  • C: Blood work is used to separate septic arthritis from transient synovitis and does not show the femoral head.

preamble.html: A 4-year-old child presents to the clinic with a painless limp. His parents report that the limp has become more obvious over the past 6 months. He has no history of fever. Physical examination reveals limited abduction of the right hip. When he walks, he seems to "hop over" his left leg. Later: Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease is the most likely cause.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: NSAID and reassurance, as it settles in 7-10 days
Stop weight-bearing and pin the hip in situ
Refer to orthopedics, physio to keep motion
Pavlik harness until the hip is stable

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. Perthes disease is referred to orthopedics, and physiotherapy keeps the hip's range of motion (better motion, better outcome), with weight taken off by crutches, a brace, swimming or cycling, NSAIDs or acetaminophen, and an osteotomy for some. Poorly treated, it leads to early osteoarthritis, as taught in 09 - Child with a Limp.

  • A: NSAID and reassurance with recovery in 7-10 days is transient synovitis, which has a sudden onset after a virus, not a limp worsening over 6 months.
  • B: Stopping weight-bearing and pinning in situ is the emergency plan for slipped capital femoral epiphysis in an 8-15-year-old.
  • D: The Pavlik harness treats developmental dysplasia of the hip up to 6 months of age (08 - Pediatric Orthopedics).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 51 year-old electrician slipped on the stairs and fell onto her outstretched hand. Her wrist is swollen and deformed and she refuses to move it. Her neurovascular exam distal to the deformity is normal.

stem:
Describe the x-ray.

Stand-in film from this year's Clinical Approach to the Wrist and Hand Part 1 deck; the handout's own X-ray is not printed.

options.html: Fracture of the scaphoid waist, with the distal radius intact
Distal radius fracture, the distal fragment angled volarly (Smith's)
Distal radius fracture, the distal fragment angled dorsally (Colles')
Dislocation of the lunate, with the radius and ulna intact

answer:
The correct answer is C. On the lateral film the joint surface of the distal radius is tilted 20° dorsally, where a normal wrist tilts about 12° palmar. The lecture: Colles' = distal radius angled dorsally ("dinner fork") vs Smith's = angled volarly, and look for an ulnar styloid fracture alongside. Deformity is always described as the distal fragment relative to the proximal.

  • A A FOOSH can break the scaphoid, but this film shows the break in the radius.
  • B Smith's is the mirror image, angled toward the palm.
  • D The carpus sits in line with the radius on both views.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 51 year-old electrician: a closed, dorsally angulated distal radius fracture after a fall on the outstretched hand. Her distal neurovascular exam is normal.

stem: What is your management plan?

options.html: Splint in the position found and book an outpatient MRI of the wrist
Open reduction and internal fixation before any attempt at closed reduction
Sling for comfort and early range of motion, with no reduction
Closed reduction under a hematoma block, splint, then a post-reduction X-ray

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's order: adequate analgesia (hematoma block, 1% lidocaine into the fracture hematoma, or conscious sedation) → closed reduction: traction, increase the deformity, correct it → splint or cast → always a post-reduction X-ray and a repeat neurovascular exam. ORIF or external fixation come in if alignment fails or cannot be held.

  • A A displaced fracture is reduced, not splinted where it lies; MRI adds nothing to a fracture already seen on X-ray.
  • B Surgery is for a reduction that fails or will not hold, not the first step.
  • C A displaced, angulated fracture will not heal well on its own.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 51 year-old electrician with a Colles' fracture of the distal radius, now reduced and splinted.

stem: Which of these is a recognised complication of this fracture that needs urgent action if it appears?

options.html: Median nerve compression with numbness in the thumb, index and middle fingers
Avascular necrosis of the distal radius
Growth arrest at the distal radial physis
Ulnar nerve palsy from the fracture fragment in Guyon's canal

answer:
The correct answer is A. The vault's distal radius fracture note: damage to the median nerve can occur, and swelling under a splint at the wrist compresses the nerve in the carpal tunnel (carpal tunnel syndrome). The other complications the lecture lists for any fracture apply too: mal-union, stiffness, complex regional pain syndrome and post-traumatic arthritis.

  • B The avascular necrosis sites are the femoral head, talus and scaphoid, the bones with a retrograde blood supply.
  • C She is 51; growth arrest is a risk only while the physis is open.
  • D The ulnar nerve runs on the other side of the wrist, away from a dorsally angled radius.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 75 year-old woman missed a step going down about 5 stairs and landed on her left lateral hip. She is in excruciating pain. No loss of consciousness, no head strike, no previous falls or steroid use.

stem: Which physical finding would most strongly suggest a hip fracture?

options.html: Leg shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated
Leg shortened, externally rotated and abducted, unable to bear weight
Tenderness over the pubic symphysis with full hip range of motion
Leg lengthened and externally rotated with a palpable mass in the groin

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's hip fracture exam: look: the leg is shortened, externally rotated and abducted, and she cannot bear weight; feel: tender over the hip; move: painful range. An impacted or non-displaced neck fracture can show almost none of this, which is why the X-ray is still needed.

  • A Shortened, flexed, adducted and internally rotated is the posterior hip dislocation.
  • C Pubic tenderness with a hip that moves freely points to a pubic rami fracture.
  • D A lengthened, externally rotated leg is an anterior dislocation, which is rare in a native hip at low energy.

preamble.html: A 75 year-old woman missed a step going down about 5 stairs and landed on her left lateral hip . She is in excruciating pain. No loss of consciousness, no head strike, no previous falls or steroid use. Later: her leg is shortened, externally rotated and abducted, and she cannot bear weight.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: CT of the hip before any plain film
X-ray of the AP pelvis and the hip
MRI of the hip and lumbar spine

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. A suspected hip fracture is imaged with an X-ray of the AP pelvis and hip, and the fracture's level on that film picks the operation. CT is added only if the X-ray is negative and suspicion stays high, as taught in 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint.

  • A: CT is the second step, after a negative X-ray, not the first film.
  • C: MRI is not the taught workup for a suspected hip fracture, and nothing points to the spine.
  • D: Bone density matters later, since a fragility fracture counts as osteoporosis, but it does not diagnose the fracture.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 75 year-old woman: her X-ray shows a displaced femoral neck fracture.

stem: How will you manage this patient?

options.html: Bed rest and traction for 6 weeks, then mobilize
Closed reduction and a hip spica cast
Surgery within 24-48 hours, a hemiarthroplasty or total hip replacement
Cannulated screw fixation after 1 week of observation

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: surgery within 24-48 hours: displaced neck → arthroplasty; intertrochanteric or subtrochanteric → intramedullary nail. A displaced neck fracture needs urgent surgery because it cuts the retrograde supply to the head (osteonecrosis). Afterwards: early mobilization, heparin for 14-30 days, falls and fracture prevention.

  • A Prolonged bed rest brings every complication of immobility (VTE, pneumonia, pressure sores, delirium), which is why nearly every hip fracture goes to surgery.
  • B A hip is not held by a cast in an adult.
  • D Screws are for the non-displaced neck fracture, and delay raises mortality.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 42 year-old man was hit by a car while walking. His leg is bleeding from a 0.5 cm laceration over the anterolateral leg. HR 95, BP 138/75, temperature 37°C. No other injuries.

stem:
What is your initial management plan for this patient?

Stand-in film from this year's Fracture Management and Complications Part 1 deck (slide 12, "Let's Review a Case!": an open spiral fracture of the distal third of the tibial diaphysis).

options.html: Close the laceration in the ED, cast the leg and arrange outpatient follow-up
IV cefazolin, tetanus prophylaxis, sterile dressing, splint, then urgent debridement and stabilization
Oral antibiotics and a CT of the leg before deciding whether the fracture is open
Probe the wound to see whether it reaches the bone, then decide on antibiotics

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture: any fracture with a wound is open, however small, until proven otherwise. Early antibiotics (the lecture's case: 2 g IV cefazolin) · tetanus prophylaxis in the emergency department · closed reduction and splint while waiting for orthopedics · then early surgery: remove devitalized tissue including bone fragments, gently irrigate with sterile saline, and stabilize (the case: an intramedullary nail).

  • A An open fracture is never closed in the ED and sent home; it needs the operating room.
  • C The wound sits over the fracture, so it is treated as open now; antibiotics are IV and early.
  • D Probing adds contamination and does not change the plan.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 42 year-old pedestrian with an open tibial fracture, now splinted on the ward.

stem: Which signs are the earliest and most reliable warning of compartment syndrome?

options.html: Loss of the dorsalis pedis pulse and a pale foot
Fever and redness spreading from the wound
Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch of the muscles

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's compartment syndrome: pain out of proportion to the injury · pain on passive stretch of the compartment's muscles (its example is a tibial fracture with rising narcotic needs). It is a clinical diagnosis, and an open wound does not decompress the compartments.

  • A The pulse is lost late, if at all: do not wait for the pulse to go.
  • B Fever and spreading redness are infection, the other complication of an open fracture.
  • C Paralysis is a late sign, by which time muscle may be dying.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Overnight the same patient needs more and more opioid; his leg is tense and stretching his toes is agony.

stem: How is compartment syndrome treated?

options.html: Elevate the leg well above the heart and reassess in the morning
Increase the opioid dose and add an NSAID
Remove the cast or dressing, call orthopedics, urgent fasciotomy
Start IV antibiotics and repeat the X-ray

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: remove the cast, call orthopedics, fasciotomy; it is an emergency, and do not wait for the pulse to go.

  • A Elevating the limb lowers its perfusion pressure; keep it at heart level.
  • B Masking the pain hides the one early sign while the muscle dies.
  • D Neither treats rising pressure in the compartment.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 10 year-old boy injured his leg playing soccer. He is crying and unable to walk. His right leg is swollen around the ankle and distal tibia, but the skin is intact.

stem:
Describe the x-ray. Using the Salter-Harris classification, what type is this?

Stand-in film from this year's Pediatric Orthopedics deck (slide 36, "Physeal Injury SH II").

options.html: Type I: straight through the physis, with no bone fragment
Type II: through the physis and out through a piece of metaphysis
Type III: through the physis and into the epiphysis, intra-articular
Type V: a crush of the physis

answer:
The correct answer is B. A fracture of the distal tibia that runs along the growth plate and exits through a triangle of metaphysis is Salter-Harris II, the most common type. The lecture's mnemonic: Straight (I) · Above (II) · Lower (III) · Through (IV) · Rammed (V). The classification matters because the risk of growth disturbance rises from I to V, and III and IV are intra-articular and need an anatomic reduction.

  • A Type I has no fracture line into the bone either side, and is often missed as a "sprain".
  • C Type III exits through the epiphysis into the joint.
  • D Type V is often invisible at first and diagnosed late, by the growth arrest.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 10 year-old boy injured his leg playing soccer. He is crying and unable to walk. His right leg is swollen around the ankle and distal tibia , but the skin is intact. Later: the X-ray shows a Salter-Harris type II fracture of the distal tibia.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Open reduction and internal fixation today
Compression bandage and walk on it as a sprain
Cast for 6 weeks, then discharge from follow-up
Cast, check films, and follow for 1-2 years

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. Type II is the most common Salter-Harris injury and is usually stable with closed reduction (if it needs one, under a hematoma block or conscious sedation), then a splint or cast with post-reduction and post-casting films. Every growth plate injury is serious, so follow it at least 1 year and preferably 2, and warn the family about growth arrest, as taught in 08 - Pediatric Orthopedics.

  • A: Anatomic reduction is what types III and IV need, as they are intra-articular; type II is usually stable closed.
  • B: Sprains are rare in children because the growth plate fails before the ligament; calling a physeal injury a sprain is the classic miss.
  • C: About 10% develop a growth disturbance, so discharging him after the cast misses growth arrest.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 10 year-old boy with a Salter-Harris fracture of the distal tibia.

stem: What is a common complication of this fracture?

options.html: Growth arrest, leading to a leg length discrepancy or angular deformity
Non-union, because children's fractures heal slowly
Heterotopic ossification of the ankle joint

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's major complication of a physeal injury is growth arrest → leg length discrepancy or angular deformity; about 10% develop a growth disturbance, which is why every growth plate injury is followed for 1-2 years.

  • A The talus is an avascular necrosis site, but after a talar neck fracture, not a tibial physeal one.
  • C Children heal faster than adults, with a thick periosteum.
  • D Heterotopic ossification is not the complication the lecture ties to the growth plate.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 30 year-old man after a motor vehicle accident, cleared by the trauma team for an isolated femur fracture. His thigh is swollen and obviously deformed. His distal neurovascular exam is normal.

stem:
Describe the x-ray.

Stand-in film: "Medical X-Ray imaging IYN05 nevit.jpg" by Nevit Dilmen, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. No deck this year shows a femoral shaft fracture, and the handout prints none.

options.html: Transverse fracture of the proximal femoral diaphysis, undisplaced
Intertrochanteric fracture of the left hip
Long oblique fracture of the left femoral diaphysis at the junction of its middle and distal thirds, displaced and shortened
Supracondylar fracture of the distal femur extending into the knee

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture's order: region and views (an AP of the left femur, with the hip on the film) · location (diaphysis, divided into thirds; here the middle-distal junction) · type (long oblique) · displacement, distal relative to proximal (the distal fragment is translated and overriding, so the femur is shortened, which thigh muscle pull causes). Always check the hip on the same film: an ipsilateral femoral neck fracture is easy to miss.

  • A The fracture line is long and slanted, not transverse, and the ends have moved.
  • B The trochanteric region is intact on this film.
  • D The break is in the shaft, well above the condyles and the joint.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 30 year-old man with an isolated, displaced femoral shaft fracture. His pain is controlled and he is haemodynamically stable.

stem: Patients with femur fractures need to be treated surgically as soon as possible. Why?

options.html: Early fixation lowers the risk of pulmonary complications (fat embolism, VTE) and lets him mobilize
The femoral head loses its blood supply within hours of a shaft fracture
A femoral shaft fracture will not unite without surgery in any patient
Surgery is needed to rule out a pathological fracture

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture's complications of fractures start with venous thromboembolism: orthopedic trauma meets all of Virchow's triad (injury, stasis, hypercoagulability), and lying in traction is stasis. Fixing the femur with an intramedullary nail early lets him get up, and early mobilization is the lecture's answer to every complication of bed rest. ⚠ Fat embolism is not in the vault's lecture note; it is the session's own teaching point (a long-bone fracture releasing marrow fat, with hypoxaemia, confusion and a petechial rash 24-72 hours later), and is why the option names it.

  • B Avascular necrosis threatens the femoral head after a neck fracture, not a shaft fracture.
  • C Shaft fractures can unite in traction; it is the months in bed that make surgery the standard.
  • D Nothing in a 30 year-old's car accident suggests pathological bone.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 22 year-old university student felt his right shoulder "pop" when he was hit from behind into the boards while reaching for the puck with his arm outstretched. There is a large bulge in the anterior shoulder, and the arm is held slightly abducted and externally rotated. Passive range of motion is limited. Radial and brachial pulses are present.

stem:
Interpret the x-ray. What is the diagnosis?

Stand-in film from this year's Clinical Approach to Osteology and Joints of the Proximal Upper Extremity deck, also a hockey player.

options.html: Fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus

answer:
The correct answer is B. The humeral head sits in front of and below the glenoid. The lecture: traumatic instability is unidirectional, anterior >> posterior, "torn loose", and its degree runs reduced → subluxated → dislocated. The arm held in abduction and external rotation is the position the anterior capsule fails in. Look for a Hill-Sachs lesion on the back of the head and a fractured glenoid rim.

  • A A posterior dislocation holds the arm in internal rotation and follows a seizure or electric shock.
  • C The AC joint sits on top of the shoulder, with a step at the end of the clavicle.
  • D The neck of the humerus is intact; the head has left the socket.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 22 year-old hockey player with an anterior shoulder dislocation.

stem: What is your initial management plan?

options.html: Sling and early exercises, reducing it only if it fails to relocate in a week
Immediate arthroscopic labral repair, before any closed reduction
Monitors and analgesia, closed reduction, then re-examine the nerves and get a post-reduction X-ray
Closed reduction first, then the X-ray only if the neurovascular exam changes

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture's reduction: safety first (monitors) · analgesia · manipulation to correct the deformity · re-examine after: check neurovascular status · and a post-reduction X-ray. The nerve to check is the axillary nerve, which wraps around the neck of the humerus: sensation over the lateral deltoid and deltoid contraction, before and after.

  • A A dislocated joint is reduced now, not left out.
  • B Labral repair comes later for the young or recurrent, never instead of reduction.
  • D Every reduction is confirmed on X-ray.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 22 year-old hockey player, now reduced. This is his first dislocation.

stem: What is the prognosis with respect to recurrence, and what does it mean for his management?

options.html: High risk of recurrence because he is young; refer to orthopedics to consider labral repair
Low risk of recurrence because it was traumatic; no follow-up is needed
High risk of a rotator cuff tear because of his age; MRI before he leaves
Recurrence is rare after a first dislocation; physiotherapy alone is always enough

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: surgery often, for young or recurrent dislocators → capsule-labral repair, 85% success. Young age is the strongest risk factor for re-dislocation, and a contact athlete is the classic referral after a first episode. A Hill-Sachs lesion raises the risk further.

  • B Traumatic "torn loose" instability is the kind that recurs in the young.
  • C Rotator cuff tears are the concern after a dislocation over 40.
  • D Rehabilitation first is the lecture's plan for the atraumatic, multidirectional "born loose" shoulder.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 27 year-old man, his knee dislocation now reduced under conscious sedation.

stem: Knowing what runs behind the knee, which structure is the biggest concern to check first?

options.html: The femoral artery in the femoral triangle

answer:
The correct answer is A. The popliteal fossa holds, deep to superficial, the popliteal artery, popliteal vein, tibial nerve and common fibular nerve, and a knee dislocation stretches or tears them. The session notes on this slide: "Popliteal artery biggest concern - massive bleeding!!" The tibial nerve runs with the posterior compartment and the common fibular nerve to the lateral and anterior compartments, which is where this patient's tingling already is.

  • B The saphenous nerve is sensory, on the medial side, and away from the fossa.
  • C The femoral artery becomes the popliteal at the adductor hiatus, above the injury.
  • D The great saphenous vein runs medially and superficially, out of harm's way.
