preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
After reduction, the same 27 year-old man's exam:

  • MSK: anterior and posterior drawer signs positive; varus stress test significant laxity, no end feel; valgus stress test unremarkable.
  • Neuro: ankle dorsiflexion, toe extension and ankle eversion 0/5; plantar flexion 5/5; ankle inversion 4/5; decreased sensation over the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
  • Vascular: good popliteal and distal pulses.

stem: What are your diagnoses?

options.html: ACL and MCL tears, with a tibial nerve palsy
ACL, PCL and LCL tears, with a common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy
PCL tear alone, with an L5 radiculopathy
ACL and PCL tears, with a deep fibular nerve palsy sparing sensation

answer: The correct answer is B. Slide 11, "Diagnoses": ACL complete tear · PCL complete tear · lateral instability contributors: LCL complete tear, likely biceps femoris complete tear, likely full or partial IT band tear · common fibular (peroneal) nerve palsy. The positive anterior and posterior drawers are the two cruciates; laxity to varus is the lateral side; loss of dorsiflexion, toe extension and eversion with numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot is the common fibular nerve (deep and superficial branches together).

preamble.html: A 32 year-old woman with 8 weeks of lower right low back, hip and buttock pain: a deep ache with sharp exacerbations, 2-7/10, in episodes lasting hours, worse lying supine and bending, better with NSAIDs, radiating to the buttock. Whether she has travelled abroad recently
Her history of sexually transmitted infection

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same woman, 28 weeks pregnant. Look: visibly pregnant, exaggerated lordosis. Feel: tender over the PSIS and lateral sacrum. Move: pain with forward flexion and extension. Positive FABER test. Neurovascular screen unremarkable. No groin pain.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The released slides list the differential (slide 18: facetogenic, discogenic, muscular, SI joint; radiculopathy; piriformis; gluteal tendinopathy; IT band) without naming a winner, but the management slide reaches for an SI belt. The lecture: sacroiliac joint dysfunction is seen in pregnancy and elite athletes, with SI tenderness, treated with physio and a belt in pregnancy; on the FABER test, back-of-pelvis pain = SI joint, groin pain = hip.

  • A Slide 18: "No groin pain, so intra-articular hip problem less likely."
  • B Her neurovascular screen is normal and the pain does not run down the leg.
  • D Gluteal tendinopathy is lateral hip pain over the greater trochanter, not the PSIS.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 76 year-old woman tripped on a curb yesterday: no loss of consciousness, no head strike, no presyncope. Knee and inner thigh pain, 5/10, much worse on weight bearing, though she can do it. Rheumatoid arthritis on prednisone, HTN, CAD, hypothyroidism. She lives alone. On exam she lies fairly comfortably, with bruising around the knee and lateral hip, tenderness along the medial thigh, the distal lateral femoral condyle and the greater trochanter, and pain when the right leg is moved passively. Her foot is neurovascularly intact.

stem: What does the X-ray show?

options.html: A normal pelvis; the pain is referred from the knee
A displaced fracture of the right femoral neck
A fracture of the left superior pubic ramus
An undisplaced fracture of the right greater trochanter

answer:
The correct answer is B. The released slide shows the film (labelled only "(A)") without a caption. On the patient's right (the left of the image) the femoral neck is broken through and the shaft has ridden up, so the leg is shortened. The lecture: knee pain can be a hip problem, and a hip fracture patient sometimes still walks on it. Prednisone and rheumatoid arthritis are her risk factors for weak bone.

  • A The right femoral neck is not intact.
  • C The pubic rami are intact on both sides.
  • D The trochanter is tender because she landed on it, but the break is in the neck.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The same 76 year-old woman with a displaced right femoral neck fracture.

stem: What's the risk without surgery?

options.html: Heterotopic ossification of the hip capsule
Osteonecrosis of the femoral head and non-union, plus the complications of prolonged bed rest
Injury to the sciatic nerve from the fracture fragment

answer:
The correct answer is C. The slides ask the question and send you to "Anatomy Time!", which is blank. The anatomy: the femoral head's main supply, the medial circumflex femoral artery, runs up the neck in a retrograde direction, so a displaced neck fracture cuts it: osteonecrosis of the head, one of the lecture's three avascular necrosis sites. Slide 33 lists what bed rest costs her: "weakness, wounds, urinary retention/UTIs, DVT, reduced cardiorespiratory capacity, pneumonias, delirium".

  • A Thigh compartment syndrome follows high-energy crush, not a low fall.
  • B Heterotopic ossification is a complication after surgery, not of leaving the hip alone.
  • D The sciatic nerve is at risk in a posterior hip dislocation.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 24 year-old university student landed on someone else's foot playing volleyball and fell. She was carried off the court. Severe lateral ankle and lateral leg pain with any movement of the foot or ankle, and significant swelling around the ankle.

stem: When does she need an ankle X-ray series?

options.html: Always, since the swelling is significant
Only if the pain is still present after a week
If there is malleolar pain and either bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of a malleolus, or she cannot bear weight for four steps
Only if the base of the 5th metatarsal is tender

answer: The correct answer is C. Slide 37, "The Ottawa Ankle Rules": "An ankle X-Ray series is only required if there is any pain in the malleolar zone and... bone tenderness at the posterior edge or tip of the lateral malleolus OR of the medial malleolus OR an inability to bear weight both immediately and in the emergency department for four steps." The base of the 5th metatarsal (D) belongs to the foot series of the Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules. Swelling (A) is not one of the rules.

preamble.html: The same 24 year-old volleyball player. Her Ottawa ankle rules are negative: a lateral ankle sprain.

stem: What are you thinking for management?

options.html: Protected weight bearing as needed, RICE, analgesia, and physio progressing to proprioception
Early surgical repair of the lateral ligaments
Strict non-weight bearing and an MRI

answer: The correct answer is B. Slide 40, "Management": Education: "This will get better! But might be a nuisance long term" · Non-pharm: protected weight bearing PRN, RICE, physio ROM → strength → proprioception → sport specific · Pharm: acetaminophen, NSAIDs · Surgical/intervention: "Almost never". Lateral, because an ankle sprain is usually an inversion injury tearing the ATFL first.

stem: A 73-year-old patient comes to you with a several year history of bilateral knee pain that is worse on the right side. On examination you find MRC 5 for knee extension and flexion as well as a normal neurologic examination. On palpation you see his knees are slightly swollen but not red or hot. You find there is joint line tenderness and crepitus with passive movement. There is no sign of patellar apprehension or grinding. Anterior and posterior drawer tests are negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Central medial meniscal tear from twisting

answer:
The correct answer is D. Arthritis — the patient's age 73 (over 50), the long history without trauma, crepitus on movement and joint line tenderness all point there.

B is the most likely meniscal injury for an elderly patient, but there is no history of trauma and no evidence of true locking. C is unlikely with no grinding or patellar apprehension on exam.

stem: A patient comes to you with an antalgic gait and some swelling over the great toe of the left foot. She had become upset during a personal matter and kicked her door. Upon examination you find that the toe is extremely painful for the patient and you decide to get an x-ray. You see a transverse fracture of the distal phalange of the great toe with no involvement of articular surface. How do you manage?

options.html: Do nothing, toe injuries generally require no treatment
Buddy tape the great toe to the next toe
Activity modification, physio and no weight bearing

answer:
The correct answer is B. Buddy taping is appropriate when there is no displacement and no involvement of the articular surface. Note the two escalation triggers embedded in that rule:

  • displacement → surgery
  • articular surface involvement → foot and toe cast

stem: A 16 y.o. F. pianist came in with progressive swollen joints (multiple) over the last three months, more than 6 joints involved in her hands, they feel warm and tender on palpation, what are your top 3 differential diagnoses?
answer:
The correct answers are B, E, F. The patient demographic (female, late teen) fits RA, SLE and JIA best. The condition is chronic (over three months) with multiple joints involved.

Each exclusion turns on one feature:

  • A Infectious — ruled out by the chronic, polyarticular course
  • C AS — more likely in the lower back
  • D Acute gout — usually one joint, and this is a chronic patient
  • G Chondrosarcoma — a large mass around bigger joints, not a polyarthritis

weekLabel: Week 11 - Arthritis, Connective Tissue Disease & Vasculitis
lectureMeta: Workbook Q33, Q37, Q49, Q56. Tests [[08 - Acute Monoarthritis]], [[04 - Osteoarthritis]], [[02 - Approach to Polyarthritis]], [[03 - Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis]].
stem: A 50-year-old female patient comes to you complaining of aching in her knees and feet that has been occurring daily, she has minor pains in the morning but the pain progresses with activity throughout the day especially with walking. In history you get the impression that this pain is bothersome but is not limiting her function. On exam you notice slight bowing (varus deformity) in her knees. Overall outside the pain, the patient does not complain of fever, nausea, or fatigue. You order a radiograph to assess her knees and ankles, what do you expect?

options.html: Subchondral sclerosis, cysts, osteophytes, eccentric cartilage loss, loose bodies
Osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling

answer:
The correct answer is A. We suspect osteoarthritis because of the daily pain that progresses through the day and worsens with activity, supported by the absence of systemic symptoms (fever, fatigue, nausea) that would point toward rheumatoid arthritis.

Note that B and C are the RA radiographic picture — osteopenia, bony erosions, soft tissue swelling and symmetric joint space narrowing — whereas OA gives eccentric cartilage loss with osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis.

stem: A 63 y.o Finnish patient presents to the ER with sudden painless vision loss, an awful headache, pain with chewing, and pain with laying his head on their pillow at night. He also mentions pain in his shoulders and hips and classic B symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats)! What should the next steps be? Choose 3

options.html: Consult oncology urgently due to risk of intracranial malignancy
Consult ophthalmology for a temporal artery biopsy

answer: The correct answer is A, E, F. This patient has giant cell arteritis. Low-dose prednisone is only reserved for cases where other options don’t work or there are difficulty discontinuing steroids. Medium-dose prednisone is for RA flares, polymyalgia rheumatica and acute gout flare. Remember to not wait for ESR/CRP results and to start high dose corticosteroids immediately! Patients who are of Northern European descent (e.g. Finnish in this case) are at greater risk of giant cell arteritis. Intracranial malignancies need to be ruled out but doesn’t require oncology consult.

stem: Which of the following is false?

options.html: Prior to diagnosing primary vasculitis, serum protein electrophoresis, urine toxicology screens, sputum cultures, Hep B+C serology, and HIV testing must be taken.
Common signs of primary vasculitis includes ecchymosis, intracranial hemorrhages, cranial nerve neuropathies, and concurrent infections.
Giant cell arteritis cannot affect people who are 49 years old or younger.
A patient with ANCA vasculitis can still have a negative ANCA.
Patients with primary vasculitis need to have the following investigations to check for organ involvement: ALT, albumin, Cr, urinalysis, chest x-ray.
Vasculitis involves blood vessel thickening from inflammation and a resulting turbulent blood flow.

answer: The correct answer is B. Common signs of vasculitis are actually petechial/purpural rashes and B-symptoms (infections must actually be ruled out to make a diagnosis of primary vasculitis). Clots, occlusions/ischemia and aneurysms are more of a concern than bleeding manifestations in vasculitis. A is true because infection and underlying malignancy/drugs must be ruled out.

stem:
Match the complication (a,b,c,d,e) to the condition (i, ii, iii, iv). Warning: there may be repeats (e.g. one condition has 1+ complications)

  1. SLE
  2. Scleroderma
  3. inflammatory myositis
  4. Sjogren’s
answer:
The correct answer is A. iii, B - iv, C - i, D - i & ii, E - ii

From 06 - Connective Tissue Disorders. Each complication is a signature of one disease:

  • A → iii (myositis): pharyngeal and cardiac muscle involvement (aspiration, arrhythmia) plus the paraneoplastic link of dermatomyositis in the elderly.
  • B → iv (Sjogren's): ↑ risk of non-Hodgkin, specifically MALT lymphoma.
  • C → i (SLE): 50x cardiovascular risk; accelerated atherosclerosis is the commonest cause of death, worsened by steroids.
  • D → ii (scleroderma): significant ILD in ~15%, tracked by anti-Scl-70.
  • E → ii (scleroderma): renal crisis in diffuse disease (RNA-polymerase), now rarer thanks to ACE inhibitors.

flags.title: The key looks wrong on D
flags.html: The key maps interstitial lung disease to SLE and scleroderma. 06 - Connective Tissue Disorders and its embedded disease notes attach ILD to scleroderma, myositis (anti-Jo1) and Sjogren's; the SLE lung section lists pleuritis and pulmonary capillaritis, not ILD. Scleroderma is the safe answer for D; SLE is not supported by the notes.

stem: Which of the following are not appropriate treatment plan for CPPD?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Colchicine is used to treat gout.

From 08 - Acute Monoarthritis and the MSK summary notes. An acute pseudogout (CPPD) attack is treated like an acute gout attack: NSAIDs (indomethacin), colchicine, or steroids (intra-articular or oral prednisone). What does not carry over from gout is urate lowering (allopurinol), which is for gout only.

  • A (colchicine) is on the notes' acute-attack list for pseudogout.
  • B, D are both listed: IA injection and a short oral prednisone taper.
  • C is an NSAID; a COXIB belongs to the same class as the indomethacin in the notes.

So on the notes, every option is an appropriate treatment for CPPD.

stem: Your 65 year old patient has early stage Osteoarthritis. She strongly asks you if she could get a joint replacement surgery. What would be your response?

options.html: No - we should perform knee arthroscopy.
No - treatment for early stage OA is monitoring & reassurance with absolutely no intervention

No - joint replacement surgeries are advised on end-stage OA patients who have tried every other non-invasive methods and still have failed to improve. We can instead try other methods like Tai-Chi and physiotherapy first.

answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 04 - Osteoarthritis. OA treatment is staged first (early, late, end stage), then goes in order: non-pharmacologic, pharmacologic, surgical. Arthroplasty is a salvage procedure for end-stage disease no longer controlled by other therapies, and early OA starts with active, neuromuscular-control exercise (Tai Chi is the lecture's example), weight loss and assistive devices.

  • A fails: early-stage disease is not an indication for replacement.
  • B fails: the notes say only arthroplasty has real benefit; arthroscopy is not recommended.
  • C fails: early OA is actively treated (exercise, weight management, topical NSAIDs), not just watched.

stem: Which of the following should we try to avoid for medical treatment of early-middle stage OA?
answer:
The correct answer is E. We should generally avoid tramadol (opioid).

stem: Which of the following affects Sacroiliac joints?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 02 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The lecture's rule is flat: whenever the sacroiliac joint is involved, think seronegative spondyloarthropathy (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, IBD-associated, reactive). Axial disease with asymmetric large peripheral joints is their pattern, and inflammatory back pain (better with movement, worse in the second half of the night) goes with it.

  • A, B fail: CTD arthritis and RA are symmetric small- and large-joint peripheral diseases.
  • D fails: OA targets weight-bearing joints, the 1st CMC and DIPs; its spine disease is facet OA, not sacroiliitis.

From 02 - Approach to Polyarthritis. The distribution table is the discriminator: MCP joints point to RA, and the DIP joints are usually SPARED in RA and other connective tissue diseases. Symmetric small- and large-joint involvement completes the RA pattern.

stem: A 68-year-old man with diabetes has had a foot ulcer for several months. It is now infected, with erythema and purulence but no systemic features. Because the ulcer is chronic, the infection is likely polymicrobial. Which antibiotic is most appropriate?
answer: The correct answer is E. A wound alone does not mean infection. Mild, monomicrobial infections (S. aureus, S. pyogenes) can be treated with cefazolin; chronic ulcers are more likely polymicrobial (including gram-negatives) and need amoxicillin-clavulanate. Pip-tazo is for Pseudomonas. Start imaging with x-ray, then MRI for osteomyelitis; debridement is often needed.

stem: A 70-year-old man has a hot, red, swollen knee and a fever. Aspiration shows cloudy fluid with gram-positive cocci in clusters. He has no MRSA risk factors. Along with blood cultures, what is the most appropriate management?

options.html: Oral cephalexin and repeat aspiration in a week

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.html: Lyme arthritis after a tick bite
Acute gouty arthritis of the knee

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes do not name the diagnosis in the case itself; the answer table that follows does, where disseminated gonococcal infection is tenosynovitis, dermatitis with a pustular rash, and polyarthralgia in the young with multiple partners (gonococcal arthritis: large-joint monoarthritis, knee, wrist, ankle). Workup: blood culture, gonorrhea NAAT or culture of urine, rectum and throat, joint fluid (positive in 50%); treatment ceftriaxone for 10-14 days. Lyme arthritis (A) is a large-joint monoarthritis without a pustular rash. Reactive arthritis (C) follows a gut or genitourinary infection by days to weeks, with conjunctivitis and urethritis. Gout (D) gives urate crystals, which the notes say distinguish it from septic arthritis.

The lecture, severe infections: exclude necrotizing fasciitis, blood cultures, swab only if a good (deeper) specimen can be obtained, consider calling orthopedics (or vascular), and start piperacillin-tazobactam (± vancomycin if MRSA history or risks). Oral cefazolin-class drugs (A) are for mild, monomicrobial infection, and a superficial swab always grows bacteria. Amoxicillin-clavulanate (B) covers a chronic polymicrobial ulcer but not a severe infection, and antibiotics alone will not save you. Imaging starts with an X-ray, and a severe infection is not left untreated for it (D).

A tagged white cell scan right away
An MRI of the foot before antibiotics
Blood cultures and a deep specimen

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. For a severe diabetic foot infection the lecture sends blood cultures and takes a swab only when a good deep specimen can be had 01 - MSK Infections. stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Serum uric acid, then treat as gout
MRI of the knee before aspirating
A plain X-ray of the knee on its own

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. A hot, red, swollen joint is infected until the fluid says otherwise, so it is aspirated and the fluid sent for the 3 C's (cell count, culture with Gram stain, crystals), along with blood cultures, blood count, creatinine and CRP 08 - Acute Monoarthritis 01 - MSK Infections. Type 2 diabetes is a risk factor for septic arthritis, and he cannot bear weight.

  • B: uric acid can be normal during a gout attack and high uric acid alone does not diagnose gout; only crystals in the fluid prove it.
  • C: imaging is optional in the septic arthritis workup; it does not replace or delay the aspirate.
  • D: an X-ray cannot tell infection from crystals; the needle decides.

stem:
A 45 yo M presents to hospital with new onset lumbar back pain. He reports the pain is 10/10. Yesterday morning he had fever and chills. He does not report any lower limb weakness, or bladder or bowel dysfunction. He has a history of opioid use, and reports injecting drugs.

Which three investigations are most useful now? (the module poses no question here; this line is written for this bank)
answer: The correct answers are A, B, and C. CBC, CRP and blood cultures will help to determine the presence of an infection and the causative agent, and CBC and CRP may need to be monitored over time to assess his progress with treatment. CK and urine culture will not be helpful in making the diagnosis of infection (particularly in the absence of any urinary symptoms). Urine tox screen may be needed for other reasons, but will not help elucidate the cause of his current symptoms.

stem: Moishe is a 62 yo M with type 2 diabetes. His most recent A1C was 9.2%. He is prescribed Metformin 1 g PO BID, but often forgets to take it. He recently started a new job as a grocery store cashier, and now spends 8 hours per shift on his feet. He wears running shoes to work that he ties tightly so they don't rub his feet. He purchased some new foot orthotics as recommended by his podiatrist. Each night he inspects his feet. Which of the following are significant steps that Moishe has taken to prevent the development of diabetic foot ulcer? (choose all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are A, C, and D. Visiting a professional who can care for the feet is very helpful in preventing diabetic foot ulcers. This ensures regular foot checks (in addition to those that Moishe is doing on his own) and quick response to any developing issues. Orthoses can help protect any vulnerable areas of the feet from breakdown. Just having a metformin prescription doesn't help overly - regular compliance with the recommended dose will!

stem: A 52-year-old man has an exquisitely painful, red first MTP joint that started overnight after a weekend of heavy drinking. Aspiration shows urate crystals. His serum uric acid today is normal. What should be done about the uric acid level?

options.html: Nothing more; a normal level excludes gout
Start allopurinol today to lower it
Repeat it once the attack has settled
Repeat it daily until it rises

answer: The correct answer is C. Serum uric acid can be normal during an acute gout attack, so check it during and again after the attack. The diagnosis rests on urate crystals in joint fluid. Triggers follow SMARTS (surgery, mechanical injury, alcohol, recent illness, travel, starting or stopping allopurinol); allopurinol prevents recurrence but is not started for the acute attack.

stem: A 78-year-old woman with knee osteoarthritis develops an acutely swollen, warm knee over a day and a low-grade fever. Aspiration shows rhomboid-shaped crystals and a negative gram stain. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Pseudogout (CPPD) is caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals, typically in older patients with OA, most often the knee. It is less intense than gout but lasts longer, and can cause fever, so it must be separated from sepsis by aspiration. Rhomboid crystals = CPPD; needle-shaped crystals = gout. Treat like gout (indomethacin, IA or oral steroid).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Williams' sore ankle: 62 yr old man, lives alone. Has diabetes (Metformin & Glyburide). Right knee has been replaced due to osteoarthritis. Not feeling well, left ankle has recently become much more painful, warm, and red. Recent pedicure for diabetes. Physical: temp 38.6 C, flushed and in pain. Left ankle is warm, red, and extremely painful. Cannot put much weight on the ankle.

stem: What do you want to do? (stem copied from the lecture; options written for this bank)

options.html: Check a serum uric acid and wait
Aspirate the joint and send the fluid
Inject a corticosteroid into the ankle

answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "Aspirate the joint (i.e. take a sample of fluid from the joint). IF THE JOINT IS RED, ASPIRATE IT!", and send it for the 3 C's: cell count, culture and sensitivity (with Gram stain), crystals. The differential for an acute hot, red monoarthritis is infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout, and he is febrile with diabetes and a prosthetic joint. A serum uric acid (A) cannot diagnose gout and may be normal during an attack. Allopurinol (B) is never started during an acute attack. Injecting a steroid (D) before infection is excluded treats the wrong disease: "to inject is human, to aspirate divine".

Not feeling well, left ankle has recently become much more painful, warm, and red. Recent pedicure for diabetes. Physical: temp 38.6 C, flushed and in pain. Left ankle is warm, red, and extremely painful. Cannot put much weight on the ankle. Joint aspirated. Cell count: 59 x 109 cells/L (inflammatory). Crystals: Negative. Gram Stain: Gram +ve cocci in clusters. Culture: Pending.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture sends him to the emergency department with "Suspected left ankle infection": septic arthritis, a medical emergency. Gram-positive cocci in clusters are staphylococci, 60%+ of septic arthritis, and his risks are systemic (diabetes, age) and local (a prosthetic joint). Gout (B) needs needle-shaped negatively birefringent crystals, and pseudogout (C) rhomboid positively birefringent ones; the crystals are negative. Reactive arthritis (D) is one of the rare causes and has no organisms in the joint.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Williams, above: suspected left ankle infection, Gram-positive cocci in clusters, culture pending, orthopedics consulted.

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management? (the notes reveal the management without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: Inject the ankle with a corticosteroid, then discharge home
Admit, urgent incision and drainage, empiric IV antibiotics
Oral colchicine, then review in the clinic in one week's time
Oral antibiotics at home until the culture result comes back

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes: admitted to hospital, taken to the OR that evening for urgent incision and drainage (I&D), "an infected joint is actually an infection in a closed space and usually requires drainage", started on empiric IV cefotaxime, with analgesia and rest. Then repeat I&D until the surgeon is confident the joint is clean, and IV antibiotics for 4-6 weeks. The MSK Infections lecture gives the usual empiric choice as cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, or vancomycin + ceftriaxone. A steroid injection (A) and colchicine (C) treat crystal arthritis; oral antibiotics at home (D) leave a closed-space infection undrained in an emergency that can quickly cause fulminant joint damage.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mike's Toe Woes: 48 yr old married man. Works at Labatt Brewery. Hypertensive (high blood pressure) on 25 mg Hydrochlorothiazide. Two days post cholecystectomy severe pain, swelling and redness 1st MTP joint. No HCT for 2 days. Similar episode on a trip to Mexico 2 years ago. Took OTC medication which helped. The joint is aspirated. Cell Count: 15 x 109 cells per litre (inflammatory). Culture: No growth at 24 hours. Crystals: Needle shaped negatively bi-refringent crystals.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The case's answer: "Diagnosis: Acute Gout", an acute inflammatory arthritis caused by uric acid crystal deposition in the joint. Needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals prove it; the big toe (1st MTP) is affected in 50%; he is a man of 35-50 on a diuretic, with alcohol exposure, and the trigger is surgery (SMARTS). Pseudogout (A) has rhomboid, positively birefringent crystals and favours the knee of an older person. The culture shows no growth, against septic arthritis (B). Cellulitis (C) does not put crystals in the joint fluid.

stem: Which of the following should NOT be started during this acute attack? (the lecture teaches the acute treatment without posing a question; stem written for this bank)
answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: allopurinol (a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, "turning off the tap") is "Do Not Start During an Acute Attack"; when it is started later, it is covered with an NSAID or colchicine and aims for the lower limit of the laboratory reference range. The acute attack is "mopped up" first with an intra-articular corticosteroid, indomethacin 50 mg PO TID (B), colchicine 0.6 mg PO q8h (C) or prednisone 30 mg OD x 2 days then reduced by 5 mg every 2 days (D).

preamble.html: Mary's Sore Knees: 78 year old woman lives with her husband. Has diabetes (Metformin). Has hypercholesterolemia. Has had mild chronic bilateral knee pain which has been worse with activity. After a recent brisk walk developed severe right sided knee pain and significant swelling. On examination the right knee is very swollen and noticeably warm and mildly red. She has difficulty flexing the right knee past 100 degrees. The left knee has a small effusion, it is cool and has slightly reduced flexion. Otherwise early changes of osteoarthritis (degenerative arthritis) in the hands. The knee is aspirated. Cell Count: 18 x 10^9 cells per litre (inflammatory). Culture: No growth at 24 hours. Crystals: Rhomboid shaped intracellular positively bi-refringent crystals.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The notes: "Diagnosis: Acute Pseudogout", an acute inflammatory arthritis caused by calcium pyrophosphate crystals. Rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent crystals prove it; it favours older people with osteoarthritis, and the knee is the most common joint. Gout (A) gives needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. The culture shows no growth (B). Osteoarthritis (D) is not inflammatory and gives a cool joint, while this fluid is inflammatory with crystals.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Inject a steroid into the knee
Admit for I&D and IV cefazolin

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. The lecture treats an attack of pseudogout with rest, ice, elevation and hydration plus a corticosteroid injected into the joint, an NSAID such as indomethacin, or a prednisone taper 08 - Acute Monoarthritis. The injection is safe here because the fluid has shown the crystals and the culture has not grown anything.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Sam is a 2-year-old male presenting to the Emergency Department with a new onset limp. He is previously healthy, but does have language delay and is awaiting an audiology appointment. Mom reports he had an upper respiratory tract infection ~2 weeks ago, with low grade fevers at that time. On exam, he is afebrile and looks well. Mucous membranes are moist. Cardiac exam shows a II/VI SEM at the LLSB border. Respiratory and abdominal exams are benign. He is reluctant to have his legs examined, and does seem to favour the left. He walks with an antalgic gait.

stem: The most appropriate treatment is?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain, "Transient Synovitis"): it "occurs 7-10 days after viral infection", the child "walks with limp", is "afebrile/low grade fever (<38)" and appears "non-toxic". The treatment slide reads "NSAIDs" and "self resolves in 7-10 days". Ibuprofen is the NSAID. The murmur and the language delay are distractors.

  • A Antibiotics treat a septic joint. The MSK Infections slides (Devlin) give the red flags for infection as fever, pain and a significant loss of motion; Sam is afebrile, well and walking.
  • C The slides' "self resolves" makes reassurance part of the conversation, which makes it the closest competitor, but the only treatment the slide names is the NSAID.
  • D Incision and drainage is for septic arthritis.

The same deck's "Hip pain in children" table puts transient synovitis first in the under 4 column, so Sam's age fits.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Jane is a 3-year-old female who is being seen for a limp. Dad believes Jane began complaining of leg pain about 1 month ago. Jane began limping yesterday afternoon. Dad does not believe there has been an injury.

stem: What is the biggest "do not miss" question on history?
answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain, "Hip pain in children"): under 4 years the "uncommon" causes are leukemia, eosinophilic granuloma and metastatic neuroblastoma. Slides (Berard, Pediatric Arthritis, "Red Flags"): the features that "should prompt clinicians to consider an alternate diagnosis" open with "Constitutional symptoms" and include night time pain causing sleep disturbance. A month of leg pain, now a limp, and no injury is the story where malignancy must be excluded, and constitutional symptoms are how you ask about it.

  • B Travel and sick contacts point to infection, which matters, but a month-long course in a child not described as unwell makes malignancy the bigger miss.
  • C and D are routine history, not a question aimed at a specific dangerous diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are seeing Jason, a 9-month-old boy, in the emergency department after he fell off the bed. He has bruising on his right cheek and is refusing to move his right leg. He cries in discomfort when you attempt to manipulate the leg. His exam is otherwise unremarkable. His CBC shows a white cell count of 12x10⁹/L.hemoglobin of 120g/L, and platelets of 365*10⁹/L. CRP is slightly elevated at 6 mg/L. His XR is shown: a fracture of the right femur. (the source's image is not reproduced; finding described from the case and session notes)

stem: Most appropriate next step is?
answer:
The correct answer is A. The slides name the concern but not the step. Slides (Cassidy, Pediatric Orthopedics, "Pediatric MSK Trauma"): the mechanisms include "NAI infants/toddlers"; Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, "Hip pain in children"): non-accidental injury is in the under-4 column. The paper's own tutor note settles the reading: "a femur fracture in a non-walking child is NAI until proven otherwise". The slides do not say what to do next; admission rests on the session notes ("admit him so he's safe"), with a skeletal survey and a head CT and a report to child protection, and the fracture treated in a spica cast.

  • B A cast is the right fracture treatment, but sending him home with follow-up returns him to an unsafe setting before abuse is excluded.
  • C Orthopedics will be involved, but a consult alone does not address his safety, which is the point of the question.
  • D An infant femur fracture is casted; it does not need urgent surgery.

⚠ The skeletal survey, head CT and admission are from the session notes; no MSK slide deck covers the non-accidental injury workup.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are seeing a 3-year-old child with an ongoing complaint of being clumsy. He was born at term and is otherwise healthy. He started walking at 14 months of age. Physical exam reveals a well grown child with the following deformity: bowed legs (genu varum), read in the session notes as tibia vara (Blount's disease) with medial beaking of the proximal tibia. (the source's image is not reproduced; finding described from the case and session notes)

stem: The most appropriate initial treatment is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. The slides do not cover Blount's disease or its treatment, so the key rests on the session notes: "under about 3, or early stage: a brace (KAFO); persistent or advanced: proximal tibial osteotomy". What the slides do give is the age rule. Slides (Cassidy, Pediatric Orthopedics, "Angular Variation"): genu varum is "normal from birth to 2 years old" and genu valgum is "normal from 3 to 7 years old", so a 3-year-old should be heading into knock knees, not still bowed. The "Angular Variation Warning Signs" slide lists progressive genu varum and asymmetry. Bowing at 3 with medial beaking is outside the normal pattern, and the brace is the first step for early tibia vara.

  • B Reassurance fits physiologic bowing, which the slide limits to birth to 2. The deck's "avoid overtreatment of normal variants" applies only if this is a normal variant, and at 3 with beaking it is not.
  • C Surgery (proximal tibial osteotomy) is for persistent or advanced disease, not the first step (the session notes).
  • D Clumsiness here is the bowing, and nothing in the case suggests injury or abuse.

flags.title: Slides silent on treatment
flags.html: The slides settle only that bowing at 3 is outside the normal window. Bracing rests on the session notes and the Blount's disease condition note. If the image showed plain physiologic bowing, the slides' normal-variant rule would argue B, so the key depends on the image showing tibia vara, as the session notes say.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: An 8-year-old boy presents to the Emergency Department with a 1 day history of fever and refusal to walk. His symptoms started yesterday, when he developed a low grade fever of 38.3C, and pain in his right knee. Today he is refusing to weight bear, complains of severe pain in his right hip and knee and his temperature was 39.8C when mom took it in the morning. On exam, he looks unwell. Heart rate is 130 bpm, blood pressure 102 /68, respiratory rate is 20. Temperature is 39.7C. He is holding his right hip flexed and externally rotated.

stem: The most important diagnostic test is:
answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Red Flags for Infection"): fever, pain and a significant reduction in motion, all present here, so this is septic arthritis of the hip until proven otherwise. The "Investigating" slide lists CBC, electrolytes, creatinine, CRP, blood cultures, joint aspirate and imaging, and the next slide, "Interpreting a joint aspirate", reads the cell count, microscopy and Gram stain. Only the aspirate examines the joint itself and finds the organism. The Kocher criteria are from the session notes; the slides do not name them.

  • A The CBC is on the slide's list but rises in any infection or inflammation; the transient synovitis slide (Stiller-Moldovan) shows blood work only slightly abnormal in a non-infected hip too.
  • B Blood cultures are on the list, but they do not prove the hip is the source.
  • D The slides list imaging as "+/-" in septic arthritis, and the osteomyelitis imaging slide calls X-ray "not sensitive enough".

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 8-year-old boy above, febrile and unwell, holding his right hip flexed and externally rotated: septic arthritis of the hip.

stem: Referring to the above case, appropriate empiric antibiotic choice would be:
answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Empiric Therapy", septic arthritis): "Ancef 2g IV q 8h vs Vancomycin 15mg/kg & Ceftriaxone 2g IV". Ancef is cefazolin, the first of the slide's two choices. The organism slides put Staphylococcus aureus first, with group A streptococcus among the rarer causes, and the pediatric slide reads "S. aureus (!) always". The session notes add that cefazolin is the Canadian choice for children over 3 months because MRSA is uncommon here; that age cut-off is from the session notes, not the slides.

  • A On the slides ceftriaxone is a partner to vancomycin in the alternative regimen, and alone for gonococcal and Lyme arthritis, not the empiric drug for a child's septic hip.
  • B Vancomycin appears only paired with ceftriaxone in the alternative regimen; it is not first-line on its own.
  • C Ciprofloxacin is not on any of the slides' regimens and does not reliably cover S. aureus or streptococci.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: You are seeing a 6-week-old baby boy for a well -baby check. Weight is 5kg, height is 59cm and head circumference is 37cm. The child is breastfed and takes 400IU of vitamin D daily. You note the following on exam: a positive Galeazzi sign, the knees at unequal heights with the hips and knees flexed. (the source's image is not reproduced; finding described from the case and session notes)

stem: The next best step in management is:
answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Cassidy, Pediatric Orthopedics, "Physical Exam" for DDH): leg length discrepancy is tested with the Galeazzi test. "DDH Management": "Diagnose early!", "prevent long-term disability", and treatment by age, starting with the Pavlik harness (up to 6 months), then closed reduction and spica cast, then open reduction. Every treatment on the slide is orthopedic, and at 6 weeks he is inside the harness window.

  • B Waiting a month works against the slide's "diagnose early" and spends harness time.
  • C The slides do not mention hip ultrasound. The session notes say orthopedics will arrange it, so the referral is the step the slides support.
  • D MRI is not on the slides' DDH workup.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 6-week-old boy above has a positive Galeazzi sign: one hip is already dislocated.

stem: If the left limb were affected in the above case, you would expect:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Cassidy, Pediatric Orthopedics, "Physical Exam - Ortolani Test"): "Sign of entry", a "reduction test for dislocated hip": thigh lifted and abducted, positive "if head of femur felt to slip back into acetabulum". A hip that is already out, as the Galeazzi sign shows, is the hip Ortolani finds.

  • A Slides ("Physical Exam - Barlow Test"): "Sign of exit", a "dislocation test for reduced but dislocatable hip". This one is already out.
  • C Galant is a newborn reflex, not a hip test (the session notes; the slides do not mention it).
  • D The case already shows a positive Galeazzi sign.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: An 8 year old boy presents with a gradual onset of left hip pain. The pain began approximately 4 weeks ago and involved the left groin. The child describes the pain as intermittent in nature. He remembers falling while playing at recess about a month ago. Mom reports intermittent episodes of tactile fever during this time. In terms of past medical history, he was diagnosed with Type I DM at 3 years of age. He is currently on an insulin pump. His HbA1C was checked at his last clinic appointment was 8.6%. He is on no other medications, his immunizations are up to date and he has no allergies. He lives at home with both parents and a healthy 5 year old sister. On exam, the child looks well and vitals are stable. Cardiac, respiratory and abdominal exams are within normal limits. He weight bears with an antalgic gait. On examination of the left leg, there is decreased range of motion at the left hip.

stem: Which of the following is the least likely diagnosis:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections): septic arthritis sits under "Acute Monoarthritis", and its red flags are fever, pain and a significant loss of motion. A 4-week, gradual, intermittent course in a well child who still bears weight does not fit an acute septic joint.

  • A Osteomyelitis stays on the list. Slides (Devlin, "Pediatric Population"): hematogenous seeding, "typically < 12 years of age", in the metaphysis, with "S. aureus (!) always"; he has diabetes and intermittent fevers.
  • C Perthes fits best. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain): age 4-8, gradual onset hip pain, appears well, limited internal rotation and abduction.
  • D Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, "Hip pain in children"): leukemia is "uncommon" but listed in every age column.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 8 year old boy with type 1 diabetes has 4 weeks of gradual, intermittent left groin pain, tactile fevers, an antalgic gait and less left hip motion. He looks well.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain, "Leg Calve Perthes Investigations"): "Xray, AP and frog leg lateral" comes first, then bone scan and MRI; the slipped capital femoral epiphysis slide also opens with X-ray (AP and lateral). In a well child with weeks of hip pain and lost motion, that is where the workup starts.

  • A, B, C Blood work will be sent, given the fevers, but none of it images the hip, and none is the first item on either slide.

⚠ The session notes record that a group could argue for the CBC because of the fevers; the slides' investigation lists start with the X-ray.

stem: Which investigation is likely to lead to a diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain): the transient synovitis slide shows blood work that is nonspecific ("CBC usually N", "ESR/CRP slightly elevated"), while the Perthes staging slide (initial, fragmentation, re-ossification, healed) is read on the X-ray. Imaging is what names the diagnosis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 8 year old boy with 4 weeks of left hip pain. CBC shows a mildly elevated WBC at 15.2*10⁹/L (normal 5*10⁹/L -10 10⁹/L), normal hemoglobin and platelets. ESR is normal. CRP is mildy elevated at 10mg/L (normal <5mg/L). XR is shown: the left femoral head is flattened, sclerotic and fragmented, and the epiphysis is collapsed rather than slipped. *(the source's image is not reproduced; finding described from the case and session notes)

stem: You confidently diagnosis the child with?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain, "Leg Calve Perthes"): "Idiopathic avascular necrosis of the proximal femoral epiphysis", age 4-8, gradual onset, appears well, limited internal rotation and abduction; the staging slide runs initial, fragmentation, re-ossification, healed. A fragmented, collapsed head in a well 8-year-old is that disease.

  • A Slides ("Slipped Capital Femoral Epiphysis"): a shifting of the epiphysis posterior and inferior on the femoral neck, ages 8-15, peaking at about 14 in boys. The head here is collapsed, not slipped.
  • B Slides (Devlin, "Pediatric Population"): children's osteomyelitis seeds the metaphysis; a normal ESR and a collapsed epiphysis argue against it.
  • D Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (Berard slides) presents in the slides' case as months of joint swelling and a morning limp, and does not flatten and fragment one femoral head.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 8 year old boy has Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease of the left hip.

stem: Most appropriate treatment:
answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Stiller-Moldovan, Pediatric Hip Pain, "Leg Calve Perthes Treatments"): the non-operative list is close observation, activity restriction or modification, crutches, wheelchair or bracing, non-weight-bearing activities, "PT/OT: ROM & strengthening" and analgesics (NSAIDs, Tylenol). Physiotherapy is the only option here that is on that list.

  • A The same slide lists surgical management (hip arthroplasty, femoral or pelvic osteotomy, hip arthrodiastasis) separately, without saying who needs it. The session notes give the surgical group as roughly over 8 with more than 50% of the head involved, or losing motion; he sits right at that age, so expect a tutor to raise it. That cut-off is from the session notes, not the slides.
  • C Nothing here needs antibiotics: the head is avascular, not infected.
  • D Steroids are not on the slide's treatment list.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 32-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by EMS after a motor vehicle collision. He complains of tingling in his foot. The leg is shortened and internally rotated.

stem: Which diagnosis heads the differential? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)
answer:
The correct answer is C. The slides rule out the fractures but do not describe a hip dislocation. Slides (Clinical Approach to the Hip, "Hip Fracture Presentation"): a hip fracture leaves the limb "(shortened), externally rotated and abducted", so an internally rotated leg is not a fracture. The same deck's trauma step tells you, in a young high-velocity patient, to check nerve function "(especially sciatic nerve)", which fits the tingling foot. That a posterior dislocation gives a shortened, internally rotated, adducted leg comes from 03.2 - Clinical Approach to the Hip Joint and 03.1 - Anatomy of the Hip Joint, not the slides.

  • A An anterior dislocation leaves the leg externally rotated, abducted and flexed (lecture note; not on the slides).
  • B and D Slides: a hip fracture is shortened, externally rotated and abducted, and the deck frames it as the older faller's injury.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 32-year-old man from the collision has a shortened, internally rotated leg. His pelvis and hip films are up, and you are asked to describe them to the orthopedic resident over the phone. (the source's image is not reproduced; the question tests the description method the session taught)

stem: In which order should you describe the X-ray? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Views, location, fracture type, displacement, joint surface and other findings
Displacement first, then the views obtained, then the fracture type and location
Soft tissue swelling first, then the diagnosis, then the views that were obtained
The diagnosis first, then any findings on the film that support that diagnosis

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Del Balso, Fracture/Complications Review, "Describing an XR"): 1. anatomic region and views, 2. regional location, 3. fracture orientation/type, 4. displacement, 5. other findings, where displacement is the "DISTAL relative to PROXIMAL" fragment and other findings are intra-articular extension, an open fracture and hardware. Slides (Kalia, Fracture Imaging and Interpretation, "Fracture Description"): the same order with joint surface involvement as its own step 5, then other findings and bone quality, and a "Joint Involvement: Subluxation/Dislocation" slide, so a dislocation is reported under the joint.

  • B Displacement is step 4 on both decks; it means nothing until the listener knows which bone and which part.
  • C The review deck tells you to check soft tissues ("often forgotten"), but they are not where the description starts.
  • D Leading with the diagnosis skips the description both decks lay out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 32-year-old man after a high-velocity collision has a posterior hip dislocation and tingling in his foot.

stem: What are the next steps in management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Order bone mineral density testing and start an osteoporosis workup before anything else
Book him for a total hip arthroplasty within 24-48 hours, the standard for hip injuries
Skin traction, bed rest and analgesia, with a repeat X-ray of the hip in 6 weeks
Airway, breathing, circulation, a pelvic fracture check, and distal pulse and sciatic checks

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Clinical Approach to the Hip, "Approach to Suspected Hip Fracture", step 2): "Is the patient stable?" Stability is "especially important to assess in a traumatic fracture in someone young (high velocity, high trauma injuries) - ABCs"; "Is there a pelvic fracture? Vascular injury? Nerve injury?"; "Check distal pulses and nerve function (especially sciatic nerve)". Slides (Fracture Management and Complications Part 1): step 1 is "Resuscitation as needed" because "bones bleed, and sharp edges can cause vascular trauma".

  • A Slides (Hip, step 3): the osteoporosis workup is for a fragility fracture, not a 32-year-old in a collision.
  • B Slides (Hip): "surgical fixation within 24-48 hours" is the standard for hip fractures, and arthroplasty is for a displaced femoral neck fracture.
  • C Leaving a dislocated hip out for weeks is on none of the slides' plans.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 32-year-old man has been resuscitated. His sciatic nerve function is documented. The X-ray shows a posterior hip dislocation.

stem: How is this injury definitively managed? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Total hip arthroplasty, replacing both the femoral head and the acetabulum
Closed reduction under sedation, a post-reduction X-ray, and fixation of any joint fragment
Bed rest and traction until the femoral head settles back into the acetabulum on its own
Immobilise the hip in a spica cast in its current position, without reducing it

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Fracture Management and Complications Part 1): obtain a reduction (closed: "adequate analgesia and sedation", longitudinal traction exaggerating the deformity, then reverse it), maintain it, and "Obtain post-reduction X-rays" to check the reduction is adequate and held. Slides (Cassidy, Pediatric Orthopedics, "Trauma Treatment") apply the same steps to "closed reduction of dislocations or fractures", with "always get post-reduction/casting films!". Slides (Kalia, "Joint Surface Involvement"): an intra-articular fracture's "reduction must be anatomic", which for a displaced fragment means open reduction and internal fixation.

  • A Slides (Hip, "Femoral Neck Fractures"): arthroplasty is for a displaced femoral neck fracture, not a young man's dislocated hip.
  • C A dislocated hip does not reduce itself.
  • D Holding a joint that is still dislocated preserves the deformity.

flags.title: Reasoned from general principles
flags.html: No slide gives a hip-dislocation-specific plan (for example a time limit for reduction). This answer rests on the slides' general reduce, hold, check sequence and the intra-articular rule.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 32-year-old man has had his posterior hip dislocation reduced after a high-energy collision. He had tingling in his foot at presentation.

stem: Which three complications are common to this injury? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head, sciatic nerve injury, heterotopic ossification
Femoral nerve palsy, non-union of the scaphoid, and chronic olecranon bursitis of the elbow
Carpal tunnel syndrome, adhesive capsulitis of the shoulder, and an ulnar claw hand
Gout of the hip, septic arthritis of the knee, and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease

answer:
The correct answer is A. No slide lists hip dislocation complications as such; the key is assembled from the general complication slides. Slides (Fracture Management and Complications Part 3, "Avascular necrosis"): most common in the femoral head, talus and scaphoid, which all have a "retrograde blood supply". Slides (Part 3, "Heterotopic ossification"): risk factors include polytrauma, and the "joints most at risk: hip, knee, elbow". Slides (Clinical Approach to the Hip, step 2): after high-velocity trauma in the young, check nerve function "(especially sciatic nerve)", which is the nerve his tingling foot points to.

  • B The femoral nerve is not the nerve at risk behind the hip, and the other two are wrist and elbow problems.
  • C These are upper limb conditions.
  • D These are not complications of trauma; Perthes is a childhood disease.

flags.title: Not post-traumatic arthritis
flags.html: Slides (Part 3, "Post-traumatic Arthritis"): "Uncommon in hip and knee", "very common with ankle fractures (>50%)". It is left out of the key for that reason, even though many outside sources list it after hip dislocation.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 67-year-old woman presents to the emergency department after a fall on ice while shoveling her driveway. She has pain in her left lower extremity and is unable to weightbear.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Acute gout, pseudogout and septic arthritis of the ankle joint
Hip fracture, tibial or fibular shaft fracture, ankle fracture
Plantar fasciitis, Achilles tendinopathy and Morton's neuroma
Deep vein thrombosis, lower leg cellulitis and chronic lymphedema

answer:
The correct answer is B. An older person who falls and cannot bear weight has a fracture until shown otherwise. Slides (Clinical Approach to the Hip, "Hip Fracture Presentation"): onset "sudden, after a fall/trauma", "unable to weight bear", and "high suspicion in the elderly even if pain is minimal or trauma was minimal". Slides (Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, "Ottawa Foot and Ankle Rules"): "inability to bear weight both immediately and in emergency department" is a trigger for an ankle X-ray series.

  • A These are atraumatic causes of a hot joint.
  • C These are overuse foot problems, not an injury from a fall.
  • D These are swelling and skin causes, not why someone cannot stand after a fall.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 67-year-old woman who fell on ice has an ankle series: AP, lateral and mortise views. There is a fracture of the lateral malleolus. (the source's image is not reproduced; the question tests how the fracture is described)

stem: What determines the Weber type of her fibular fracture? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Whether the fibular fracture line is transverse, oblique or spiral on the AP view
How far the distal fragment is displaced or angulated relative to the proximal one
The level of the fibular fracture relative to the tibiofibular syndesmosis
Whether the skin over the fracture is broken, making it an open fracture

answer:
The correct answer is C. The Weber classification is not on any slide deck available for checking: the Lower Extremity Radiology deck is not in the OCR set, and none of the other decks name Weber. The key rests on 02 - Lower Extremity Radiology: Weber grades a lateral malleolus fracture by its level against the syndesmosis: A below (usually stable, walking boot for 6 weeks), B at (depends on the medial malleolus and deltoid ligament), C above (unstable, usually open reduction and internal fixation). Slides (Kalia, Fracture Imaging and Interpretation, "Special views") do list the ankle mortise view.

  • A Slides (Del Balso review and Kalia): orientation/type is its own step in the description and does not set the Weber type.
  • B Slides: displacement (distal relative to proximal) is a separate descriptor.
  • D Slides (Kalia): an open fracture is listed under "other findings", a separate label.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 67-year-old woman's X-rays show a displaced ankle fracture, and the ankle is visibly deformed. (⚠ assumed for this question: the handout's X-rays are not reproduced and it does not state the findings, so the fracture is taken as displaced to give one answer)

stem: What are the next steps in management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Walking boot and weight-bearing as tolerated
MRI of the ankle before anything else is done
Leave the ankle as it lies until the swelling settles, then reassess it in clinic
Analgesia, closed reduction and a splint, then a post-reduction X-ray

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Fracture Management and Complications Part 1): obtain a reduction ("adequate analgesia and sedation", longitudinal traction exaggerating the deformity, then reverse it), maintain the reduction (casting/splinting among the options), and "Obtain post-reduction X-rays" to verify the reduction is adequate and is being maintained.

  • A A boot with weight-bearing is the plan for a stable, undisplaced Weber A fracture (02 - Lower Extremity Radiology; not on the slides).
  • B Plain films have already made the diagnosis; MRI adds delay and is on none of the slides' fracture steps.
  • C Slides (Part 1): reduction is needed whenever the fracture is displaced; a deformed ankle is reduced now, not left out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 67-year-old woman's ankle has been reduced and splinted. Her films show both malleoli fractured, with the fibular fracture above the syndesmosis. (⚠ assumed for this question: the handout's X-rays are not reproduced and it does not state the pattern, so a bimalleolar Weber C fracture is taken to give one answer)

stem: How is this injury definitively managed? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Walking boot for 6 weeks, weight-bearing as tolerated

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Clinical Approach to the Ankle and Foot, "What if a Sprain Isn't Just a Sprain?"): a bimalleolar fracture (medial and lateral malleolus) "typically required surgical management", while a unimalleolar fracture "may be managed non-operatively (determined by stability of talus)". Slides (Fracture Management Part 1): surgical maintenance is internal fixation, ORIF. The Weber C reading (above the syndesmosis, unstable, usually ORIF) is from 02 - Lower Extremity Radiology; no available slide names Weber, so the bimalleolar slide is what settles the key.

  • B The boot is for a stable fracture; the slides keep non-operative care for the unimalleolar fracture with a stable talus.
  • C No fracture is casted for life; the cast would also not hold an unstable mortise.
  • D Slides (Part 1, step 5): physiotherapy is rehabilitation after the fracture is stabilised, not the fixation.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 67-year-old woman has had her ankle fracture fixed.

stem: What is the most common complication following this injury? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Heterotopic ossification around the ankle joint
Compartment syndrome of the anterior forearm

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Fracture Management and Complications Part 3, "Post-traumatic Arthritis"): arthritis after a peri-articular fracture, "Uncommon in hip and knee" but "Very common with ankle fractures (>50%)": pain, especially with weight-bearing, and reduced motion, managed like degenerative osteoarthritis.

  • A Slides (Part 3, "Avascular necrosis"): the talus is a retrograde-supply site, but the slides give no figure for it after an ankle fracture.
  • B Slides (Part 3, "Heterotopic ossification"): risk factors are polytrauma, head injury and burns, and the joints most at risk are the hip, knee and elbow, not the ankle.
  • D Slides (Part 3, "Compartment Syndrome"): most common in the lower leg or forearm, but a forearm compartment follows a forearm injury, not an ankle fracture.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: At the 6 week post-operative visit, the 67-year-old woman describes pain which is not being controlled by her routine analgesia. She has a swollen ankle, and foot with shiny, mottled skin. She has pain elicited by light touch, and extreme sensitivity to cold.

stem: What is the diagnosis? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Deep surgical site infection of the ankle

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Shoesmith, Neuropathic Pain, slide 10 "Complex regional pain syndromes (CRPS)"): "Focal tissue or nerve injury can uncommonly lead to a chronic pain syndrome associated with inflammatory and autonomic features", with pain "greater than expected from injury" that "lasts longer than typically healing would occur". The affected limb can have severe pain and allodynia, swelling, temperature changes, colour changes, and skin and hair changes; slide 11's photo shows oedema, discoloration and shiny skin. Pain from light touch is allodynia. Treatment is "challenging and requires multidisciplinary pain management". The CRPS slides are in the Neuro block deck, not the MSK chronic pain decks (Viana, Jarmain), which do not cover CRPS.

  • A Infection would bring a red, hot wound and fever, not touch-evoked pain and cold sensitivity.
  • C A clot swells the calf but does not change the skin texture or make light touch painful.
  • D Slides (Fracture Management Part 3): non-union is failure to heal in twice the expected time; at 6 weeks it is too early to call, and it does not cause allodynia.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. G. Gutna, 81, lives in a retirement home and comes to the emergency department with anterior right knee pain and swelling for three days. The pain is constant, worse with any activity and getting worse; ice and ibuprofen help a little. He has had right knee pain with activity for years, but this is worse. No injury. He has had chills but no fever, and is tired. No other joint hurts now; no rash, eye, bowel or urinary symptoms. History: hypertension, STEMI and triple bypass, atrial fibrillation, diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, left hip replacement, mild psoriasis in his 50s (in remission), BPH. Medications include apixaban 5 mg twice a day and ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily as needed. He drinks 1-2 beers a night.

stem: Based on Part 1, which is the best differential diagnosis for his right knee? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus, polymyalgia rheumatica
Meniscal tear, collateral ligament sprain, patellar fracture
Septic arthritis, pseudogout, gout, hemarthrosis, a flare of osteoarthritis
Deep vein thrombosis of the calf, cellulitis of the shin, and prepatellar bursitis of the knee

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Rohekar, Acute Monoarthritis): an acute monoarthritis is "a single inflamed joint for less than six weeks", and its differential is "Infection, Infection, Infection, Gout, Pseudogout". Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Acute Monoarthritis"): the list adds "Blood: Hemarthrosis", and the "Investigating" slide asks you to consider coagulopathy: he takes apixaban, so a bleed into the joint belongs on his list. Slides (Rohekar, Part 3): pseudogout affects "older individuals" who "often have associated osteoarthritis", and the knee is the most common joint, which fits his years of activity-related knee pain. His chills, diabetes and age keep infection at the top.

  • A These are systemic polyarthritides. He has one joint and no rash, eye or other joint symptoms.
  • B The MSK Infections slide does list trauma, but these are injuries and he denies any.
  • D None of these is an effusion in the joint, and the list leaves out septic arthritis, the diagnosis that must be excluded.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Gutna, 81, has three days of worsening right knee pain and swelling, with chills, on a background of years of activity-related knee pain. Exam: temperature 37.8 °C, pulse 90, BP 113/64, irregular rhythm. Bony enlargement at the DIPs of both hands. Left knee: bony enlargement and crepitus, no effusion, no warmth. Right knee: a small effusion, slightly warm, no redness, tender medial and lateral joint lines, positive ballottement, passive flexion only 0° to 70°. The left hip scar is well healed and non-tender.

stem: How does the examination refine the differential for the right knee? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: An osteoarthritis flare alone, explained by the bony changes in his hands and in his other knee, so no further workup is needed
An acute warm monoarthritis on an osteoarthritic knee: exclude septic arthritis first, and pseudogout leads the rest
Gout as the most likely cause, since he drinks beer every night and the effusion is warm
A psoriatic arthritis flare, since he has a history of psoriasis and a single swollen joint

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Appleton, Chronic Monoarthritis): the osteoarthritis effusion is "cool to similar temperature (not warm/hot)", so his cool, crepitant left knee and DIP enlargement are background osteoarthritis, but his warm right knee is not. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Red Flags for Infection"): fever, pain, "significant reduction in ROM", and he has a low-grade temperature and flexion only to 70°. Slides (Rohekar, Part 3): the "Mary's Sore Knees" case is the same picture (an older diabetic woman with activity-related knee pain, a warm swollen right knee, a cool left knee effusion and hand osteoarthritis), and it turns out to be acute pseudogout once infection is excluded by aspiration.

  • A Slides (Appleton): osteoarthritis "MUST NOT HAVE" other causes of arthritis, infections included, and a warm effusion with a temperature does not fit osteoarthritis alone.
  • C Slides (Rohekar, Part 2): the first attack of gout is in men aged 35 to 50, the 1st MTP in 50% of cases, and the risk factor is "excessive alcohol intake", not two beers a night. Warmth does not separate gout from infection or pseudogout ("it can look just like an infected joint!").
  • D His psoriasis has been in remission for decades, and Slides (Rohekar) keep psoriatic arthritis among "a couple of rare things", after infection and crystals.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Gutna, 81, with diabetes, has a warm right knee effusion, painful flexion limited to 70°, chills and a temperature of 37.8 °C, on a background of knee osteoarthritis. He takes apixaban.

stem: Which investigation is most important to order now? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A knee X-ray to look for chondrocalcinosis, and treat as pseudogout if it is present
An MRI of the right knee to look for a meniscal tear or spontaneous osteonecrosis of the knee before any procedure
A corticosteroid injection into the knee, then reassess the pain in 48 hours
Aspiration of the right knee for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystals, with blood cultures

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Boyd, Intra-articular Injections): "Always aspirate initial presentation of acute monoarthritis to rule out infection!", and send fluid for only three things, cell count, crystals, culture and Gram stain (C3G). Slides (Rohekar): "If the joint is red, aspirate it!", and the three teaching cases show why the fluid decides: the cell count is inflammatory in the septic ankle, the gout and the pseudogout alike, so the Gram stain and culture find infection and the crystals name the crystal disease. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Investigating"): CBC, lytes, creatinine, CRP, blood cultures, joint aspirate, with coagulopathy in mind. His knee is warm rather than red, which is why the Boyd slide's "always aspirate" is the one that applies.

  • A Slides (Rohekar, "Pseudogout vs Chondrocalcinosis"): chondrocalcinosis is "a radiographic finding" of calcium pyrophosphate in the cartilage; the diagnosis needs intracellular crystals in aspirated fluid, and an X-ray cannot exclude infection.
  • B Slides (Appleton): MRI in osteoarthritis is "almost never" used, only "when the diagnosis of osteoarthritis is in DOUBT"; it does not answer infection versus crystals.
  • C Slides (Rohekar): "To inject is human, to aspirate divine." Slides (Boyd): a "septic joint (or high suspicion)" is a contraindication to a steroid injection, so "wait until culture negative before injecting steroid". The same slide lists a bleeding disorder; his anticoagulant is not named there.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Gutna, 81, has a warm, swollen right knee. History: diet-controlled type 2 diabetes, years of right knee pain with activity, a left hip replacement, atrial fibrillation on apixaban, a childhood penicillin allergy, and a new relationship with a woman in his building.

stem: Which features of his history raise his risk of septic arthritis in the right knee? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: His age over 80, his diabetes and the existing arthritis in that knee
His penicillin allergy, his statin and his tamsulosin
His new sexual partner, which makes gonococcal arthritis the leading concern
His left hip replacement, a prosthetic joint that seeds infection to the other joints

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Devlin, MSK Infections, "Etiology"): the risk factors are "Immune compromise, T2DM, EtOH, Age (>80), IVDU, RA". Slides (Rohekar, "Risk Factors for Septic Arthritis"): the systemic factors include diabetics and the "very young or old", and the local factors include an "underlying joint abnormality (i.e. arthritis)". His right knee has years of osteoarthritic pain.

  • B None of these is on either slide's list; the medications that do count on the Rohekar slide are methotrexate, leflunomide, prednisone and the biologics. The penicillin allergy matters later, when choosing an antibiotic.
  • C Slides (Devlin, "Other Infectious Etiologies"): gonococcal arthritis is the exposure history of the "young, multiple partners, MSM". It is not his leading concern.
  • D Slides (Rohekar): a prosthetic joint is a local factor, so it raises the risk of infection in that joint. His hip scar is well healed and non-tender, and the knee is not a prosthesis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: During a difficult delivery, a 10 pound baby's shoulders get stuck behind the mother's pubic symphysis, and the obstetrician needs effort and maneuvers to free him. After delivery he cannot move his left upper limb: the shoulder is adducted and medially rotated, the elbow extended, the forearm pronated, the wrist dropped, but grip is normal and he can move his fingers.

stem: Where is the nerve lesion? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Radial nerve in the radial groove

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Martin, Neurovascular Supply to the Distal Upper Extremity, "Testing Myotomes & Dermatomes"): C5 deltoid and biceps, C6 biceps and wrist extensors, C8 finger flexors, T1 interossei. His lost movements are all C5-C6 (shoulder abduction and lateral rotation, elbow flexion, supination, wrist extension) and his C8-T1 movements (grip, fingers) are intact. Slides (Martin, Brachial Plexus): the superior trunk is formed by C5 and C6. The slides do not name the injury; the eponym Erb-Duchenne palsy and the "waiter's tip" come from the lecture's detailed notes and 01.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 2.

  • A C8 drives the finger flexors and T1 the interossei on the myotome slide; his grip is normal.
  • C Slides (Martin, Proximal Upper Extremity): the radial groove is a site at risk for the radial nerve, which drops the wrist but does not adduct and medially rotate the shoulder or stop elbow flexion.
  • D A median nerve lesion weakens grip and thumb opposition, and spares the shoulder.

Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The newborn with a superior trunk (C5-C6) injury holds the left shoulder adducted and medially rotated with the elbow extended.

stem: Which muscles have lost their supply to produce this posture? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Interossei, lumbricals, hypothenar muscles and the finger flexors
Triceps, anconeus, latissimus dorsi and the long finger extensors
Pectoralis major, teres major, subscapularis and latissimus dorsi
Deltoid, supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and biceps

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Martin, Brachial Plexus): the suprascapular nerve (C5,6) leaves the superior trunk, and the axillary nerve is C5,6. Slides (Martin, Proximal Upper Extremity): the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior compartment of the arm, and the bicipital reflex "tests integrity of C5 & C6". Slides (Payne, Nerve Injuries, "Radiculopathy: key terms"): the C6 myotome includes "deltoid, supra/infraspinatus, biceps". Lose the abductors and lateral rotators and the arm falls adducted and medially rotated; lose biceps and the elbow stays extended. The muscle-by-muscle supply (axillary to deltoid and teres minor, suprascapular to supraspinatus and infraspinatus) is from 01 - Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus; the slides give the nerves and roots.

  • A On the myotome slide these are C8 and T1 hand muscles; his grip is normal.
  • B Slides (Martin, myotomes): triceps and the finger extensors are C7, which the superior trunk does not carry.
  • C These are adductors and medial rotators, so losing them cannot produce an adducted, medially rotated arm. The Brachial Plexus deck does give the upper and lower subscapular nerves as C5,6, so subscapularis and teres major are weakened too, but that works against the posture; pectoralis major and latissimus dorsi keep supply from lower roots and pull the arm in.
