Case 2 (motorcyclist with a claw), prompt a. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 28-year-old falls off her motorcycle onto an outstretched right arm. She has a claw of the 4th and 5th digits: in those digits the metacarpophalangeal joints are hyperextended and the interphalangeal joints flexed. She cannot move her 5th digit at all and has no sensation over the 5th digit. The lab files this case under brachial plexus injury.

stem: Where do you expect the nerve injury to be? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Inferior trunk of the brachial plexus (C8-T1)
Superior trunk of the brachial plexus (C5-C6)
Median nerve in the carpal tunnel
Ulnar nerve at the elbow (medial epicondyle)

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Martin, Wrist & Hand Pt 2, "Nerve Lesions: Ulnar Nerve"): the 4th and 5th digit claw is the sign pictured for an ulnar nerve lesion, and the sites at risk are posterior to the medial epicondyle, between the 2 heads of flexor carpi ulnaris and Guyon's canal. Slides (Martin, Distal Upper Extremity, "Nervous Supply: Ulnar Nerve"): in the forearm the ulnar nerve supplies flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial part of flexor digitorum profundus; she cannot move her 5th digit at all, so those forearm branches are lost too, which puts the lesion at the elbow rather than at the wrist. An inferior trunk lesion would not stop at two digits: on the myotome slide C8 drives the finger flexors and T1 the interossei of the whole hand, and the root-contribution slide (Brachial Plexus) sends C8 and T1 into the median nerve as well.

  • A No slide in the brachial plexus, wrist and hand or neurovascular decks describes an inferior trunk (Klumpke) injury; a C8-T1 lesion would weaken median as well as ulnar hand muscles and give more than a 4th and 5th digit claw. The sensory test in the next question confirms the level.
  • B A superior trunk injury takes the C5-C6 shoulder and elbow muscles and spares the hand.
  • C Slides (Martin, Wrist & Hand Pt 2): carpal tunnel syndrome numbs median territory and may weaken the thumb (APB), not the little finger.

flags.title: Slides vs the lecture note
flags.html: 01.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 2 (from Dr. Martin's detailed notes) gives Klumpke paralysis (C8-T1), from grasping something to break a fall, as a cause of claw hand, and this question was keyed to the inferior trunk to match the lab's "brachial plexus injury" heading. The slides never mention Klumpke or the inferior trunk as an injury; they show the 4th and 5th digit claw only under ulnar nerve lesions. The slides were followed, so the key moved from the inferior trunk to the ulnar nerve.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 28-year-old motorcyclist has a claw of digits 4 and 5: metacarpophalangeal joints hyperextended, interphalangeal joints flexed.

stem: Which impaired muscles explain the claw? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: The thenar muscles and the 1st and 2nd lumbricals, supplied by the median nerve
The long finger extensors, which can no longer pull the 4th and 5th digits straight
The interossei and the 3rd and 4th lumbricals, supplied by the ulnar nerve
Flexor carpi radialis and palmaris longus, which normally hold the wrist in flexion

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Martin, Wrist & Hand Pt 2, "Nerve Supply: Ulnar Nerve"): the deep branch supplies "ODM, ADM, FDM, 3rd & 4th Lumbricals, Interossei, AP". The slides picture the claw but do not explain it; the mechanism comes from the lecture's detailed notes and 01.1 - Anatomy of the Wrist and Hand - PART 2: with the interossei and medial lumbricals wasted, the long extensors and flexor digitorum profundus act unopposed, so the MCP joints overextend and the IP joints cannot straighten.

  • A Slides (Martin, "Nerve Supply: Median Nerve"): OP, APB, FPB and the 1st & 2nd lumbricals are median; losing them does not claw the 4th and 5th digits.
  • B The extensors are working; they are what overextends the MCP joints.
  • D Slides (Martin, Distal Upper Extremity): the median nerve supplies the anterior forearm muscles "except 1½ muscles"; these wrist flexors are median and do not shape the fingers.

Tests 07.2 - Clinical Approach to the Neurovascular Supply of the Distal Upper Extremity, 01 - Anatomy of the Brachial Plexus, 03 - Nerve Injury. Case 2 (motorcyclist with a claw), prompt c. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 28-year-old motorcyclist has a 4th and 5th digit claw and no sensation over her 5th digit. You want to know whether the lesion is in the plexus (C8-T1) or in the ulnar nerve.

stem: Which sensory finding best separates the two? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Sensation over the pulp of the thumb
Sensation over the first dorsal web space

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Martin, Distal Upper Extremity, "Motor and Sensory Features"): ulnar sensory loss is "NOT MCNFA and NOT C8", and the map on the same slide labels the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm (C8, T1), a medial cord branch on the cutaneous supply slide. Slides (Martin, "Testing Myotomes & Dermatomes"): the T1 test point sits on the medial forearm. So a numb medial forearm puts the lesion in the plexus, and a spared medial forearm with a numb little finger puts it in the ulnar nerve. Slides (Payne, Nerve Injuries): a mononeuropathy has a "well circumscribed area of sensory abnormality" and weakens only that nerve's muscles.

  • A The thumb is the C6 test point on the dermatome slide and median territory; neither lesion touches it.
  • C Slides (Martin, Distal Upper Extremity): the superficial radial branch is "sensory to dorsum of hand lateral to 4th digit", so the first dorsal web space is radial.
  • D Slides (Payne, "numb thumb" case): the LCNFA is musculocutaneous and C6, the test for the numb-thumb problem, not this one.

The UNE "Clinical Features" slide does list tingling "medial forearm into ring and small finger", but Payne's mononeuropathy slide explains that a nerve lesion may radiate as subjective complaints "but not usually objective signs" outside its territory; the objective test here is sensory loss.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 31-year-old woman, 26 weeks pregnant, has a week of pain radiating down her left medial thigh and feels she is walking funny. She has decreased sensation over the left medial thigh and weak adduction on the left. You cannot recreate the pain, and all other hip movements are full strength.

stem: Which nerve is implicated, and where is it most likely being impaired? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Femoral nerve, where it passes under the inguinal ligament
Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, beside the anterior superior iliac spine
Sciatic nerve, where it leaves the pelvis below piriformis
Obturator nerve, in the pelvis before the obturator foramen

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Martin, Gluteal Region and Thigh, "Thigh Organization"): the medial compartment functions to "adduct hip" and its innervation is the obturator nerve. The "MC: Nerve Supply" slide gives the obturator nerve (L2-L4), "motor to medial compartment muscles", drawn running through the pelvis, with a patch of medial thigh skin shaded beside it. The medial compartment slides list adductor longus and brevis, adductor magnus (adductor part: obturator nerve) and gracilis.

  • A Slides: the femoral nerve supplies the anterior compartment, which flexes the hip and extends the knee.
  • B The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is drawn on the anterior compartment nerve slide at the inguinal ligament; it cannot weaken adduction.
  • C Slides: the sciatic nerve supplies the posterior compartment (extend hip, flex knee), and only the hamstring part of adductor magnus (tibial nerve).

⚠ The slides give the nerve's course, not compression by the pregnant uterus; that mechanism is the lab's implication.

Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 26-weeks-pregnant woman has left medial thigh numbness and weak hip adduction. All other hip movements are full strength.

stem: Which finding best shows this is a peripheral nerve injury and not an L3 radiculopathy? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Hip flexion and knee extension (same roots, femoral nerve) are full strength
The weakness and the numbness are both on the left side only, with the right leg normal
The pain cannot be recreated on examination by moving or loading the left hip
The symptoms began suddenly a week ago, at a clear point in the pregnancy

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Payne, Nerve Injuries, "Clinical Presentation of a Mononeuropathy"): "weakness of muscles taken care of by that peripheral nerve but NOT of other muscles from the same nerve root that are managed by a different peripheral nerve"; a myotome is the muscles of one root "regardless of the related peripheral nerve". Slides (Martin, Gluteal Region and Thigh): the medial compartment myotome is L3, quadriceps L3/4 and iliopsoas L1/2, with the femoral and obturator nerves both L2-L4. Full-strength hip flexion and knee extension with weak adduction confines the lesion to the obturator nerve.

  • B Both a root and a single nerve are usually one-sided.
  • C Not reproducing the pain does not tell root from nerve.
  • D Slides (Payne): a radiculopathy's onset "may be sudden or insidious", and a mononeuropathy's is "variable".

Payne's other discriminators: a radiculopathy brings neck or back pain radiating down the limb, "fuzzy" borders and myotomal reflex loss; a mononeuropathy gives a well circumscribed area of sensory loss.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 22-year-old collided with a friend while snowboarding. Since then he trips over his right foot and cannot lift the toes of his right foot well.

stem: Which muscles are implicated? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Tibialis posterior, flexor digitorum longus and flexor hallucis longus
Tibialis anterior, extensor digitorum longus and extensor hallucis longus

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Martin, Anatomy of the Leg, "Muscles: Anterior Compartment"): four muscles, "primarily responsible for dorsiflexion of the ankle", "all innervated by: Deep Fibular Nerve": tibialis anterior (L4 & L5), extensor digitorum longus with fibularis tertius (extends the lateral four digits) and extensor hallucis longus (L5, extends the great toe). Slides (Payne, "Case: Foot Drop"): "Foot drop = dorsiflexion weakness". The gait descriptions (slapping foot, high steppage) are not on the slides.

  • A Slides: the superficial posterior compartment plantarflexes, all on the tibial nerve.
  • B Slides: the deep posterior compartment is also tibial nerve and passes under the flexor retinaculum.
  • D Slides (Gluteal Region): gluteus medius and minimus abduct the thigh and stabilize gait (superior gluteal nerve); they do not lift the toes.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: The 22-year-old snowboarder has a right foot drop after a collision. You suspect the common fibular nerve at the fibular neck, but need to exclude an L5 radiculopathy.

stem: Which finding would point to an L5 radiculopathy instead? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Weak eversion of the foot from fibularis longus and brevis
Weak inversion and hip abduction as well as dorsiflexion
Sharp-bordered numbness over the dorsum of the foot
Numbness confined to the first dorsal web space of the foot

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Payne, Nerve Injuries, "Case findings: abnormal in RED"): abnormality confined to peroneus longus, tibialis anterior and extensor digitorum brevis is "Common Peroneal Neuropathy at Fibular Head". The "Case: Alternate Ending" slide adds gluteus medius, semimembranosus, tibialis posterior and the L5 paraspinals (one root, several nerves) and labels it "L5 Radiculopathy". Tibialis posterior (inversion) is tibial nerve and gluteus medius (hip abduction) superior gluteal nerve, so neither can fail from a fibular nerve lesion.

  • A Slides (Martin, Leg): the lateral compartment everts and is supplied by the superficial fibular nerve, a branch of the common fibular; peroneus longus is abnormal in Payne's fibular head case.
  • C Slides (Payne, foot drop case): the fibular head lesion gave "reduced pinprick sensation dorsum of foot, clear borders"; the Leg deck's sensory slide gives that skin to the superficial fibular nerve.
  • D Slides (Martin, Leg, "Sensory Nerve Supply"): the first web space is deep fibular skin, also a branch of the common fibular.

lectureMeta: Source: Schulich Reviews - MSK Review (Schulich Reviews, December 18, 2024), slide 116.
stem: A 40-year-old man has swelling of several DIP joints, one whole "sausage" toe, and pitting of his fingernails. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. DIP involvement points to psoriatic arthritis or OA; RA and the other CTDs usually spare the DIPs. Psoriatic arthritis adds dactylitis, enthesitis and nail changes (pitting, onycholysis) and is a clinical diagnosis. RA is symmetric small-joint arthritis of the hands and feet with more than an hour of morning stiffness.

stem: A patient presents with persistent right wrist pain and swelling. 3 weeks later, the right 2nd to 5th MCPs become affected, in addition to the existing right wrist pain. Another 6 weeks later, the left knee and left wrist also start to swell and become painful. The course of this patient’s arthritis is best described as…
answer: The correct answer is D. The patient has had symptoms for at least 9 weeks, so this is considered chronic polyarthritis. The joints symptoms are persistent and there are progressively more joints becoming involved in the disease process. This is a common pattern for rheumatoid arthritis

stem: A 24-year-old man has 6 months of low back and buttock pain that wakes him in the second half of the night, with over an hour of morning stiffness that improves with exercise. Last year he had anterior uveitis. Chest expansion is reduced. Which investigation is most useful next?
answer: The correct answer is C. Inflammatory back pain (better with movement, second-half-of-night pain, long morning stiffness) with anterior uveitis and reduced chest expansion suggests ankylosing spondylitis. Investigate with a pelvic x-ray for sacroiliitis, CRP/ESR and HLA-B27; some patients show changes only on MRI.

stem: Three weeks after an episode of urethritis, a 26-year-old man develops a painful swollen knee and ankle, red eyes and dysuria. Joint aspirate culture is negative. What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. Reactive arthritis follows a GI or GU infection by 1-3 weeks and is not an infection of the joint itself: "can't see" (conjunctivitis/uveitis), "can't pee" (urethritis), "can't climb a tree" (large-joint oligoarthritis). It is a clinical diagnosis and is often HLA-B27 positive.

stem: A 48-year-old woman has dry eyes, a dry mouth with dental caries, and bilateral parotid swelling. Which antibody pair is most characteristic of her likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is E. Sjögren syndrome: sicca (dry eyes and mouth), salivary gland involvement, Raynaud's, arthritis. Most patients are ANA and RF positive, and anti-Ro and anti-La are characteristic. Treatment includes artificial tears and saliva.

stem: A 55-year-old woman has Raynaud's phenomenon, tight skin of the fingers, telangiectasias, calcium deposits in the fingertips and heartburn from esophageal dysmotility. Which antibody is most associated with this presentation?
answer: The correct answer is A. This is CREST (calcinosis, Raynaud's, esophageal dysmotility, sclerodactyly, telangiectasia), the limited form of systemic sclerosis, associated with anti-centromere antibodies. Almost all SSc is ANA positive; anti-Scl-70 goes with diffuse disease and pulmonary fibrosis.

stem: A 62-year-old woman has 2 months of difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms. She has a violaceous rash on her upper eyelids and red papules over her knuckles. CK is markedly raised. Which association must be investigated?
answer: The correct answer is B. Inflammatory myositis causes proximal (shoulder and hip) weakness with raised CK. Dermatomyositis adds the heliotrope rash, Gottron papules and dilated nailfold capillaries, and in older adults it is associated with cancer, so screen for malignancy. Polymyositis has no rash or photosensitivity.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 22 year old college student. New onset of: red rash on the cheeks (malar rash); maculopapular rash in the sun; fatigue; hands turning white in the cold (Raynaud's); weight loss; hair loss; stiff hands in the morning and swelling of knuckles. Her cousin has Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (JIA).

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis in this patient and why?
answer: The correct answer is C. The case answers "Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE)", and the lecture gives the why: a malar rash, a rash in the sun (photosensitivity), stiff swollen hands in the morning (possible inflammatory arthritis), hair loss (alopecia) and Raynaud's, with fatigue and weight loss. Alopecia and Raynaud's are common in SLE but are not classification criteria. Sjögren's syndrome (A) is dry eyes and mouth; dermatomyositis (B) is proximal weakness with a high CK, and its photosensitive rash is a V-neck or shawl rash with Gottron's papules over the knuckles, not a malar rash that spares the nasolabial folds; systemic sclerosis (D) is tight skin, dysphagia and fingertip ulcers.

preamble.html: 22 year old college student. stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: An anti-DNA antibody on its own
A skin biopsy of the malar rash
A kidney biopsy before any bloods

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. The lecture's lupus tests serve diagnosis, prognosis and treatment safety: a blood count, ESR, creatinine and urinalysis, and the ANA as the screening test, positive in over 95% of SLE 06 - Connective Tissue Disorders. A negative ANA makes SLE highly unlikely.

  • A: anti-DNA is not ordered unless the ANA is positive, since it cannot be positive with a negative ANA.
  • B: the malar rash is diagnosed by its look (fixed redness sparing the nasolabial folds); a skin biopsy is not in the lecture's workup.
  • D: the kidney is assessed first with creatinine and urinalysis; a biopsy is not the starting test.

stem: Does she have SLE? (the first line of the case is a recap written for this bank; the results and the question are copied from the lecture)

options.html: Yes: she meets at least 5 criteria
No: her anti-DNA antibody is negative
No: her kidneys are not involved
Not until a kidney biopsy is done

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "Yes This patient has SLE." It counts: positive ANA; low white cells and platelets; positive anti-Smith and low complement (C3 and C4); malar rash; photosensitivity; possible inflammatory arthritis, "at least 5 criteria" where 4 of 11 are needed. A negative anti-DNA (B) does not exclude SLE: anti-Smith satisfies the same immunologic criterion. Kidney involvement (C) is one criterion among eleven, not a requirement, and nothing here calls for a biopsy (D).

Low-dose prednisone and an oral NSAID
Long-term warfarin plus a low-dose aspirin daily

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Blood and protein in the urine mean glomerulonephritis, major organ disease, which the lecture treats with high-dose steroids plus mycophenolate or azathioprine, on top of hydroxychloroquine, the anchor drug for every lupus patient 06 - Connective Tissue Disorders.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Woman with severe retrosternal dysphagia, tight skin on hands, arms and face, crackles on auscultation of lung bases, +ANA nucleolar pattern, +Scl70 (topoisomerase 1)

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. The case answers: "Systemic sclerosis". Tight skin reaching the arms is diffuse cutaneous disease, and its antibodies are an ANA with a nucleolar pattern and anti-Scl-70, which "correlates with pulmonary fibrosis", the crackles at the lung bases (interstitial lung disease, "mostly at bases of lungs"). Dysphagia is common in scleroderma. Dermatomyositis (B) can cause swallowing trouble and lung disease, but through proximal weakness with anti-Jo-1, not tight skin; Sjögren's (C) and SLE (D) do not tighten the skin.

preamble.html: Woman or man with proximal muscle weakness, problems getting out of bed (due to core strength weakness), new Raynaud's, rash over knuckles, elevated CK

stem: What is the likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "DERMATOMYOSITIS". Proximal weakness with an elevated CK is inflammatory myositis, and the rash over the knuckles (Gottron's papules or sign) makes it dermatomyositis. Polymyositis (A) has the same weakness and CK but "no rash or photosensitivity". The SLE photosensitive rash (B) is not a knuckle rash, and systemic sclerosis (D) brings Raynaud's but not a myopathy with a rash.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mrs. Tran's painful knee: 52 years old, female. History of type 2 diabetes. Knee pain since age 45, now getting worse and more frequent. Pain is limiting her from daily walks and using the stairs. Stiffness in the knee in the morning for 5 minutes after waking. Appears well, but walking with a slight antalgic gait. On examination, the right knee is slightly swollen but feels cool. Tender to palpation along the joint line. Crepitus is noted on passive flexion.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The notes: "Mrs. Tran has chronic monoarthritis caused by knee OA." Pain brought on by activity (walks, stairs), morning stiffness under 30 minutes (usually under 5), and a tender joint with a cool effusion are the OA presentation, with no red flags. OA is a clinical diagnosis. Infection (A) gives a warm or hot joint. Rheumatoid arthritis (C) is an inflammatory polyarthritis, and chronic crystal arthritis (D) is the fourth item on the differential after "osteoarthritis" three times.

options.html: MRI of the knee to confirm the diagnosis
Aspirate the knee for the 3 C's
A bone scan of both of her knees
Plain X-ray of the knee to stage it

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. Osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis, and the X-ray does not make it; the X-ray is used to stage it (early, late or end-stage), and staging is the first of the lecture's four treatment questions 04 - Osteoarthritis.

  • A: MRI is almost never used in OA and only when the diagnosis is in doubt; hers is typical.
  • B: aspiration is for a red, hot joint; her knee is cool, with activity-related pain and 5 minutes of morning stiffness.
  • C: a bone scan, like MRI, is expensive and kept for when other problems need ruling out.

stem: What is the most appropriate initial management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. The lecture's first-line OA treatment is non-drug: 150 minutes of activity a week with neuromuscular control exercise (Tai-Chi, GLA:D), plus joint protection education 04 - Osteoarthritis. Only active, exercise-based physiotherapy works.

preamble.html: Ms. Markus' intermittent knee pain: 36 years old, female soccer star. No medical problems, but tore ACL in a soccer match at age 23. Pain only with running for 5 years, now increasing swelling. Stiffness in the knee in the morning for 5 minutes after waking. No red flags for other types of arthritis.

stem: Does Ms. Markus have knee OA? (stem copied from the lecture; options written for this bank)

options.html: No, she is too young to have osteoarthritis
No, osteoarthritis needs X-ray changes first
No, her pain is intermittent, not daily

answer: The correct answer is D. The lecture: "Yes, she has post-traumatic knee OA - Not too young for that!" Her risk of needing a knee replacement by age 55 is over 50%. Post-traumatic OA after an ACL or meniscus tear is secondary OA, and most symptomatic knee OA starts between 35 and 55 (A). OA is a clinical diagnosis; X-ray changes alone do not diagnose it (B). Her symptoms are activity-related with brief morning stiffness and no red flags, the OA pattern (C).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mr. Liebowitz' progressive knee pain and stiffness: 68 male with chronic left knee pain and stiffness, worse after activity, with occasional "flare ups" of knee pain and swelling. Medical history includes dyslipidemia, chronic renal failure, and left total hip arthroplasty for hip OA (2001). Medications include atorvastatin 40 mg daily. Pain and stiffness has progressed to such an extent that he moved out of his 2-storey house into a retirement home. No red flags for other causes of arthritis. Left knee exam demonstrates varus knee alignment. Tenderness and crepitus on the knee examination and limitation in passive left knee flexion due to pain. X-ray: joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

stem: Which of the following best describes his diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is C. The lecture: "Mr. Liebowitz has late stage knee OA." The X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes, staged on the early / late / end-stage scale. End-stage (B) is where he is two years later, with bone-on-bone contact, a cane and symptoms uncontrolled despite every non-surgical treatment. There are no red flags for other causes of arthritis (D).

stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate plan? (the lecture gives "You recommend he try" without posing a question; stem written for this bank)

options.html: Neuromuscular physiotherapy, OT education, topical NSAID
Regular oral naproxen, with tramadol for any breakthrough pain
Arthroscopic debridement of the knee with a meniscectomy
Passive therapy: ultrasound, TENS and acupuncture sessions

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: physiotherapy for neuromuscular strength and stability training for at least 3 months, OT to educate on safe movements, consider topical NSAIDs BID to TID (avoid oral NSAIDs for chronic renal failure), a corticosteroid injection if refractory, and an SNRI trial for 2-3 months if still refractory. Oral NSAIDs are out with his kidneys, and opioids including tramadol are generally avoided (risks > benefit) (B). Knee arthroscopy has strong level 1 evidence of no meaningful benefit (C). Passive therapies are not shown to be beneficial (D).

preamble.title: The cases
preamble.html:
Case 1. 5 year old girl previously well. Presents with a 3 month history of bilateral knee swelling and morning limp. She is otherwise systemically well. O/E there are multiple active joints: bilateral knees, left wrist, many small joints of the hands.

Case 2. 3 year old boy previously well. Presents with: 3 months of intermittent fevers; 2 months of joint pain and swelling involving both knees and ankles; several episodes of faint rash, lasting up to a few hours. O/E he appears fatigued, pale; splenomegaly; effusions of both knees and ankles.

stem: Do these patients have JIA?

options.html: Only Case 1: Case 2's fevers rule out JIA
Only Case 2: Case 1 has too many joints
Neither: both have lasted too short a time
Both fit, once other causes are excluded

answer: The answer is D, reasoned from the lecture; the lecture asks the question and says "We will return to this case at the end", but never states an answer. The lecture's criteria are onset under 16, arthritis in one or more joints, duration over 6 weeks, and other causes excluded. Case 1 (age 5, 3 months) and Case 2 (age 3, 2 months of joint swelling) both meet the first three, and JIA is "a diagnosis of exclusion", so both fit once other causes are ruled out. Fever does not rule JIA out (A): high spiking fevers define systemic JIA, which is often first thought to be infection or leukemia, so those must be excluded. No joint count is too many (B): one or more joints qualifies, and 5 or more is polyarticular JIA. Both have lasted well over the 6 weeks the criteria need (C).

stem: If this is JIA, what is the most likely subtype?
answer: The answer is B, reasoned from the lecture; the session poses the question without an answer. Both knees, the left wrist and many small joints of the hands are 5 or more joints, which is polyarticular JIA (the notes: "joint pain and swelling in 5 or more joints during the first 6 months"); a younger child with polyarthritis fits the rheumatoid factor-negative group, though the case gives no rheumatoid factor result here. Oligoarticular JIA (A) is 4 or fewer joints. Systemic JIA (C) needs high spiking fevers and rash, and she is systemically well. Enthesitis-related arthritis (D) is more common in boys, usually over 10, with enthesitis and sacroiliitis.

answer: The answer is D, reasoned from the lecture; the lecture poses the question without an answer. Systemic JIA is "the most serious and potentially life threatening subtype", and the summary names its unique consideration: "macrophage activation syndrome in the context of SJIA". Silent uveitis (B) is the risk of oligo- and polyarticular JIA; in the screening table systemic JIA has the longest interval, every 12 months. Micrognathia (C) is a local growth disturbance any subtype can cause, not the complication particular to systemic JIA.

Three months of fever, two of joint swelling and a big spleen are not a passing virus (D), and the lecture gives no reason to treat this as septic arthritis (C).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 45 year old man with a 6 week history of a painful, non-blancheable rash on his legs. Over this time period, he has felt generally unwell with significant fatigue. He has pain and swelling in his ankles bilaterally. The rash is purpura.

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is B. The lecture reveals it on its classification chart: cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis is "Diagnosis of case 1", a small vessel vasculitis that "can occur on its own or be a manifestation of other vasculitis types". The lecture frames the rash's differential as "coagulopathy or vasculitis". Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (A) is an ANCA-associated vasculitis whose common features are sinonasal, eye, lung and kidney disease, none of which he has. Polyarteritis nodosa (C) is a medium vessel vasculitis. Henoch-Schönlein purpura (D) is a small vessel vasculitis with purpura too, but the lecture marks it as one of the two most common in children. The module carries this same man forward, where hepatitis C turns out to be the cause (module Q161-162).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html:
75 year old female with prior history of high blood pressure treated with a small dose of hydrochlorothiazide. Patient developed a right-sided temporal headaches that quickly got worse over 1 week. She has never had a headache like this before. She noticed that it hurt to brush her hair. She was having trouble eating because of jaw pain. 2 months ago she complained of shoulder and hip pain and stiffness worse in the morning. She was very fatigued and had lost same weight.

Laboratory investigations: Hemoglobin 99 (115-145) · WBC normal · Platelets normal · ESR 70 mm/hr (normal < 20) · CRP 50 (normal <5)

stem: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is D. The case: "The family doctor was concerned about giant cell arteritis." She is over 50 with a new headache unlike any before, scalp tenderness (it hurt to brush her hair), jaw claudication, polymyalgia rheumatica symptoms (shoulder and hip pain and stiffness, worse in the morning), weight loss and fatigue, with anemia and a high ESR and CRP. All three distractors are on the notes' differential of a cranial presentation: temporomandibular arthritis (A) would explain jaw pain but not the scalp tenderness, the girdle stiffness or the inflammatory markers; a migraine (B) does not start for the first time at 75 with raised markers; sinusitis (C) does not cause jaw claudication or limb girdle stiffness.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 75 year old female with prior history of high blood pressure treated with a small dose of hydrochlorothiazide. Patient developed a right-sided temporal headaches that quickly got worse over 1 week. She has never had a headache like this before. She noticed that it hurt to brush her hair. She was having trouble eating because of jaw pain. 2 months ago she complained of shoulder and hip pain and stiffness worse in the morning. She was very fatigued and had lost same weight. Laboratory investigations: Hemoglobin 99 (115-145) · WBC normal · Platelets normal · ESR 70 mm/hr (normal < 20) · CRP 50 (normal <5). Later: the diagnosis is giant cell arteritis, and she is started on prednisone today.

stem: Which investigation best confirms the diagnosis? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Repeat the ESR and CRP in two weeks' time
CT of the sinuses for sinusitis

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. Giant cell arteritis is confirmed by a temporal artery biopsy within 1-2 weeks: transmural inflammation with giant cells is 100% specific, though 50-70% are negative from skip lesions, so a negative biopsy does not rule it out 07 - Vasculitis. Prednisone is started first and the biopsy arranged after.

  • A: the ESR and CRP are already high; repeating them adds nothing, and normal values would only have made GCA unlikely.
  • B: ANCA is ordered only when a small vessel vasculitis is suspected; GCA is a large vessel vasculitis.
  • D: scalp tenderness, jaw pain on eating and morning girdle stiffness with a high ESR point to GCA, not sinusitis.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The 75 year old woman with a new right temporal headache, scalp tenderness, jaw pain on eating, morning shoulder and hip stiffness, and an ESR of 70 and CRP of 50. Her family doctor is concerned about giant cell arteritis.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step? (stem written for the lecture's answer; the lecture poses no question)

options.html: Prescribe prednisone today, then refer to rheumatology
Book a biopsy; start prednisone only if it is positive
Repeat the ESR and CRP in 2 weeks, then decide on treatment
Start prednisone 15 mg daily and review in 2 weeks

answer: The correct answer is A. The lecture: "The patient was given a prescription that day for 50 mg daily of prednisone. A referral to Rheumatology was made. The patient felt 100% better after 5 days of prednisone." The lecture gives the rule: as soon as GCA is suspected, measure the ESR and CRP and start prednisone 1 mg/kg (max 60 mg daily) once the blood is drawn, and do not wait for results; then protect against steroid side effects (proton pump inhibitor, calcium and vitamin D, bisphosphonate) and arrange a temporal artery biopsy or Doppler ultrasound. Waiting for a biopsy (B) or for repeat markers (C) risks vision loss, which in 15-20% is permanent; a negative biopsy would not rule GCA out anyway, since 50-70% are negative from skip lesions. 15-20 mg (D) is the polymyalgia rheumatica dose, and polymyalgia with GCA needs high-dose prednisone "to decrease the risk of blindness" (Rheumatology Treatments, steroids lecture).

preamble.title: The case - purpura and ankle swelling
preamble.html:
The case. 45 year old man with a 6 week history of a painful, non-blancheable rash on his legs. Over this time period, he has felt generally unwell with significant fatigue. He has pain and swelling in his ankles bilaterally. The rash has the appearance of purpura. Prior to developing the rash, the patient felt well. He has no past medical history and avoids going to see the doctor. He works in sales and is married with two children aged 3 and 5. He has a family history of heart disease in his father; no family history of cancer or rheumatologic disease. He denies any recent travel outside of Canada. He drinks 2-3 alcoholic beverages daily and smokes a pack-a-day of cigarettes. He uses marijuana recreationally once a month. He denies any other drug use but did use i.v. drugs 10 years ago. He has several tattoos. He denies any unprotected sex other than with his wife.

Regarding his current symptoms, these are getting worse over the last week. The bilateral ankle pain is worse in the morning and associated with 2 hours of stiffness. He has been using ibuprofen 800 mg, 3 times daily for the pain in his legs. He did not find that acetaminophen helped his symptoms and he has not been using it. He does not take any other medications, vitamins or herbals. He denies any history of red, painful eyes, headaches, sinus congestion or epistaxis. He has no hearing problems. He denies dyspnea, cough or chest pain. He has no hemoptysis. He has no abdominal pain, vomiting, diarrhea or blood per rectum. Other than the ankle pain, he has no other joint involvement. He denies parasthesias and has no limb weakness. He does not have symptoms consistent with Raynauld’s phenomenon or digital ischemia. On exam, his vitals are stable. He has leg edema to his knees. His rash in non-blancheable and painful to touch. It is worse around ankles and he has no lesions above knees. His ankles are swollen and warm. He has difficulty with both passive and active range of motion at the ankles. He can weight bear but has an antalgic gait. The rest of the exam was normal.

stem: What investigations should be ordered initially (check all that apply)
answer: The correct answers are A, B, C, D, E, F, G, I, J, N, O, and P. The CBC determines if the white count is elevated, which may suggest an infection and whether the hemoglobin is low and platelets high, which can be seen in inflammation from infection or autoimmune disease. Similarly, elevations in ESR and/or CRP tells us if there is systemic inflammation. It is important to ensure that there is no coagulopathy, which can cause purpura; thus, look for low platelets and/or elevated INR and PTT. ALT can be high and albumin low in liver dysfunction that can occur with some types of primary and secondary vasculitis. To rule out infections that commonly cause purpura, blood cultures, hepatitis and HIV should be tested (even in patients without risk factors; however, this patient does have risk factors, including prior i.v. drug use and tattoos). Given the prior use of i.v. drugs and because cocaine use can cause purpura, it should be discussed with the patient whether he consents to have a urine toxicology screen. The patient has ankle pain and swelling; thus, bilateral ankle X-rays should be performed to assess for evidence of arthritis. Because asymptomatic manifestations of vasculitis can occur in the lungs and kidney, it is important to obtain a serum creatinine, urinalysis and a chest X-ray in all patients suspected of vasculitis. A skin biopsy is helpful to confirm a diagnosis of vasculitis; however, it does not need to be performed with the initial investigations. Less invasive tests can sometimes identify the underlying cause making the skin biopsy unnecessary. It is also not recommended to perform a skin biopsy for non-severe (non-ulcerating) purpura with a duration of symptoms less than 4-6 weeks because often these resolve on their own and are due to unspecified viral infections or hypersensitivity reactions. The urine cultures do not need to be done unless the urinalysis shows evidence of infection, RF and ANCA do not need to be tested before the results of the other investigations. If the initial investigations do not identify a cause, serology for autoimmune disease can be considered depending on symptoms. In this case, the patient had evidence of inflammatory arthritis; therefore, ANA, RF and/or anti-CCP2 can be ordered. ANCA can be ordered by the specialist once secondary causes of vasculitis are ruled out. The patient has no respiratory or abdominal complaints; therefore, the CT scan is not indicated.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The case. The results revealed an elevated ALT of 70 (normal <30) and a CRP of 50 (normal <5). He had a positive anti-HCV antibody, suggesting a prior or current hepatitis C infection. The rest of his labs and X-Rays were normal. The treating physician contacted rheumatology on-call who advised that blood be sent for hepatitis C viral load and cryoglobulins. The rheumatologist explained that hepatitis C infection can directly cause vasculitis and inflammatory arthritis, or it can be associated with cyroglobulins that causes a small vessel vasculitis. Either way, the first-line treatment for the arthritis and purpura associated with hepatitis C is to treat the underlying infection with antivirals.

stem: The patient is very bothered by his rash and ankle pain and he is not getting relief from ibuprofen. What can be prescribed to relieve symptoms while the patient awaits the investigations? (select all that apply)

options.html: Another oral non-steroidal anti-inflammatory (i.e. diclofenac, naproxen, etc.)

answer: The correct answers are A, D, E, and F. Acetaminophen is minimally effective for the pain of inflammatory arthritis and does not treat cutaneous vasculitis. There is no evidence for cannabinoids for this indication. Methotrexate takes a long time to start working; thus, it is not useful to manage acute symptoms. Given that this patient’s likely diagnosis is an underlying infection (hepatitis C), methotrexate which is an immunosuppressant that can also cause liver toxicity should not be used. In other patients who have primary cutaneous vasculitis, methotrexate can be used for non-resolving, scarring or severe skin disease. Topical corticosteroids can be used first line for non-severe cutaneous vasculitis. If it is not effective, NSAIDs can be tried in patients that do not have contraindications. Another anti-inflammatory is colchicine and it can be used for cutaneous vasculitis and arthritis (0.6 mg twice a day with dose adjusted for renal disease) with the major side effect being diarrhea. Oral corticosteroids are very effective for cutaneous vasculitis and arthritis; however, there are significant side effects, and should be avoided if possible. If other agents fail, infection has been ruled out and the skin disease is severe, moderate doses of prednisone can be used with taper (30 mg for 1 week then decrease by 5 mg every 5 days until off).

stem: A 65-year-old woman presents with new right-sided headache and pain and stiffness in her shoulders and hips that is worse in the morning and improves with activity. She has been very fatigued but has no other symptoms. She weighs 70 kg. What is the initial management plan (select all that apply):

options.html: Urgent laboratory investigations (CBC, Creatinine, ALT, ESR, CRP and a urinalysis) to be performed at this clinic visit.
Urgent referral for temporal artery biopsy
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations are available and only if the ESR or CRP is elevated
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations and temporal artery biopsy are available and only if the ESR or CRP is elevated
Start prednisone 50 mg daily after the results of the laboratory investigations and temporal artery biopsy are available and only if the biopsy is consistent with GCA
Start calcium, vitamin D and a proton pump inhibitor to protect from steroid side effects

answer: The correct answers are A, B, D, H, and J. GCA should be suspected in this patient because she has new onset headache and symptoms that would be consistent with PMR, which is frequently associated with GCA. It is critical to test for ESR and CRP immediately to ensure accuracy of the test. A negative ESR and CRP in a patient who is not on steroids, makes GCA very unlikely. After the blood is drawn for the inflammation markers, the patient should be started immediately on high dose steroids (1 mg/ kg daily to maximum of 60 mg daily); a delay in starting steroids can lead to severe complications, such as blindness and/or stroke. If the blood cannot be drawn immediately, then the steroid should be started, and the laboratory investigations completed as soon as possible. It is important to confirm the diagnosis with a temporal artery biopsy; however, steroid treatment should not be delayed waiting for the biopsy to be performed. Because steroids have serious side effects, particularly in the elderly: calcium and vitamin D should be started to prevent fractures and a proton pump inhibitor to prevent gastritis and peptic ulcer disease. It is not necessary to start a bisphosphonate for bone protection immediately; this can be started later after the diagnosis is confirmed. All patients with GCA should be referred to rheumatology or another specialist with an interest in GCA (could be general medicine, neurology, ophthalmology) for confirmation of diagnosis, additional medical management and monitoring).

preamble.title: The case - joint pain after a non-resolving sinus infection
preamble.html:
The case. 55 year old woman presents with joint pain and swelling. You had been following her for the last 2 months for a non-resolving sinus infection for which she had already received 2 courses of antibiotics. She did not have fevers but felt chills. The symptoms of her sinus infection were facial pain, frontal headache, nasal congestion, purulent discharge and nasal crusting. In the last week she was also complaining of epistaxis and right ear fullness with hearing loss. A CT of her sinuses showed opacification of her sinuses. You had referred her to ENT, but the appointment was pending. The joint pain and swelling came on subacutely a week ago. It involved the wrists, right knee, left ankle and some of her PIPs. Her symptoms were worse in the morning and associated with 1 hour of morning stiffness. Her symptoms improved with ibuprofen. She is not any other medications, does not have any past medical history and her cancer screening is up to date. She has no significant family history. She does not drink, smoke or use any drugs or herbals. She works as a PSW and has travelled to the Philippines.

She has felt terrible the last several months with no energy and decreased appetite. She has lost 10 kg. She denies dyspnea but has not been active. She has some mild cough, worse in the morning and she feels it dripping down from her nose. She has no chest pain and no abdominal complaints. She denies any ocular complaints. She has no parasthesias and no focal weakness. On physical exam, the patient’s vitals are stable and she is afebrile. She is not in respiratory distress. She has tenderness over her sinuses. The tympanic membrane on the left was cloudy and bulging. She had several swollen tender joints. The rest of the exam was non-contributory. You had sent basic laboratory investigations and found that she was anemic with a hemoglobin of 100, platelets and WBC were slightly elevated at 520 and 13, respectively. Her liver enzymes and creatinine were normal. CRP was 80 (normal <5)

stem: What additional investigations should be ordered? (click all that apply)

options.html: Biopsy of sinonasal tissue to send for pathology and culture

answer: The correct answers are A, B, D, F, I, J, and O. The patient has non-resolving sinusitis with inflammatory arthritis and systemic symptoms. The differential diagnosis includes an infection, vasculitis, sarcoidosis or lymphoma. She could also have two processes occurring - a resistant/atypical sinus infection and causes of inflammatory arthritis (RA, lupus, CPPD, etc.). Blood cultures are important to assess for systemic infection. Sputum cultures are low yield and usually contaminated with oral flora. Given her travel history, a TB skin test is indicated. She does not have risk factors for HIV, but it can cause the patients symptoms and would be recommended to test for it. Vasculitis and lupus can be asymptomatic in the lungs and kidneys; therefore, the patient should have a urinalysis and chest X-Ray. The CT chest and PFTs do not need to be ordered right away but can be considered if the chest X-ray is normal because it is difficult to assess for dyspnea given the low activity level. The patient has evidence of inflammatory arthritis; thus, RF/anti-CCP2 and ANA should be ordered. Anti-ENA should only be done if ANA is positive. The complement levels are non-specific and do not need to be ordered unless ANA is positive and there is concern for lupus. ANCA would be helpful, but it is not reimbursed. It can be ordered once infectious and other causes are ruled out. There is concern for autoimmune disease, a biopsy of the sinuses is necessary to rule out atypical infections such as fungal and TB before starting immunosuppressive agents.

preamble.title: The case, continued
preamble.html: The case. The investigations showed negative blood cultures and TB skin test. Her HIV, ANA, RF and anti-CCP2 were negative. A chest X-Ray showed multiple cavitary lesions and the urinalysis showed blood and protein.

stem: What is the differential diagnosis?
answer: The correct answers are A, C, D, E, F, and G. The patient is ANA negative, which would make lupus highly unlikely. Similarly, rheumatoid vasculitis generally does not occur in patients who are RF negative. The patient’s investigations were concerning for renal disease and she also had cavitary lesions in her lungs. These findings are non-specific and can be seen in GPA, infections and cancer. TB is not ruled out because there are false negatives with TB skin tests.

stem: The patient has multi-organ involvement and the cause is not yet identified, as a primary care provider, what is the next step?

options.html: Arrange for the patient to be admitted to hospital
Call nephrology for an urgent referral
Send the patient for further investigations to identify the underlying cause
Wait for the ENT appointment before taking further action
Call ENT to update on patient status and inquire about a more urgent appointment
Refer to rheumatology and respirology for an urgent assessment

answer: The correct answers are B, F, and G. The patient is stable with no respiratory distress and her creatinine is normal; it is not necessary for urgent admission at this time. However, the patient needs to be monitored closely and she should be advised to go to the emergency department if she develops serious symptoms (i.e. dyspnea, hemoptysis, chest pain, fevers, syncope, vision loss, severe headache, focal neurologic signs, etc.). Her most pressing issue is the evidence of renal dysfunction with proteinuria and hematuria because she is at risk for rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Therefore, nephrology should be contacted urgently. It would not be appropriate to wait for the pending ENT visit as the patient has multi-organ involvement and needs rapid assessment by other specialties. However, since the patient has already been referred to ENT and a sinonasal biopsy would be helpful to assist with diagnosis, it would be beneficial to contact ENT with an update on the patient’s condition and request a more urgent appointment. In addition, given that vasculitis is on the differential and that the patient has lung involvement, rheumatology and respirology should be consulted. It is not necessary for the primary care physician to initiate further investigations at this point as the specialty providers can manage going forward. It would also not be advisable to start high dose prednisone before evaluation by specialty care because infection remains on the differential and corticosteroids can worsen infections.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding steroid use for rheumatologic disease is FALSE?

options.html: Intramuscular injections work better for patients who are non-compliant with oral steroids
Acute gout flare is an indication for high dose steroids
Side effects from chronic steroid use include weight gain, osteoporosis, and GI upset
Polymyalgia rheumatica is an indication for medium dose steroids
Recurrent UTIs are a contraindication for steroids

answer: The correct answer is B. An acute gout flare is an indication for medium dose steroids (25-30 mg daily x 3 weeks → taper by 5 mg every 3 days). High dose steroid indications include ANCA-associated vasculitis, lupus nephritis, inflammatory myositis, and giant cell arteritis.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding intra-articular injections is FALSE?

options.html: A red, hot, swollen joint should never receive an intra-articular steroid injection
Uncommon complications of intra-articular injections include tendon ruptures, post-injection flares, and infection
A diagnostic arthrocentesis should be sent for culture (+ Gram stain), cell count, and crystals
Hyaluronic acid injection can help relieve joint pain and is a form of therapeutic arthrocentesis
A joint aspirate containing a high number of neutrophils indicates a septic joint

answer: The correct answer is A. A red, hot, swollen joint could benefit from an intra-articular steroid injection if the patient is experiencing an acute gout flare or pseudogout, etc. Not every red, hot, swollen joint is a septic joint, but this should be ruled out by performing a diagnostic arthrocentesis.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding medications for rheumatological conditions is FALSE?

options.html: Pregnancy is a contraindication for NSAID use
Opioids are uncommonly used in rheumatological disease
A patient with chronic kidney disease would be better off on a COXIB over an NSAID for their osteoarthritis
Acetaminophen is an anti-inflammatory that can be used safely up to 3g/day in divided doses in a healthy person
NSAIDs are indicated in rheumatoid arthritis but do not delay radiographic changes to bones and joints

answer: The correct answer is D. Acetaminophen is not an anti-inflammatory medication. It is an analgesic. It can be used safely up to 3g/day in divided doses in a healthy person but should be reduced in liver disease.

stem: How would you treat this? 65 year-old woman with acute-onset pain in pelvic and shoulder girdles bilaterally. ESR 50 mm/hr

options.html: Prednisone ~1 mg/kg daily, then a slow taper
Prednisone 15-20 mg daily, then a slow taper
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily x 3 days
Prednisone 25 mg daily x 3 days, then taper

answer: The correct answer is B. The notes on polymyalgia rheumatica: it "typically does not require high-dose prednisone"; the standard dose is 15-20 mg daily, then a rapid taper to 10 mg, then a slow taper by 1 mg every 4 weeks until off. It is self-limited (6 months to 2 years). A (high dose) is needed only if giant cell arteritis is also present (~15%), to decrease the risk of blindness. C (pulse steroids) is for an emergency such as giant cell arteritis with vision involvement. D is the short acute gout course.

flags.title: The notes give two schedules
flags.html: One part of the notes says 15-20 mg daily x 4 weeks then taper quickly to 10 mg; the polymyalgia rheumatica section says x 2 weeks then a rapid taper to 10 mg "weekly" over a couple of weeks. Both continue with 1 mg every 4 weeks. The options avoid the duration.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: 65 year-old woman with acute-onset pain in pelvic and shoulder girdles bilaterally. ESR 50 mm/hr

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Pain of the shoulders and hips in someone over 50 with a raised ESR is polymyalgia rheumatica. Its mimics differ: fibromyalgia has normal inflammatory markers, myositis gives proximal weakness and is usually painless, and inflammatory arthritis affects the distal joints 03 - Body Pain.

  • A: Fibromyalgia has normal inflammatory markers and stiffness everywhere, not just proximally.
  • C: Myositis presents with proximal weakness and is usually painless.
  • D: Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis involves the distal joints, not the girdles.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mrs. Avery Smith is 70, active and on no medications. 3 months ago she began to notice pain and stiffness in her shoulders in the morning that got progressively worse. She had fatigue, lost her appetite and lost 10 lbs. Two months later her family doctor found a normal physical exam.

stem: Which of the following is the best differential diagnosis for Avery's presentation?

options.html: Polymyalgia rheumatica, inflammatory myositis, inflammatory arthritis, fibromyalgia, cancer
Septic arthritis, gout, pseudogout, reactive arthritis
Rotator cuff tear, adhesive capsulitis, acromioclavicular osteoarthritis
Cervical radiculopathy, brachial plexopathy, thoracic outlet syndrome

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slide 48, "How to differentiate PMR from other disorders", lists exactly these as the conditions to sort out: fibromyalgia, myositis, inflammatory arthritis, osteoarthritis, cancer and infection. Bilateral girdle pain and stiffness with weight loss and fatigue in an older woman is a systemic, inflammatory-sounding picture.

  • B is the differential of an acute hot monoarthritis. Avery has no swollen joint, and her onset is insidious over months.
  • C are local shoulder problems. They do not explain the fatigue, weight loss or bilateral morning stiffness.
  • D are nerve problems. Her exam is normal, with no sensory or motor finding.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avery, 70, has 3 months of progressive shoulder pain and morning stiffness, fatigue, poor appetite and 10 lbs of weight loss. Her exam is normal, with no weakness. Blood tests: hemoglobin 103 (low), platelets 489 (high), normal white cells, ESR 73 mm/hr, CRP 65 mg/L.

stem: What is the most likely diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Slide 43, "What is wrong with Avery?": older woman (> 50) · pain and stiffness in the hips and shoulders · profound morning stiffness · insidious onset · fatigue · weight loss · elevated ESR/CRP, anemia, thrombocytosis. Slide 46: in PMR "there is NOTHING wrong with the muscles · no weakness · other than pain, examination of muscles and joints is normal".

  • A Fibromyalgia has no elevation of inflammatory markers, and its stiffness is everywhere, proximal and distal (slide 48). Avery's ESR and CRP are high.
  • B Myositis is weakness of proximal muscles, usually without pain (slide 48). Avery has pain and no weakness.
  • D Inflammatory arthritis involves distal joints with reduced active and passive range of motion (slide 48). Avery's exam is normal.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avery, 70, has shoulder girdle pain and profound morning stiffness, a normal exam with no weakness, anemia, high platelets, and an ESR of 73 and CRP of 65. Her family doctor suspects polymyalgia rheumatica.

stem: Which statement about her investigations is correct?

options.html: A normal creatine kinase would be needed before the diagnosis can be made
The raised ESR and CRP alone are enough to start treatment without looking further
A muscle biopsy is needed to confirm the diagnosis
The raised ESR and CRP separate her from fibromyalgia, but other causes of raised markers, such as cancer, must be excluded

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slide 48: fibromyalgia has no elevation of inflammatory markers, so Avery's raised ESR and CRP point away from it. Slide 54: "Never treat based on an elevation of inflammatory markers alone; make sure there are no other reasons to explain the elevation", and always reassess to rule out other causes of pain. Slide 48 names cancer (asymmetric, other symptoms) and infection among the mimics.

  • A PMR is a clinical diagnosis. Creatine kinase belongs to the workup of muscle pain for myositis (the fibromyalgia section's targeted tests), but no rule makes it a prerequisite.
  • B is exactly what slide 54 forbids.
  • C In PMR the muscles are histopathologically normal (slide 47), so a biopsy would show nothing.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avery, 70, is diagnosed with polymyalgia rheumatica. Other causes of her raised inflammatory markers have been considered. She has no headache, jaw pain or visual symptoms.

stem: What is the best next step in management?

options.html: Prednisone 1 mg/kg daily and an urgent temporal artery biopsy
Prednisone 20 mg daily, held until she feels well and her markers settle
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily and review in 6 weeks

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slide 50: "Avery was prescribed 20 mg of prednisone per day", and in 12 hours she felt almost completely normal. Slide 52: prednisone 15-20 mg per day, depending on the patient's size, held on that dose until the patient is feeling well and the inflammatory markers have normalized, then a slow wean, usually after a month or two. Slide 49: PMR is exquisitely sensitive to corticosteroids, 90% better in 48 hours.

  • A High-dose prednisone is for giant cell arteritis. Avery has no cranial symptoms.
  • C No NSAID gives PMR's dramatic response; none of the mimics improves as quickly with steroids (slide 48), which is itself diagnostic.
  • D The deck treats PMR with prednisone alone.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Avery, 70, felt almost completely normal within 12 hours of starting prednisone 20 mg daily for polymyalgia rheumatica. She has now been well on that dose for a month and her inflammatory markers have normalized.

stem: Which plan for the rest of her treatment is best?

options.html: Stop prednisone now, since her symptoms and markers have resolved
Taper by 5 mg every week until off, then stop follow-up
Taper over 16-18 months (15, then 12.5, then 10 mg a month each, then down 1 mg a month), with calcium, vitamin D and an antiresorptive
Continue 20 mg daily for 2 years, then stop

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slide 53: prednisone 15 mg × 1 month, 12.5 mg × 1 month, 10 mg × 1 month, then down 1 mg per month, 16-18 months in total. Slide 51: Avery was treated for 18 months in all before stopping. Slide 55: anyone expected to take more than 7.5 mg of prednisone for more than 3 months needs bone protection: calcium 1500 mg a day, vitamin D 1000-2000 IU a day, and anti-resorptive therapy. Slide 54: the average course is about 2 years, some patients need low-dose prednisone much longer, and relapses are common.

  • A Stopping abruptly invites relapse; the deck tapers slowly over many months.
  • B is far too fast, and the deck keeps reassessing because relapse is common.
  • D Holding a high dose for 2 years ignores the taper and maximizes steroid harm.

Tests 08 - Acute Monoarthritis. Case 1, prompt 1. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ian McClellan, a 52-year-old businessman, woke this morning with an acutely swollen right 1st MTP joint. He recalls a similar episode 6 months ago that subsided over ten days. He has mild hypertension and recently started hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily. He drinks 8-12 beers, mainly on weekends, and this past weekend had "a couple of dozen". His father had a few attacks like this. BP 160/100. The medial right forefoot is fiery red and diffusely swollen, most intense over the 1st MTP; even gentle palpation hurts.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Ian's problem?

options.html: Plantar fasciitis, Morton's neuroma, stress fracture

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture's differential for an acute (under 6 weeks) red, hot, swollen single joint is "infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout", and the three look alike at the bedside.

  • B are chronic arthritides. Osteoarthritis is a chronic, activity-related, cool joint; rheumatoid and psoriatic arthritis are usually polyarticular and not this explosive.
  • C are mechanical forefoot problems without a hot, swollen joint.
  • D Cellulitis can mimic a red forefoot, but a DVT does not, and the list omits septic arthritis, the one diagnosis that must be excluded.

Tests 08 - Acute Monoarthritis. Case 1, prompt 2. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ian, 52, woke with a fiery red, swollen right 1st MTP after a weekend of heavy drinking. He had a similar attack 6 months ago that settled in ten days, recently started hydrochlorothiazide, and his father had similar attacks.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it?

options.html: Pseudogout: his age and the acute onset
Gout: the 1st MTP, a recent thiazide, an alcohol binge, a prior self-limited attack and a family history
Septic arthritis: the redness and the severe pain
Reactive arthritis: the alcohol and a single lower-limb joint

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's gout: lower limb, 1st MTP in 50%, men aged 35-50, diuretics (hydrochlorothiazide by name), alcohol and family history as risk factors, an attack that comes on over hours and, untreated, lasts about 7-10 days. His triggers fit the lecture's SMARTS list (Alcohol, and the new drug).

  • A Pseudogout favours the knee of an older person with osteoarthritis and is less intense and slower to peak.
  • C Redness and pain do not separate infection from crystals; nothing here (no fever, no portal of entry, no immunosuppression) points to infection, though only the fluid can exclude it.
  • D Reactive arthritis follows a gut or genital infection, not alcohol, and is a large-joint oligoarthritis.

Tests 08 - Acute Monoarthritis, 01 - Rheumatology Investigations. Case 1, prompt 3. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ian, 52, has a fiery red, swollen right 1st MTP, his second attack in 6 months, after a weekend binge and a new thiazide. You suspect gout.

stem: Which investigation will confirm the diagnosis?

options.html: Aspiration of the 1st MTP for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystals under polarized light

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: "If the joint is red, aspirate it" and send the 3 C's (cell count, culture with Gram stain, crystals). Finding urate crystals is the only proof of gout: needle-shaped and negatively birefringent. The Gram stain and culture exclude infection at the same time.

  • A Uric acid may be normal during an attack, and high uric acid alone is not gout. It is a useful baseline blood test, not a diagnosis.
  • B X-ray changes take years; it does not separate an acute crystal attack from infection.
  • D Inflammatory markers rise in all three diagnoses on the differential.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ian, 52, has an acute gout attack of the right 1st MTP. Aspiration shows needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals, and the Gram stain is negative. Kidney function is normal.

stem: What is the best immediate management?

options.html: Start allopurinol today to lower his uric acid
Rest, ice, elevation and an anti-inflammatory: indomethacin 50 mg three times daily or colchicine 0.6 mg every 8 hours
Admit for IV cefazolin and incision and drainage
Reassure him and offer acetaminophen only, since the attack will settle on its own in 10 days

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's acute gout treatment: rest, ice, elevation, then a steroid injected into the joint, an oral NSAID or COXIB (indomethacin 50 mg three times daily), colchicine 0.6 mg every 8 hours, or prednisone 30 mg daily for 2 days, then down 5 mg every 2 days. In the sink analogy, mop up first.

  • A ⚠ Never start allopurinol during an acute attack.
  • C is septic arthritis treatment; his Gram stain is negative and the crystals explain the joint.
  • D The attack is self-limited, but it is very intense, and leaving it untreated is not the lecture's management.

Tests 08 - Acute Monoarthritis. Case 1, general treatment. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ian's attack of gout settles. This is his second attack in 6 months. He drinks heavily on weekends and takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best?

options.html: Nothing more: treat each attack as it comes
Lifelong colchicine at full attack dose
Start allopurinol whenever his uric acid is high, even without attacks
Less alcohol, hydration and diet; review the diuretic; offer allopurinol, started under NSAID or colchicine cover, if attacks keep affecting his life

answer:
The correct answer is D. Gout recurs in 60% within 1 year, 80% within 2 and 90% within 5. The lecture's prevention: diet (meat and seafood bad, vegetables and low-fat dairy good), less alcohol, good hydration, and attention to risk factors such as diuretics. Allopurinol is considered for recurrent attacks affecting lifestyle, tophi, or harm from repeated acute treatment, in a patient who accepts lifelong treatment. Cover the start with an NSAID or colchicine, and aim for a uric acid at the lower limit of the reference range.

  • A ignores how likely recurrence is and his modifiable triggers.
  • B Colchicine at attack dose is for the attack and for covering an allopurinol start, not lifelong.
  • C Isolated hyperuricemia is not treated.

Tests 04 - Osteoarthritis. Case 2, prompt 1. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Stan Humphreys, a 65-year-old retired OPP officer, has had mild right knee pain for 5 years, worse over the last 2. A hockey player in his youth, he recalls no specific injury. The pain is worst when he is out hunting, the knee sometimes swells, and he can no longer squat. He takes acetaminophen and glucosamine and is asking for a cortisone injection. He is 170 cm and 100 kg. The knee is slightly warm and tense, lacks 10° of extension and 30° of flexion, has palpable crepitus, and valgus stress opens the joint.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Stan's chronic monoarthritis?

options.html: Osteoarthritis, chronic crystal arthritis, inflammatory arthritis, an old mechanical injury
Patellofemoral pain syndrome, Osgood-Schlatter disease, osteochondritis dissecans

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's chronic monoarthritis differential: "1. osteoarthritis · 2. osteoarthritis · 3. osteoarthritis", then chronic crystal arthritis (gout, pseudogout), first telling it apart from mechanical or sports causes, then less commonly inflammatory arthritis, a neuropathic joint, chronic infection, neoplasm and avascular necrosis.

  • A is the differential of an acute hot monoarthritis. Stan's knee has hurt for 5 years.
  • C are systemic connective tissue diseases that present as polyarthritis with extra-articular features.
  • D are conditions of children and adolescents.

Tests 04 - Osteoarthritis. Case 2, prompt 2. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Stan, 65, 100 kg, has 5 years of right knee pain worse with activity, intermittent swelling, crepitus, lost range of motion (lacks 10° extension and 30° flexion) and valgus laxity. He played hockey in his youth.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it?

options.html: Chronic gout: male sex and intermittent swelling
Knee osteoarthritis: chronic activity-related pain, crepitus, lost range of motion, obesity and possible old sports trauma
Rheumatoid arthritis: the swelling and the loss of motion
Avascular necrosis: his age and the hockey history

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's chronic OA monoarthritis: knee >> hip, pain brought on or worsened by activity, chronic (over 6 weeks), exam with an effusion, joint thickening and crepitus. His risk factors: obesity (a BMI near 35), age, male occupation and mechanical factors, and youth hockey, since post-traumatic OA is never "too young". ⚠ OA's effusion is classically cool; his "slightly warm" knee is a reason to aspirate the effusion and look for crystals, not a reason to drop OA.

  • A Gout favours the 1st MTP with explosive, self-limited attacks, not 5 years of activity pain.
  • C Rheumatoid arthritis is a symmetric small-joint polyarthritis.
  • D Avascular necrosis is on the list, but crepitus and activity pain building over years point to OA.

Tests 04 - Osteoarthritis. Case 2, prompt 3. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Stan, 65, has years of activity-related right knee pain, crepitus and lost range of motion. You think he has osteoarthritis.

stem: Which investigation is most useful?

options.html: MRI of the knee to confirm osteoarthritis
Weight-bearing X-rays of the knee to stage the disease

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture: OA is a clinical diagnosis, and the X-ray stages it (early, established, late or end-stage; Kellgren-Lawrence 1-2 early, 3-4 late to end-stage) by showing joint space narrowing and osteophytes. Staging is the first of the lecture's four treatment questions, and it decides whether surgery is on the table.

  • A and B ⚠ MRI or bone scan: almost never; expensive, and only to rule out other problems when the diagnosis is in doubt.
  • C Autoantibodies are ordered only when an inflammatory polyarthritis is suspected; a positive ANA or rheumatoid factor in a 65-year-old would prove nothing.

Tests 04 - Osteoarthritis. Case 2, prompt 4. Written for this bank 2026-11-19.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Stan, 65, 100 kg, has knee osteoarthritis. His X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes, not bone on bone. He asks you for a cortisone injection because he heard it might help.

stem: What is the best response?

options.html: Refuse: corticosteroids have no role in osteoarthritis
Book an arthroscopic washout and debridement
An injection can give short-term relief, but the core treatment is active exercise therapy and losing weight

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture lists intra-articular corticosteroid for short-term relief among the drugs for hip and knee OA, but the foundation is non-drug: lose 5% of body weight, 150 minutes of activity a week, neuromuscular training, and physiotherapy that is active (exercise-based) for at least 3 months.

  • A Intra-articular steroid is on the lecture's list of recommended drugs.
  • B ✘ Knee arthroscopy has strong evidence of no meaningful benefit.
  • D Joint replacement is a salvage procedure for end-stage disease with unacceptable symptoms; his X-ray is not end-stage, and he has not had a trial of conservative care.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Stan, 65, 100 kg, has non-end-stage knee osteoarthritis. He takes acetaminophen as needed and glucosamine 500 mg three times daily.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best supported?

options.html: Weight loss, regular exercise and active physiotherapy; topical NSAID, then oral NSAID or duloxetine if needed; replacement only if he reaches end stage
Continue glucosamine and add chondroitin to rebuild cartilage
Ultrasound, TENS and acupuncture for pain, with a scheduled opioid
Rest the knee as much as possible to protect the cartilage

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture's hip and knee plan: lose 5% of body weight, 150 minutes of activity a week, neuromuscular control (Tai-Chi, GLA:D), walking aids or an unloader brace; drugs: topical NSAIDs, oral NSAIDs if no contraindication, duloxetine, intra-articular steroid for short-term relief; joint replacement only for end-stage disease. No treatment preserves the joint; the goal is to live better with it.

  • B Glucosamine is inconclusive and chondroitin is not recommended.
  • C Passive therapies (ultrasound, TENS, laser, acupuncture) are not recommended, and opioids are generally avoided.
  • D OA is a "sick joint" that fails to heal; inactivity impairs healing, and activity is treatment.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Dorothy Blonde, a 61-year-old lab technologist, was out for a run when her left knee began to hurt; by the time she got home it was significantly swollen. It is her first episode. In the ER the knee was grossly swollen, warm and red; white cells 11.6, other routine labs essentially normal. The X-ray showed faint linear calcification in both the medial and lateral menisci, joint space otherwise normal. She has been well, with no fevers or chills. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times daily and is allergic to penicillin (rash).

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Dorothy's knee?

options.html: Septic arthritis, pseudogout, gout, a traumatic injury such as a meniscal tear
Prepatellar bursitis, pes anserine bursitis, Baker's cyst
Patellofemoral pain syndrome, iliotibial band syndrome

answer:
The correct answer is B. An acute, warm, red, swollen single joint is "infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout" in the lecture, and because it started on a run, a mechanical injury belongs on the list too.

  • A are chronic arthritides; this is a first, acute episode.
  • C Bursitis sits outside the joint; she has a joint effusion (positive patellar tap and ballottement).
  • D Neither causes a red, hot effusion.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Dorothy, 61, has a first, acute, warm, red, swollen left knee that came on during a run. She is afebrile and well. Her X-ray shows faint linear calcification in both menisci.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it?

options.html: Gout: the acute onset and the redness
Septic arthritis: the raised white count
Pseudogout: an older patient, the knee, and chondrocalcinosis on X-ray
Meniscal tear: the onset while running

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture's pseudogout: lower limb, knee most common, older people, often with osteoarthritis. Chondrocalcinosis is calcium pyrophosphate seen in cartilage on X-ray; the lecture's own knee film shows a line in the joint cartilage. The attack is less intense than gout and slower to peak.

  • A Gout favours the 1st MTP, and in women it comes after menopause with risk factors such as diuretics; her X-ray points to calcium pyrophosphate instead.
  • B A white count of 11.6 is mildly raised in any inflammatory arthritis; she is afebrile and well. Infection is still not excluded until the fluid is back.
  • D A tear would not make the joint red and hot, and it would not explain the meniscal calcification.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Dorothy, 61, has an acute, warm, red left knee effusion and chondrocalcinosis on X-ray. You suspect pseudogout.

stem: Which investigation is most important, and what would confirm pseudogout?

options.html: Serum uric acid; a normal level confirms pseudogout
MRI of the knee; a meniscal signal confirms it
Aspirate the knee for the 3 C's; rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent crystals with a negative Gram stain and culture
No test is needed; the X-ray is diagnostic

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: "If the joint is red, aspirate it" and send the 3 C's. Pseudogout is diagnosed by intracellular calcium pyrophosphate crystals: rhomboid and positively birefringent. The cell count is inflammatory in septic arthritis, gout and pseudogout alike, so the Gram stain and culture are what exclude infection.

  • A Uric acid cannot diagnose gout, let alone exclude it.
  • B MRI does not separate crystals from infection.
  • D Chondrocalcinosis shows calcium pyrophosphate in the cartilage, but it does not prove the crystals caused this attack, and it never excludes infection.
