preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Dorothy, 61, has an acute left knee effusion. The aspirate shows an inflammatory cell count with rhomboid, intracellular, positively birefringent crystals; the Gram stain is negative and the culture is pending. She is already taking ibuprofen 400 mg two or three times daily without relief.

stem: What is the best immediate management?

options.html: Inject a corticosteroid into the knee, with rest, ice and elevation
Start IV cefazolin until the culture returns

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture's acute pseudogout treatment: rest, ice, elevation, hydration, a steroid injected into the joint, an oral NSAID or COXIB (indomethacin 50 mg three times daily), or the same prednisone taper as gout. With infection excluded on the Gram stain and the crystals found, injecting is safe; "to inject is human, to aspirate divine" means aspirate first.

  • B Allopurinol lowers uric acid; it has no role in calcium pyrophosphate disease.
  • C Her Gram stain is negative and the crystals explain the joint. Had infection been likely, her penicillin allergy (a rash, not anaphylaxis) would matter when choosing between cefazolin and vancomycin.
  • D ✘ Arthroscopy is not a treatment for crystal arthritis.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Dorothy's acute pseudogout settles after the injection. Her X-ray showed chondrocalcinosis.

stem: Which statement about her ongoing care is best?

options.html: She needs allopurinol to prevent further attacks
Treat future attacks the same way, and screen for conditions linked to calcium pyrophosphate disease (hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism)

answer:
The correct answer is B. Pseudogout attacks are treated as they come (rest, ice, elevation, hydration, joint injection, NSAID or prednisone taper), and the lecture lists no preventive drug for it, unlike allopurinol for gout. The polyarthritis lecture's special tests for CPPD look for underlying causes: hemochromatosis, hyperparathyroidism, hypothyroidism.

  • A Allopurinol is for urate, not calcium pyrophosphate.
  • C Long-term steroids have no place after a single, settled attack.
  • D Activity is not the cause; nothing in the lectures asks her to stop.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John Tupper, a 73-year-old family doctor, has developed over 48 hours a very sore, painful right ankle and has trouble bearing weight. He has some fatigue and had a few chills last night. He had a tooth extracted 48 hours ago. He has hypertension, high cholesterol, hypothyroidism and mild asthma, and takes hydrochlorothiazide 12.5 mg, metoprolol, atorvastatin, levothyroxine and salbutamol. His father had severe gout. He had a remote fracture of that ankle. Exam: BP 155/90, pulse 95, temperature 37.6 °C; a very warm, red, painful ankle; the other joints are normal; a new grade 2/6 systolic ejection murmur at the apex.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis?

options.html: Osteoarthritis after his old fracture, nothing else
Ankle sprain, Achilles tendinopathy, plantar fasciitis

answer:
The correct answer is A. An acute red, hot, swollen single joint is "infection, infection, infection, gout, pseudogout". John has a reason for each: a possible bacteremia from the dental extraction, a thiazide and a family history of gout, and his age for pseudogout.

  • B Post-traumatic OA is chronic and activity-related with a cool effusion, not a hot joint over 48 hours.
  • C He recalls no injury, and none of these makes a joint red and hot.
  • D These are polyarthritides with systemic features; this is a single acute joint.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 73, has a 48-hour hot, red right ankle two days after a tooth extraction, with chills, a temperature of 37.6 °C, a pulse of 95 and a systolic murmur at the apex. He takes hydrochlorothiazide, and his father had gout. He has never had gout.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it?

options.html: Gout: the thiazide and the family history
Septic arthritis: a likely bacteremia after dental work, chills, low-grade fever, tachycardia and a murmur, in a first-ever attack
Cellulitis of the ankle: the redness and warmth

answer:
The correct answer is C. The lecture: bacteria most often reach a joint through the blood from a remote site (#1), and age is a risk factor. Dental extraction can seed the blood; chills, a low-grade fever and a fast pulse suggest systemic infection, and a murmur raises the question of endocarditis. Septic arthritis is a medical emergency, so it is the diagnosis to act on until the fluid says otherwise.

  • A Gout is on the list (thiazide, father), but he has never had an attack, and gout does not explain the chills or the murmur.
  • B Pseudogout favours the knee and does not explain the systemic signs.
  • D Cellulitis can sit over a joint, but he cannot bear weight and resists range of motion, which point to the joint itself.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 73, has a hot, red right ankle with chills, a temperature of 37.6 °C, a pulse of 95 and a new apical systolic murmur, two days after a tooth extraction. You suspect septic arthritis.

stem: Which set of investigations is best?

options.html: Serum uric acid and an ankle X-ray only
MRI of the ankle, then decide on aspiration
Start antibiotics now and aspirate in a week if he is no better
Aspirate the ankle for cell count, Gram stain and culture, and crystals; blood cultures; blood count, electrolytes, creatinine and CRP

answer:
The correct answer is D. The lecture's septic arthritis workup: aspirate (3 C's), blood cultures, blood count, electrolytes, creatinine, C-reactive protein, ± imaging. The fluid also finds crystals if this is gout after all. With a new murmur after a bacteremic procedure, the blood cultures matter twice: for the joint and for endocarditis (an echocardiogram would be the natural next test, though the lectures do not discuss it).

  • A Uric acid cannot diagnose or exclude gout, and an X-ray cannot exclude infection.
  • B Imaging is optional; it must not delay the aspiration.
  • C Antibiotics before the aspirate and blood cultures can sterilize the cultures, and a week's delay risks fulminant joint damage.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 73, has a hot right ankle after a dental extraction. The aspirate shows an inflammatory cell count, no crystals, and Gram-positive cocci on Gram stain. Blood cultures have been drawn. Culture is pending.

stem: What is the best immediate management?

options.html: Indomethacin 50 mg three times daily and review in 48 hours
Admit, consult orthopedic surgery for urgent incision and drainage, and start empiric IV antibiotics (e.g. cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours)
Inject a corticosteroid into the ankle
Oral cephalexin as an outpatient, with review once the culture is back

answer:
The correct answer is B. The lecture's septic arthritis treatment: admit, urgent incision and drainage, because an infected joint is a closed space, repeated until the joint is clean, and empiric IV antibiotics: cefazolin 2 g IV every 8 hours, or vancomycin 15 mg/kg plus ceftriaxone 2 g IV every 24 hours with MRSA risk. The lecture's own septic ankle went to the emergency department, orthopedics was consulted, and he was in the operating room that evening.

  • A treats gout; the Gram stain shows bacteria and there are no crystals.
  • C ⚠ Injecting a steroid into an infected joint treats the wrong disease.
  • D Septic arthritis is an emergency that needs IV antibiotics and drainage, not outpatient oral therapy.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 73, is admitted with septic arthritis of the right ankle. He has had incision and drainage and started empiric IV antibiotics. He has a new murmur.

stem: Which statement about the rest of his treatment is best?

options.html: Antibiotics for 4-6 weeks in all, tailored to the culture, with repeat drainage until the joint is clean, and a search for the source given the murmur
Three days of IV antibiotics, then stop once the fever settles
Start allopurinol, since his father had gout
No further drainage is ever needed after the first washout

answer:
The correct answer is A. The lecture: 4-6 weeks of antibiotics in all, with drainage repeated until the joint is clean. Culture and sensitivity (24-48 hours) let the empiric antibiotic be narrowed. Because spread is usually through the blood from a remote site, the murmur after dental work needs the source looked for (the blood cultures, and endocarditis, which the lectures do not cover further).

  • B Three days is far too short; untreated or undertreated infection causes fulminant joint damage.
  • C Isolated hyperuricemia and a family history are not indications for allopurinol, and he has never had gout.
  • D The lecture repeats drainage until the joint is clean.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John Delaney, a 26-year-old recently married man, has had 3 months of pain and swelling that began in the right index MCP and PIP, then spread to the left ring DIP, right wrist and left ankle, with two hours of morning stiffness. A year ago a right 4th toe became painful, red and swollen and was amputated as presumed cellulitis or osteomyelitis. He has had left Achilles tendonitis and recurrent plantar fasciitis. Six months ago a painful red right eye cleared with steroid drops. He has scaling behind the ears and on the scalp, pitted nails with onycholysis, and his father and brother have psoriasis. No low back problems. He takes ibuprofen 200 mg four times daily.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for John's problem? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus, Sjögren's syndrome, mixed connective tissue disease
Septic arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, cellulitis with osteomyelitis
Psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, IBD-associated arthritis, polyarticular gout
Erosive osteoarthritis, polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia, hypothyroid myopathy

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Jiang, Approach to Inflammatory Polyarthritis, "Pattern of distribution"): an "Asymmetric polyarthritis, Small and large joints" is psoriatic arthritis (other asymmetric: gout, reactive), and over 6 weeks is chronic ("Review: Arthritis classification"). Slides (Rohekar, Spondyloarthritis, "Concept of SpA") put arthritis associated with ulcerative colitis or Crohn's disease in the same family as psoriatic and reactive arthritis, so ask about bowel symptoms. Reactive arthritis fits a young man with enthesitis and eye disease (Rohekar, Psoriatic Arthritis and Reactive Arthritis: "Most common in young men (20-40 years old)"), and its keratoderma blennorrhagicum is a "psoriasis-like" skin lesion. The session notes add the histories to take: diarrhea, urethritis and sexual history. Ankylosing spondylitis is less likely with no back pain, since it "classically begins in the sacroiliac joints" (Rohekar).

  • A These are symmetric polyarthritides (Jiang: "Symmetric polyarthritis, small and large joints: Rheumatoid arthritis (other symmetric: SLE, CTD)"), and Jiang's slide says "DIPs ... spared in RA and other CTDs". John has DIP disease.
  • B Jiang's temporal pattern: infectious arthritis is "Acute (hours to days)". Three months of additive joints with skin, nail and eye disease is not infection.
  • D None of these give warm, swollen, tender joints with dactylitis and enthesitis in a 26-year-old. The slides class osteoarthritis as non-inflammatory (Jiang) and describe PMR as over 50 with normal joints on exam (Anwar, Polymyalgia Rheumatica).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 26, has an asymmetric polyarthritis including a DIP, a past "cellulitis" of a whole toe, Achilles tendonitis and plantar fasciitis, a past painful red eye that cleared with steroid drops, scaly plaques behind the ears and on the scalp, nail pitting and onycholysis, and a father and brother with psoriasis. The involved joints have a reddish-purple hue.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Psoriatic arthritis: asymmetric with a DIP, dactylitis, enthesitis, uveitis, hidden psoriasis and nail disease
Reactive arthritis: a young man with uveitis, heel enthesitis and a lower-limb oligoarthritis after an infection
Rheumatoid arthritis: two hours of morning stiffness with warm, swollen MCP, PIP and wrist joints
Ankylosing spondylitis: Achilles tendonitis, plantar fasciitis, anterior uveitis and a man under 40

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Rohekar, Psoriatic Arthritis and Reactive Arthritis, table "Key features that help distinguish between psoriatic arthritis and rheumatoid arthritis"): psoriatic arthritis has DIP joints in 30-50%, an asymmetric "ray" pattern, enthesitis, dactylitis and periarticular erythema, and nail dystrophy. The "Extraarticular Features" slide gives nail changes in 80% of psoriatic arthritis (pitting, onycholysis) and uveitis in 7%; the "Epidemiology" slide says first-degree relatives are 50x more likely to develop arthritis; and the slides say "Remember 'hidden' Ps: umbilicus, scalp, behind ears, perianal, nails". The enthesitis sites (Achilles, plantar fascia) are on Rohekar's "Enthesitis" slide. The amputated toe was almost certainly a dactylitic sausage digit, the case's teaching moment (the session notes).

  • B Rohekar's reactive arthritis follows a GI or GU infection, with symptoms "within 1-3 weeks", and gives a "Large joint oligoarthritis". Nothing here explains the psoriasis, nails or DIP.
  • C Long morning stiffness fits any inflammatory arthritis, but rheumatoid arthritis is symmetric, a "row" pattern, with DIP involvement "uncommon" (Rohekar table), and Jiang's slide says the DIPs are spared in RA.
  • D Ankylosing spondylitis "classically begins in the sacroiliac joints and slowly ascends the spine" (Rohekar). John denies back problems, and the skin and nails point elsewhere.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 26, has a chronic asymmetric polyarthritis with DIP involvement, dactylitis, enthesitis, past uveitis, scalp and retroauricular psoriasis and nail pitting. You suspect psoriatic arthritis and expect to start a DMARD.

stem: Which initial workup is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: ANA with reflex anti-dsDNA, complement C3 and C4, and an ENA panel to screen for a connective tissue disease
HLA-B27 and an MRI of the sacroiliac joints, since a positive HLA-B27 confirms a spondyloarthritis
Serum uric acid and a repeat foot X-ray, since the amputated toe was most likely tophaceous gout
CBC, CRP, creatinine, liver enzymes, RF and anti-CCP, hepatitis B and C, and hand and foot X-rays

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Jiang, Approach to Inflammatory Polyarthritis, "Routine labs"): CBC (low hemoglobin from anemia of chronic disease, high platelets from inflammation), creatinine and liver enzymes (they affect drug clearance), and "CRP: most commonly used". RF and anti-CCP are for "clinical suspicion for rheumatoid arthritis" (Jiang, "RF and anti-CCP: When to order?"); RA is on the list for an MCP, PIP and wrist polyarthritis, and a negative result fits the spondyloarthritides, which are "often called 'seronegative spondyloarthritis' due to absence of rheumatoid factor" (Rohekar, Spondyloarthritis). X-rays help "differentiate between types of inflammatory arthritis" and give a "baseline, prior to treatment" (Jiang, "X-rays"); psoriatic arthritis shows DIP erosions and periostitis or bony proliferation (Rohekar table). Hepatitis B and C serology (± chest X-ray) is the methotrexate baseline (Boyd, Disease Modifying Drugs, "Methotrexate: Monitoring"). The session notes add uric acid (Jiang's special lab for gout), aspirating any effusion, an STI screen for reactive arthritis, and the "pencil-in-cup" X-ray sign (not on the slides).

  • A Slides (Pope, Lab tests for Connective Tissue Diseases, slide 4): order the ANA "Only when/if you suspect an autoimmune connective tissue disease", and complement is a "Waste of $ for you to order it if you are not a specialist" (slide 19). Nothing here suggests a connective tissue disease.
  • B HLA-B27 is "Present in 8% of the general Caucasian population" (Rohekar, "Epidemiology and Pathogenesis of AS"), so a positive result confirms nothing; Jiang lists it as the special lab for ankylosing spondylitis. He has no back pain to image.
  • C Uric acid is Jiang's special lab for gout and a reasonable add-on, but the skin, nails, DIP and enthesitis are not gout, and uric acid alone proves nothing.

flags.title: Slides vs the session notes: ESR
flags.html: The session notes order "CBC, ESR and CRP". Jiang's "Routine labs" slide says "CRP: most commonly used" and "ESR: not routinely ordered. Nonspecific, as it can be falsely elevated by a number of things." The slides were followed, so the keyed option leaves ESR out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 26, has psoriatic arthritis with active synovitis of the right index MCP and PIP, left ring DIP, right wrist and left ankle. He takes ibuprofen 200 mg four times daily. He was recently married and has no children. He drinks occasionally.

stem: What is the best immediate management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Keep ibuprofen 200 mg four times daily and re-examine him in 3 months before adding anything
Naproxen 500 mg twice daily, joint injections, and methotrexate with rheumatology referral
Hydroxychloroquine, the gentlest conventional DMARD, with ibuprofen kept at 200 mg four times daily
High-dose prednisone, about 1 mg/kg, for several months until all the swollen joints settle

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Boyd, NSAIDs and Acetaminophen, "NSAIDs: Examples"): the anti-inflammatory doses are ibuprofen 600-800 mg TID and naproxen 500 mg BID, and psoriatic arthritis is on the indications slide; John's 200 mg four times daily is well below that. Slides (Boyd, Steroids in Rheumatology, "Which Route to Choose?"): a cortisone injection is "often used if only a few joints are swollen", with fewer systemic adverse effects; but Boyd's Intra-articular Injections deck lists "Skin surface covered by psoriatic plaques" as a relative contraindication (bacterial skin flora in plaques), so inject only through clear skin. Slides (Rohekar, "Treatment of Psoriatic Arthritis"): "Methotrexate will treat both skin and joints." Before starting, Boyd's methotrexate slide says "Avoid in pregnancy: teratogenic" and "Avoid alcohol", so discuss family planning and drinking.

  • A "NSAIDs are not Disease Modifying in RA" (Boyd), and at this dose it is not even an anti-inflammatory.
  • C ✘ Rohekar: "Hydroxychloroquine often avoided due to case reports of severe psoriasis flares."
  • D Boyd's high dose (~1 mg/kg) is for serious or life-threatening conditions: ANCA-associated vasculitis, lupus nephritis, inflammatory myositis and giant cell arteritis. The session notes add that tapering systemic steroids can flare psoriasis (not on the slides).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: John, 26, started methotrexate for psoriatic arthritis. His peripheral joints have improved, but he still has heel enthesitis and a new sausage digit. He and his wife hope to have children.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best?

options.html: Methotrexate alone for life, since it controls his skin, peripheral joints, entheses and spine
Long-term low-dose prednisone, 5 mg or less, to keep both the skin and the joints quiet
Escalate to a TNF or IL-17 inhibitor and plan any pregnancy around the methotrexate
Add hydroxychloroquine to methotrexate as dual therapy, since both drugs help skin disease

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Rohekar, "Treatment of Psoriatic Arthritis"): "csDMARDs often used, but evidence that they prevent radiographic progression is limited." TNF inhibitors are "effective for both axial and peripheral symptoms", "Treat skin, joints, enthesitis, dactylitis, nails" and "Prevent radiographic progression"; IL-17 inhibitors are "amazing for skin" and "effective for axial and joint symptoms". Boyd (Biologics) adds that biologics usually follow failure of other DMARDs, which is John's position. Boyd's methotrexate slide: "Avoid in pregnancy: teratogenic", with folic acid and no alcohol, so pregnancy is planned around it. The treat-to-target rhythm (adjust every 3-6 months) is on Boyd's RA slide, not Rohekar's psoriatic arthritis slides. The session notes add dermatology, and ophthalmology if the uveitis recurs.

  • A Rohekar: "csDMARDs do not work for spinal disease", and the slides credit TNF inhibitors, not conventional DMARDs, with treating enthesitis and dactylitis. The session notes add that methotrexate does little for enthesitis and dactylitis.
  • B Boyd's low dose (5 mg or less) is "used chronically when other options don't work", and chronic prednisone brings osteoporosis, infection and avascular necrosis ("Good short term, not long term!").
  • D ✘ Rohekar: hydroxychloroquine is "often avoided" in psoriatic arthritis because of severe psoriasis flares.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Pauline Turner, a 42-year-old mother of 4, has 6 months of gradually progressive pain, swelling and stiffness of the MCPs, PIPs, wrists, shoulders, knees and the balls of her feet. Morning stiffness lasts until noon. She is fatigued and may have lost a few pounds. She buys artificial tears for itchy, irritated eyes, keeps water at the bedside, and has had four dental caries this year. Exam: reduced tear film, a dry mouth with no salivary pool, halitosis, warm, swollen MCPs, PIPs and wrists, bilateral knee effusions, and tender MTPs on squeeze. She takes enteric-coated aspirin.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Pauline's problem? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Polyarticular gout, pseudogout (CPPD), and septic arthritis from bacterial endocarditis
Rheumatoid arthritis, Sjögren's syndrome, SLE, and viral arthritis such as hepatitis C
Psoriatic arthritis, reactive arthritis, enteropathic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis
Polymyalgia rheumatica, fibromyalgia, generalized osteoarthritis and hypothyroidism

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Jiang, Approach to Inflammatory Polyarthritis): an "Insidious/chronic (weeks to months)", "Progressive and additive" course is RA, CTDs, and a "Symmetric polyarthritis, small and large joints" is rheumatoid arthritis (other symmetric: SLE, CTD). Sicca is on Jiang's extra-articular list (ocular), and Pope's Sjögren's slides name dry eyes, dry mouth, dental caries and halitosis, with arthritis among the extra-glandular features. Jiang's "A quick note on viral arthritis" lists hepatitis A, B, C and parvovirus among the pathogens, and "RF" lists hepatitis C among the infections that make RF positive; viral arthritis is "Self-limited", so 6 months is long for it.

  • A Jiang: crystal and infectious arthritis are "Acute (hours to days)". This came on gradually over 6 months.
  • C Jiang puts psoriatic and reactive arthritis in the asymmetric pattern and ankylosing spondylitis in the axial one; she has no skin, gut, genital or back clues.
  • D She has true synovitis and effusions. Anwar's PMR slides say "other than pain, examination of muscles and joints is normal", and fibromyalgia is the patient whose "rheumatologist said my joints aren't swollen".

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Pauline, 42, has 6 months of symmetric synovitis of the MCPs, PIPs, wrists and MTPs, with shoulder and knee involvement and knee effusions. Morning stiffness lasts until noon. She cannot make a tight finger tuck, her grip is weak, and she is off work. She has dry eyes, a dry mouth, new dental caries and halitosis. There is no rash, no mouth ulcers and no fever.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Primary Sjögren's syndrome: dry eyes, dry mouth, new caries and halitosis dominate the picture
SLE: a woman of childbearing age with fatigue, weight loss and a symmetric polyarthritis
Parvovirus B19 arthritis: a mother of four with a symmetric small-joint polyarthritis
RA with secondary Sjögren's: 6 months of symmetric small-joint synovitis and sicca

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Jiang, Approach to Inflammatory Polyarthritis): a symmetric small and large joint polyarthritis is rheumatoid arthritis, MCPs are an RA joint ("Predilection for certain joints"), the DIPs are spared, and over 6 weeks is chronic. Slides (Rohekar, table of psoriatic vs rheumatoid arthritis): RA's extra-articular features are nodules, sicca and vasculitis. Slides (Pope, Sjögren's Syndrome): the dry mouth brings halitosis and dental caries. Hours of morning stiffness fit an inflammatory arthritis; the slides give no RA-specific cut-off (Rohekar's "> 60 min am stiffness" is for inflammatory back pain).

  • A Pope lists arthritis among Sjögren's extra-glandular features, but here symmetric synovitis of the MCPs, wrists and MTPs with knee effusions is the dominant problem, and Jiang's pattern for that is rheumatoid arthritis.
  • B Pope's SLE criteria bring rash in the sun, oral ulcers, serositis or low counts; she has none.
  • C Jiang: viral arthritis is "Self-limited"; 6 months of progressive disease is too long.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Pauline, 42, has a 6-month symmetric small-joint polyarthritis with knee effusions and sicca symptoms. You suspect rheumatoid arthritis with secondary Sjögren's and expect to start methotrexate.

stem: Which investigation plan is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: RF, anti-CCP, CBC, CRP, ANA and ENA (Ro, La), hepatitis B and C, and hand and foot X-rays
HLA-B27, CRP and sacroiliac X-rays, since a polyarthritis with eye symptoms suggests spondyloarthritis
Anti-dsDNA, complement C3 and C4 and urinalysis first, and an ANA only if the anti-dsDNA is positive
A single RF now, then repeat RF titres every 3 months to judge disease activity and treatment response

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Jiang, Approach to Inflammatory Polyarthritis, "RF and anti-CCP: When to order?"): "Only for initial diagnostic purposes, when there is a clinical suspicion for rheumatoid arthritis. Eg. patient presenting with true swollen joints and have elevated inflammatory markers." Anti-CCP is the specific one ("spec. 95%"), and "seropositive" patients "are more likely to have aggressive disease". Sicca makes a connective tissue disease plausible, which is when Pope orders the ANA (Lab tests, slide 4), and the ENA follows: "Ro and La together go with Sjögren's Syndrome" (slide 18). Pope's Sjögren's lab slide: ANA positive in 80-90% and RF in 90%. Routine labs (Jiang): CBC (anemia of chronic disease), CRP, creatinine and liver enzymes. Hepatitis B and C serology (± chest X-ray) is the methotrexate baseline (Boyd, Disease Modifying Drugs), and hepatitis C is also a viral mimic (Jiang). X-rays are a "Baseline, prior to treatment" (Jiang); RA shows periarticular osteopenia and wrist erosions (Rohekar table). The session notes add aspirating a knee and a Schirmer test or ophthalmology referral.

  • B Jiang lists HLA-B27 as the special lab for ankylosing spondylitis; her eye problem is sicca, not uveitis, and she has no axial disease.
  • C ⚠ Pope (slide 14): "Only order anti DNA in the presence of a positive ANA", and complement is a "Waste of $ for you to order it if you are not a specialist" (slide 19).
  • D Jiang: when NOT to order RF and anti-CCP: "For 'monitoring' purposes. Titres are not predictive of flares or response to therapy."

flags.title: Slides vs the session notes: ESR
flags.html: The session notes list "CBC (expect anemia of chronic disease), ESR and CRP", and 01 - Rheumatology Investigations pairs RF and anti-CCP with "ESR and CRP". Jiang's "Routine labs" slide says "CRP: most commonly used" and "ESR: not routinely ordered" because it is nonspecific. ESR does appear elsewhere in the slides: Pope's Sjögren's lab slide says the ESR is "often quite high", and Boyd's DMARD monitoring includes ESR and CRP, but neither is an instruction to order it at diagnosis. The slides were followed, so the keyed option leaves ESR out.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Pauline, 42, has seropositive rheumatoid arthritis with secondary Sjögren's. Symptoms began 6 months ago. She has active synovitis of the hands, wrists and MTPs and large knee effusions (aspirate: inflammatory, no crystals, culture negative). She is off work and taking enteric-coated aspirin. Liver enzymes, creatinine and hepatitis serology are normal.

stem: What is the best immediate management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Keep the enteric-coated aspirin and reassess in 6 months, since many polyarthritides burn out
Start a TNF inhibitor now, as first-line therapy, because she is likely to be seropositive
Urgent referral, triple DMARD therapy, and a prednisone bridge or knee injections
High-dose prednisone, about 1 mg/kg, continued long term as the main treatment

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Boyd, Disease Modifying Drugs, "Approach to Treatment of Rheumatoid Arthritis"): joint damage is early ("Erosions occur in >90% of patients within 2 years"), so there is a "Window of Opportunity": treat early, aggressively and appropriately, starting DMARDs "within 3 months of symptom onset" (she is already past that). "Multiple studies have confirmed the use of 'triple therapy' in early RA is more effective than a single agent", and the "Common RA Treatment Strategies" slide says "Start triple therapy for 3-6 months" (methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine). Boyd's methotrexate slides: 20-25 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg weekly, onset 6-8 weeks. Slides (Boyd, Steroids in Rheumatology): an RA flare takes prednisone 20-40 mg daily "with taper as start DMARD", used "for 'bridging therapy' until steroid-sparing medications can be started", and a cortisone injection suits "weight-bearing joints affected". Boyd's injection deck says to "wait until culture negative before injecting steroid"; her culture is negative.

  • A "NSAIDs are not Disease Modifying in RA" (Boyd), and 6 more months would waste the window.
  • B Boyd (Biologics): "Biologics are expensive as a result, patients usually need to have failed other DMARD therapies before using them."
  • D Boyd: high dose is for serious or life-threatening conditions, and prednisone is "Good short term, not long term!"

flags.title: Slides vs the session notes: methotrexate first or triple therapy from the start
flags.html: The session notes say to start methotrexate with folic acid and add hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine as triple therapy. Boyd's slides start with triple therapy ("Start triple therapy for 3-6 months") because it beats a single agent in early RA. The slides were followed: the keyed option now reads "triple DMARD therapy" (it previously read "methotrexate with folic acid").

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Pauline, 42, has started triple therapy (methotrexate with folic acid, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine) for rheumatoid arthritis with secondary Sjögren's. Three months later she still has several swollen joints, and her dry eyes and mouth continue to bother her.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best?

options.html: Methotrexate alone at a fixed dose for life, with RF titres repeated to guide any changes
Stop the DMARD once the joints settle and restart it only for flares, to limit toxicity
Hydroxychloroquine alone, since it needs no blood monitoring and is safe in pregnancy
Treat to remission, adjusting every 3-6 months, adding a biologic if needed; sicca care

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Boyd, Disease Modifying Drugs): "Monitor patient regularly for ongoing disease activity: goal is remission (no swollen or tender joints)" and "Therapy should be adjusted every 3-6 months if treatment goal not achieved" ("Treat-to-target approach"). For an incomplete response ("Common RA Treatment Strategies"): change methotrexate from PO to SC, add leflunomide, and consider adding a biologic. Methotrexate and sulfasalazine need monthly CBC with differential, ALT, creatinine, ESR and CRP; hydroxychloroquine needs a baseline and annual eye exam. The slides do not cover sicca treatment; the sicca care rests on the session notes (artificial tears, sugar-free gum or lozenges, saliva substitutes, fluoride and close dental follow-up), which also add OT and PT and vaccines before immunosuppression.

  • A Jiang: RF titres are not for "monitoring", and Boyd says to use "combination therapy over single therapy" and adjust to target, not hold a fixed dose.
  • B Boyd: "Damage results in subsequent damage"; the goal is sustained remission, and stopping lets erosions advance.
  • C Boyd's hydroxychloroquine slide is right that it needs "No laboratory monitoring" and is "Safe in pregnancy", but a single agent is weaker than combination therapy, and she has not responded to three drugs.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ana Barclay, a 17-year-old student, has 2 weeks of severe right-sided chest pain worse with movement and deep breathing, and 3 months of painful stiff fingers, wrists and knees. She has profound fatigue. This summer she blistered on her arms and cheeks after a beach trip. She notes hair on her pillow and more mouth sores. She takes minocycline for acne and occasional ibuprofen. Exam: malar erythema, ulcers in the mouth and on the nasal septum, puffy fingers with fusiform PIP swelling, swollen wrists and bilateral knee effusions.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Ana's problem? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: SLE, minocycline-induced lupus, viral arthritis, early RA or juvenile arthritis
Septic arthritis, disseminated gonococcal infection, acute gout and pseudogout
Ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis and enteropathic arthritis
Fibromyalgia, polymyalgia rheumatica, osteoarthritis, and rosacea with costochondritis

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders): her picture matches the deck's SLE case and criteria (malar rash, photosensitivity, oral or nasal ulcers, inflammatory arthritis, pleurisy, hair loss) in a young woman ("SLE affects young people", 9:1 women to men). Pope also says SLE is "Rarely ... drug induced: often milder course, joints, skin and serositis", and Jiang's ENA slide pairs anti-histone with drug-induced lupus. The slides do not name minocycline as a cause; that rests on the vault's drug-induced lupus erythematosus note and the session notes. Jiang's inflammatory polyarthritis list includes RA, viral arthritis and polyarticular JIA. The session notes add MCTD and dermatomyositis, rosacea for the rash, and pericarditis, pleurisy, PE and pneumonia for the chest pain.

  • B Jiang: crystal and infectious arthritis are acute (hours to days), and they explain none of the rash, ulcers or pleurisy.
  • C Jiang puts the seronegative arthritides in the asymmetric or axial patterns; they do not give a malar rash or oral ulcers.
  • D She has true synovitis and effusions. Pope: rosacea "does not spare the nasolabial folds" and "is not an autoimmune rash".

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ana, 17, has pleuritic chest pain, symmetric PIP, wrist and knee synovitis, malar erythema, blistering after sun exposure, oral and nasal ulcers, hair loss, and profound fatigue. She takes minocycline for acne.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Rosacea with a coincidental viral arthritis: facial redness, acne treatment and recent joint pain
Drug-induced lupus, proven by the minocycline, so no other diagnosis need be considered
SLE: serositis, inflammatory arthritis, malar rash, photosensitivity, oral ulcers and alopecia
Dermatomyositis: a photosensitive rash, puffy fingers and difficulty making a tight fist

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders, "SLE Criteria"): malar rash, photosensitivity, oral or nasal ulcers, inflammatory arthritis (non erosive), and pleurisy or serositis ("chest pain made worse with deep inspiration"), plus hair loss, which Pope's case counts as alopecia; 9:1 women to men. On Pope's 2019 EULAR/ACR slide, the entry criterion is an ANA of at least 1:80 and a score of 10 classifies; acute cutaneous lupus scores 6 and joint involvement 6, so she reaches 12 once the ANA is positive (the session notes make the same count).

  • A Pope: rosacea "may have dilated blood vessels", does not spare the nasolabial folds, and is not autoimmune; it explains nothing below the face.
  • B Pope: drug-induced lupus is rare, with an "often milder course, joints, skin and serositis". Ana's joints, skin and pleurisy fit either, so nothing is "proven" by the drug history: the antibodies (anti-histone, per Jiang) and the course after stopping the drug must sort it out, and SLE stays first.
  • D Pope: dermatomyositis is proximal muscle weakness with an elevated CK, Gottron's papules and a heliotrope rash; she has no weakness.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ana, 17, has pleuritic chest pain, symmetric polyarthritis, a photosensitive malar rash, oral and nasal ulcers and hair loss, and takes minocycline. You suspect SLE but must exclude drug-induced lupus.

stem: Which investigation plan is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Anti-dsDNA first, then an ANA only if the anti-dsDNA comes back positive, to save on testing
ANA, then anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, anti-histone; CBC, ESR, creatinine, urinalysis; ECG, chest X-ray
RF and anti-CCP alone, since this is a symmetric small-joint polyarthritis in a young woman
No tests: lupus is a clinical diagnosis, so start high-dose prednisone and see whether she responds

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders, "SLE Initial Labs To Consider Ordering"): CBC with differential (hematologic abnormalities), ESR, creatinine and urinalysis (renal involvement), ANA as the screening test, "Maybe ENA Panel", and "Don't order anti-DNA unless if ANA is positive". Tests serve diagnosis, prognosis and treatment safety (Pope, "So what tests are you going to order?"). The ANA is positive in over 95% of SLE; anti-dsDNA is "very specific for SLE but very insensitive" (about 50%) and "correlates with renal SLE"; anti-Sm is "fairly specific for SLE" (Pope, Lab tests, slides 14, 16 and 18). Jiang's ENA slide pairs anti-histone with drug-induced lupus. Pope's hematologic criterion: hemolytic anemia is "Usually Coomb's test positive". Pericarditis has "characteristic changes on electrocardiogram" and pleuritis is "often associated with a pleural effusion", which justifies the ECG and chest X-ray. The session notes add antiphospholipid antibodies, anti-Ro and anti-La (Pope: Ro raises the risk of congenital heart block) and liver enzymes.

  • A ⚠ Pope (Lab tests, slide 22): "NO, order the ANA first and only if positive order the anti-DNA", and "A double stranded DNA cannot occur with a negative ANA" (Connective Tissue Disorders).
  • C Jiang: RF and anti-CCP are for suspected rheumatoid arthritis, and RF is also positive in SLE (Jiang's RF slide), so they cannot answer the lupus question.
  • D Pope's SLE work-up is a set of tests, and Boyd keeps high-dose steroid for serious or life-threatening disease.

flags.title: Slides vs the session notes: complement and p-ANCA
flags.html: The session notes order C3 and C4 and say minocycline-induced lupus is often p-ANCA positive with hepatitis. On complement, the slides say "Waste of $ for you to order it if you are not a specialist" (Pope, Lab tests, slide 19) and list it only as "Maybe: Complement levels: C3, C4, CH50" (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders), although low C3 or C4 scores points on the 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria and Jiang's "Lupus and seroconcordance" slide tracks it with disease activity. The slides do not link p-ANCA to minocycline: ANCA appears only in Barra's vasculitis deck (c-ANCA in GPA, p-ANCA in MPA and EGPA). The slides were followed, so the keyed option leaves both out. The option now includes ESR, which Pope's "SLE Initial Labs" slide lists.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ana, 17, has SLE (ANA 1:640, anti-dsDNA positive) with pleurisy, arthritis, a photosensitive malar rash and mouth ulcers. Urinalysis and creatinine are normal; blood counts are mildly low. She still takes minocycline for acne.

stem: What is the best immediate management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Pulse IV methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide, as for major organ lupus
Continue minocycline for her acne and add hydroxychloroquine and a sunscreen
An NSAID alone for the pleurisy and joints, waiting for the final antibody results
Stop minocycline, start hydroxychloroquine, and an NSAID or low-dose prednisone

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders, "Pharmacologic Rx in SLE"): hydroxychloroquine "may be beneficial and protective of major disease flares"; "Give to every patient with SLE unless if there is a contraindication"; it is the "Anchor drug for SLE treatment and especially helps skin and joints". Treatment "Depends on severity of disease": "NSAIDs help joint pain, swelling, stiffness", topical steroid for skin rash, "Low dose oral prednisone for mild to moderate arthritis". Non-drug care: sun avoidance and "Sunscreen with minimum SPF 30". Boyd's hydroxychloroquine slide adds a baseline and annual eye exam. The slides do not cover stopping the drug: stopping minocycline, with drug-induced lupus expected to settle over weeks to months, rests on the session notes.

  • A Pope: cyclophosphamide is "Only for serious major internal organ involvement", and Boyd keeps pulse IV methylprednisolone for life- or organ-threatening disease. Her kidneys and brain are spared.
  • B Continuing a drug that can cause lupus confounds the picture and may drive it (reasoning from the session notes; the slides are silent on this step).
  • C An NSAID helps joints, but leaving out the anchor drug and the minocycline question misses the key steps, and Boyd says NSAIDs need caution in renal disease.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Ana, 17, has SLE that settled on hydroxychloroquine and a short prednisone course after minocycline was stopped. Her antiphospholipid antibodies are positive. She is sexually active and asks about the future.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best?

options.html: Lifelong hydroxychloroquine, eye exams, sun protection, cardiovascular care, counselling
Stop all treatment once the chest pain and joints settle, and restart only if symptoms return
Long-term prednisone at 20 mg daily to prevent flares while she finishes high school
Repeat the ANA every 6 months and adjust her treatment according to the change in titre

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Pope, Connective Tissue Disorders, "EULAR guidelines for SLE treatment"): hydroxychloroquine at every severity; the target is remission (hydroxychloroquine, no glucocorticoid) or low disease activity (hydroxychloroquine, prednisone 7.5 mg a day or less); adjuncts are sun protection, vaccinations, exercise, no smoking, body weight, blood pressure, lipids, glucose, and antiplatelets or anticoagulants in aPL-positive patients. Pope's "Non-Pharmacologic Rx": education, SPF 30+, rheumatology follow-up, and cardiac risk assessment ("Assess clotting risk"); SLE prognosis brings a 50-fold increase in cardiovascular events. Boyd: hydroxychloroquine needs a yearly eye exam. Treatment depends on the organ involved, so escalate for major organ disease. The session notes add contraception counselling (avoid estrogen with positive antiphospholipid antibodies), confidentiality and transition to adult care.

  • B Pope: hydroxychloroquine "may be beneficial and protective of major disease flares"; stopping it removes that.
  • C Prednisone 20 mg misses the 7.5 mg target and brings the steroid complications Pope lists in SLE prognosis, AVN and osteoporosis.
  • D ⚠ Pope (Lab tests, slide 11): "Is there utility in following the ANA titre? No."

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary Worthington, a 48-year-old salesperson, has 11 months of pain that began in the low back and spread to her legs and arms, aching all over, worse in the morning. Her hands feel swollen and her rings tighter. She sleeps poorly, wakes unrefreshed, and feels much better after a rare good night's sleep. Walks aggravate the pain. She has chronic migraine and irritable bowel syndrome, memory difficulties, gained 20 pounds, smokes 30 pack-years, and is stressed about money. BMI about 34, BP 150/90. No swelling of any joint. 14/18 tender points. Reflexes are normal.

stem: Which is the best differential diagnosis for Mary's problem? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Rheumatoid arthritis, lupus and Sjögren's syndrome, given her morning stiffness and tight rings
Polyarticular gout, pseudogout and septic arthritis, given the swelling and severe pain
Ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic arthritis and reactive arthritis, given the back pain at onset
Fibromyalgia, hypothyroidism, sleep apnea, depression, and less likely polymyalgia rheumatica

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Anwar, Fibromyalgia): pain in multiple areas, present for more than 3 months, with other somatic symptoms; centralizing pain brings "Comorbid CNS symptoms: fatigue, sleep, memory, mood". The rule-out slide points at the mimics: for fatigue, "CBC, Ferritin, TSH, CRP, ALT, cr, Albumin, sleep study" (hypothyroidism and sleep apnea, with her BMI 34, BP 150/90 and unrefreshing sleep), and fibromyalgia is increased with "Any psychiatric disease". Slides (Anwar, Polymyalgia Rheumatica): PMR is "Older than 50", in the shoulder and hip girdles, with elevated ESR and CRP. The session notes add vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, myopathy and, with 30 pack-years, malignancy.

  • A The inflammatory arthritides need objective synovitis; she has no swelling of any joint, Anwar's "morning stiffness and hand pain but the rheumatologist said my joints aren't swollen".
  • B Jiang: crystal and septic arthritis are acute (hours to days), with hot, swollen joints.
  • C Her back pain is worse with activity, which is Rohekar's mechanical column; inflammatory back pain "Improves with activity", and the ASAS axial SpA criteria apply to back pain starting under 45. She has no skin, gut or genital clues.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary, 48, has 11 months of widespread pain that started axially and spread, unrefreshing sleep, better after a good night, fatigue and forgetfulness, migraine and IBS, a feeling of hand swelling with no objective synovitis, pain worse with exercise, financial stress, and 14/18 tender points.

stem: Which is the most likely diagnosis, and which features most strongly support it? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Polymyalgia rheumatica: morning pain and stiffness lasting hours in a woman approaching 50
Fibromyalgia: widespread pain over 3 months, unrefreshing sleep, fog, migraine and IBS
Early rheumatoid arthritis: hours of morning stiffness, hand swelling and rings getting tighter
Hypothyroidism: weight gain of 20 pounds, fatigue, forgetfulness and generalized aching

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Anwar, Fibromyalgia): widespread pain present for more than 3 months; the clinic encounter is "so tired", "I feel like I am in a fog", "Even when I sleep 8 hours, I wake feeling like I didn't sleep at all", somatic symptoms such as "Unrelenting headaches" and irritable bowel syndrome, and "I have morning stiffness and hand pain but the rheumatologist said my joints aren't swollen". The 2010/2016 criteria (widespread pain index plus symptom severity, symptoms at a similar level for at least 3 months) are the ones to "Know"; the 1990 criteria (tender in 11 of 18 locations) are "Be aware of it, but you can forget it". Her 14/18 still supports it.

  • A Anwar: PMR is "Older than 50", in the shoulder and hip girdles, with elevated ESR and CRP, whereas in fibromyalgia there is "no elevation of inflammatory markers; stiffness is everywhere (proximal and distal)". Her pain began in the back and is everywhere.
  • C Felt swelling without objective synovitis is not rheumatoid arthritis (Anwar's "joints aren't swollen" patient).
  • D TSH is on Anwar's fatigue rule-out list, but hypothyroidism does not explain the migraine and IBS cluster, and Anwar's slide says fibromyalgia is often diagnosed "plus something else".

flags.title: Slides vs the session notes: "exclude the mimics"
flags.html: The session notes head this case "Fibromyalgia (exclude the mimics)". Anwar's slide is titled "Fibromyalgia is NOT a diagnosis of exclusion": it is "common to make a diagnosis of FM plus something else", and the 2016 criteria say the "Diagnosis [is] valid irrespective of other diagnoses". The very next slide, "BUT what do we have to rule out when diagnosing a patient with fibromyalgia?", lists targeted tests (CK, metabolic work-up, exam for swelling, fatigue labs, sleep study). So the slides agree with targeted rule-out tests but frame fibromyalgia as a positive diagnosis, not one reached by exclusion. The slides' framing was followed; the key is unchanged.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary, 48, has fibromyalgia with fatigue, 20 pounds of weight gain, memory problems, unrefreshing sleep, a BMI of 34, BP 150/90, financial stress and no synovitis. Her father died of a heart attack.

stem: Which investigation plan is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: ANA, RF and anti-CCP to screen for an autoimmune cause of her widespread pain and tight rings
MRI of the whole spine and a bone scan, given the back pain at onset and her smoking history
Targeted tests: CBC, CRP, TSH, creatinine, liver enzymes, and a sleep study for suspected apnea
No tests at all, since fibromyalgia is diagnosed clinically and testing only reinforces illness

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Anwar, Fibromyalgia, "BUT what do we have to rule out"): "Fatigue: CBC, Ferritin, TSH, CRP, ALT, cr, Albumin, sleep study", "Muscle pain: CK", and "Targeted investigations according to somatic complaints (use common sense)". Normal inflammatory markers also separate fibromyalgia from PMR (Anwar, PMR: "Fibromyalgia: no elevation of inflammatory markers"). The session notes add calcium, ALP and vitamin D as indicated, PHQ-9 and GAD-7, STOP-BANG to guide the sleep study, and lipids and A1c for her cardiovascular risk.

  • A ✘ Slides (Pope, Lab tests, slide 6): "32 year old woman with fatigue and widespread pain (thought to have fibromyalgia): NO" ANA. Jiang: "Do not reflexively order ANA and RF on every patient with joint pain", and RF and anti-CCP are for true swollen joints.
  • B The slides do not cover spinal imaging here; mild pain on lumbar flexion with normal reflexes and no inflammatory back pain features does not warrant it (reasoning, not a slide).
  • D Anwar's rule-out slide still targets tests at the mimics and comorbidities (thyroid, sleep apnea).

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary, 48, has been told she has fibromyalgia. She worries the pain means her joints are being damaged. Her daily walks make the pain worse, she sleeps poorly, and she takes occasional ibuprofen.

stem: What is the best immediate management? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Validate and educate, then graded exercise with pacing, sleep hygiene and CBT
A scheduled opioid for the pain, with a plan to reassess and taper in 3 months
A prednisone trial of 15-20 mg daily, since she has hours of morning stiffness
Advise her to stop her walks and rest until the pain settles, to protect her joints

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Anwar, Fibromyalgia, "Treating Fibromyalgia"): 1. Education, 2. Exercise (weight bearing, non weight bearing, Tai Chi or yoga, warm pool), 3. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy: "Sleep hygiene", "Pacing: 'Don't over-do it'", "Mindfulness techniques for chronic pain"; the "Tricks of the Trade" slide says "Emphasize non pharmacologic therapy", and the "Expectations" slide groups exercise, CBT and education with the drugs ("50% of patients experience a 30% improvement in pain"). Slides (Viana, Chronic Pain, "Hurt Does Not Equal Harm"): pain is "due to dysfunctional pain signal modulation rather than ongoing tissue damage", and there is "Good evidence in support of return to activity", with individualized, supervised programs best. That answers her worry about joint damage.

  • B ⚠ Anwar's "Real World Use of Opioids in FM": non-opioid users had significantly better sleep, disability and pain interference, with no difference in pain severity. Viana: "Only tramadol has been found to be effective for fibromyalgia", and Boyd says opioids have a limited role in rheumatic disease. A scheduled opioid is not the immediate step.
  • C Anwar: prednisone 15-20 mg is the PMR dose, and PMR improves "quickly and dramatically with corticosteroids"; fibromyalgia has no raised inflammatory markers.
  • D Viana: "Participating in ANY regular activity is better than activity avoidance." The walks need grading, not stopping.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: Mary, 48, has fibromyalgia and is doing graded aquatic exercise and CBT. She still has poor sleep, low mood and migraine. She smokes, her BP is 150/90, and a sleep study is pending.

stem: Which longer-term plan is best?

options.html: Full-dose NSAIDs taken regularly, since her pain began as an inflammatory back problem
One low-dose drug, such as amitriptyline or duloxetine, while treating sleep and other inputs
A combination of an opioid, pregabalin and duloxetine started together to control the pain quickly
Monthly tender point counts, raising the drug dose until fewer than 11 points remain

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Anwar, Fibromyalgia, "Tricks of the Trade"): "Start with one drug", "Start with the lowest dose", "Titrate the dose slowly", "Set expectations for benefit". Low-dose tricyclics (amitriptyline, nortriptyline, cyclobenzaprine) "Improve pain, fatigue and sleep" but have "No effect on mood"; duloxetine has the "best evidence" and is "Effective in patients with or without depression" but "Not beneficial for sleep". Treat other inputs: nociceptive pain (mechanical low back pain → PT), "Treat sleep apnea", "Treat psychiatric illness". Expectations: 50% of patients get a 30% improvement. Pregabalin is on the slides only as a number needed to treat (9 for a 30% reduction) and for its side effects (somnolence, dizziness, weight gain). The session notes add that amitriptyline also helps migraine, plus smoking cessation, blood pressure, weight, work modifications and social work.

  • A Anwar's pain phenotypes: fibromyalgia is central pain, "responsive to meds that alter levels of neurotransmitters"; NSAIDs are for nociceptive pain, and she has no inflammation.
  • C Anwar says "Consider combinations" only after starting with one drug at the lowest dose and titrating slowly; starting three at once breaks that rule, and the opioid data above argue against the opioid.
  • D Anwar: the 1990 tender point criteria are "Be aware of it, but you can forget it", and counting points is not a treatment target.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 56-year-old woman with a 12-year history of seropositive rheumatoid arthritis presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and a dry cough. She takes hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate. Exam: fine bibasilar crackles. No fever.

stem: What is the most likely working diagnosis? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Pneumocystis pneumonia from her methotrexate immunosuppression

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Malette, Rheumatologic Complications, "Pulmonary Manifestations of Rheumatoid Arthritis"): interstitial lung disease heads the list, ahead of pleural effusions, nodules and methotrexate pneumonitis. The "RA: ILD" slide puts it in "10-15% of patients", "often asymptomatic", with a work-up of chest X-ray and HRCT. Slides (Polyarthritis, "RF and anti-CCP"): seropositive patients are "more likely to have aggressive disease", including extra-articular manifestations, which fits her 12 years of seropositive disease. The "Types of RA: ILD" slide lists usual interstitial pneumonia first; that it is the commonest pattern, and the "velcro" crackles of fibrosis, come from the session notes, not the slides.

  • B Slides (Malette, "Methotrexate-Induced Injury"): it "often occurs weeks to months after treatment initiation", and Slides (Boyd, DMARDs) describe methotrexate's acute pneumonitis as "dry cough, SOB, fever". She has been treated for years and has no fever. It stays on the differential, since methotrexate pneumonitis is on the lecture's own list of RA lung problems.
  • C The lecture ties Pneumocystis to corticosteroids at over 15 mg a day ("Risk of Corticosteroids"); she is not on steroids, and a slow course without fever fits fibrosis better.
  • D The lecture does list coronary disease and heart failure (a twofold increase) among RA's cardiac manifestations, but fine basal crackles with a dry cough over a progressive course point to the lung.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 56-year-old woman with long-standing seropositive RA on hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate has progressive exertional dyspnea, a dry cough and fine bibasilar crackles. You suspect RA-associated ILD.

stem: Which investigations are the key ones to order? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A chest X-ray alone, since a normal film rules out interstitial lung disease
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP titres to measure how active the lung disease is
High-resolution CT of the chest and full pulmonary function tests with DLCO
Bronchoscopy with lavage before any imaging, since infection is likeliest

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Malette, "RA: ILD"): the work-up is "Chest X-ray, HRCT", and the "Discussion: RA-ILD" slide says "Obtain baseline HRCT and PFTs in high-risk RA patients." The slides name PFTs but not the DLCO; the session notes add that PFTs show a restrictive pattern with a reduced DLCO, often the earliest abnormality, and the session's summary table gives the key test as "HRCT + PFTs (DLCO)".

  • A The slide pairs the chest X-ray with HRCT rather than letting it stand alone; the session notes add that the film can be normal early.
  • B Slides (Polyarthritis, "RF and anti-CCP"): order them "only for initial diagnostic purposes" and not for "monitoring" purposes, since "titres are not predictive of flares or response to therapy".
  • D The slides do not mention bronchoscopy. The session notes keep sputum cultures and lavage for when she is febrile or acutely unwell, which she is not.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 56-year-old woman with seropositive RA on hydroxychloroquine and methotrexate has RA-associated ILD on HRCT, with a restrictive pattern and a low DLCO on PFTs.

stem: Which management plan is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Raise the methotrexate dose, since better control of the joints will treat the lung
Shared care by rheumatology and respirology, and consider stopping methotrexate
Reassure her and repeat the CT in five years, since RA-ILD is often asymptomatic
Stop hydroxychloroquine, the drug most often responsible for lung fibrosis in RA

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Malette, "Discussion: RA-ILD"): "Consider stopping methotrexate" and "Multidisciplinary care (rheumatology + pulmonology)." The "Methotrexate-Induced Injury" slide adds that the link between methotrexate and chronic RA-ILD "remains controversial". Rituximab or abatacept for the joints, and supportive care (smoking cessation, vaccines, pulmonary rehabilitation, oxygen), come from the session notes, not the slides.

  • A Slides (Boyd, DMARDs): "Which DMARDs are associated with lung toxicity? Methotrexate & Leflunomide." The Malette deck lists pulmonary fibrosis among the types of methotrexate-induced injury. Raising the dose goes the wrong way.
  • C The slide does call RA-ILD "often asymptomatic", but she is symptomatic and progressive, and the lecture's plan is active management, not waiting.
  • D Slides (Malette, "Hydroxychloroquine"): one of the "safest medications" for systemic rheumatic disease, with serious side effects rare; its named toxicity is retinal, not lung.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 68-year-old woman with lupus takes hydroxychloroquine and prednisone 7.5 mg daily. After a recent fall she has hip pain and limited mobility.

stem: Which differential diagnosis must lead your thinking? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A lupus arthritis flare of the hip, and trochanteric bursitis
Hip osteoarthritis, and lumbar radiculopathy referring pain to the hip
Septic arthritis of the hip as the single diagnosis, since her steroids can hide the fever
A fragility fracture of the hip, and avascular necrosis of the femoral head

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Malette, "Risk of Corticosteroids"): osteoporosis at over 5-7.5 mg a day for 3 months, which is her dose, so a fall puts a fragility fracture first. Slides (Malette, "Risk Factors of Avascular Necrosis"): corticosteroids and "Autoimmune diseases: Lupus/RA" are both atraumatic risk factors, and femoral head and neck fractures are traumatic ones. Slides (Pope, CTD): lupus patients suffer "complications from steroids such as AVN and osteoporosis". The session's summary table: "AVN / fragility fracture, Steroids + SLE".

  • A The slides do not address the hip in lupus arthritis; the session notes say lupus arthritis rarely affects the hip on its own, and bursitis does not explain lost mobility after a fall.
  • B Both are on the wider differential in the session notes, but neither is the danger her fall and steroids create.
  • C The lecture lists infection among steroid risks, and the session notes keep septic arthritis on her list because steroids blunt fever, but it does not explain the fall and is not the leading concern.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 68-year-old woman with lupus on prednisone 7.5 mg daily has hip pain and limited mobility after a fall. You need to exclude a fracture and look for avascular necrosis.

stem: Which imaging plan is best? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: AP pelvis and lateral hip X-rays, then an MRI of the hip
A bone densitometry (DXA) scan alone, since a fall from standing means osteoporosis
Anti-double-stranded DNA and complement levels to look for a lupus flare in the hip
Ultrasound of the hip to look for an effusion, and no further imaging if there is none

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Malette, "Discussion: AVN"): "Early MRI critical for diagnosis." The slides do not mention the plain films; the X-ray first step rests on the session notes, whose summary table gives the key test as "X-ray, then MRI": the films rule out a fracture and show late AVN (crescent sign, collapse), while X-rays are often normal in early AVN and MRI is the most sensitive test and also finds occult fractures.

  • B The session notes do add a DXA if she has not had one recently, but it cannot show a fracture or necrosis in the hip.
  • C Slides (Pope, Investigations): low complements "may occur in active lupus esp lupus nephritis", and ordering them is a "waste of $ for you to order it if you are not a specialist". Neither test images the hip.
  • D An ultrasound neither excludes a fracture nor shows early AVN in the bone, and the lecture's slide names MRI.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 68-year-old woman with lupus on hydroxychloroquine and prednisone 7.5 mg daily has hip pain after a fall. Imaging shows avascular necrosis of the femoral head without collapse.

stem: Which plan best addresses the drug behind her complication? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Stop hydroxychloroquine, the lupus drug most linked to bone loss, and keep the prednisone
Raise prednisone to 20 mg daily, since her lupus must be active for the bone of the hip to die
Taper prednisone with a steroid-sparing agent, keep hydroxychloroquine, give a bisphosphonate
Make no change, since prednisone at 7.5 mg is too low a dose to harm bone

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Malette, "Discussion: AVN"): "Encourage steroid-sparing regimens", "Weight-bearing modification and bisphosphonates may help", and "Orthopedic referral if joint collapse suspected." Slides (Pope, CTD): give hydroxychloroquine "to every patient with SLE unless if there is a contraindication". Slides (Boyd, Steroids): steroid-sparing medications exist "because of the multiple potential side effects of chronic prednisone use", osteoporosis and avascular necrosis among them. Calcium, vitamin D and falls prevention come from the session notes.

  • A Hydroxychloroquine is the one lupus drug every patient gets (Pope), and the Malette deck calls it one of the safest; it is not the cause.
  • B More steroid adds to the risk. Slides (Malette, "Risk of Corticosteroids"): osteonecrosis risk at doses over 20 mg for a month.
  • D The same slide puts osteoporosis risk at over 5-7.5 mg a day for 3 months, so her dose is not harmless.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 52-year-old man with rheumatoid arthritis presents with chest pain. His BMI is 33 and he has type 2 diabetes.

stem: Which cause of his chest pain must you assume until it is excluded? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Costochondritis from rheumatoid arthritis of the chest wall joints
Rheumatoid pericarditis, the commonest cardiac manifestation of RA
Gastroesophageal reflux or an ulcer from his anti-inflammatory drugs

answer:
The correct answer is B. Slides (Malette, "Cardiovascular Risk in Rheumatic Disease"): "Accelerated atherosclerosis due to chronic inflammation", "Autoimmune disease equivalent CV risk to diabetes", and "Patients with RA have a relative risk of 1.5x for premature atherosclerosis." The same slide says NSAIDs and selective COX-2 inhibitors can increase cardiovascular risk and that corticosteroids aggravate hypertension. He also has diabetes and obesity. "ACS until proven otherwise" is the session notes' phrase.

  • A Chest wall involvement is on the session notes' differential, but it is a diagnosis made after the heart is excluded.
  • C Pericarditis is the first cardiac manifestation on the lecture's RA slide, but it is not the diagnosis that kills if missed. (The slides list it without calling it the commonest; that ranking is from the session notes.)
  • D GI causes are on the session notes' list, especially on NSAIDs or steroids (peptic ulcer disease is on the lecture's steroid risk slide), but they come after ischemia is excluded.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 52-year-old man with RA, type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 33 has chest pain. You are treating it as an acute coronary syndrome until proven otherwise.

stem: Which tests come first? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A D-dimer and CT pulmonary angiogram, since RA drugs cause clots
Rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP, to see whether his RA is active
An echocardiogram, to look for a pericardial effusion from RA
An ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin

answer:
The correct answer is D. The slides do not cover this step: the Case 3 slide only asks "What tests would you order?" and keys nothing. The answer rests on the session notes, "Immediately: ECG and serial high-sensitivity troponin", and the session's summary table's key test, "ECG + troponin". The vault has no note that covers the ACS workup itself.

  • A Slides (Malette, "JAK-Inhibitor Toxicities"): VTE risk, "especially PE", belongs to the JAK inhibitors, not to RA drugs in general, and he is not on one.
  • B Slides (Polyarthritis, "RF and anti-CCP"): not for "monitoring" purposes; they do not address the chest pain.
  • C An echo is on the session notes' workup list, after the ECG and troponin.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 52-year-old man with RA, type 2 diabetes and a BMI of 33 has had acute coronary syndrome excluded. You now plan to lower his long-term cardiovascular risk.

stem: Which plan best fits the lecture? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Tight RA control, risk factor management and a 1.5 multiplier on his risk score
His risk score as calculated for the general population, since his RA is treated
Stopping methotrexate, since antirheumatic drugs raise the rate of cardiovascular events in RA
Switching to regular celecoxib for his joint pain, since a COX-2 inhibitor spares the heart

answer:
The correct answer is A. Slides (Malette, "Management and Prevention Strategies for CV Risk in Autoimmune Disease"): aggressive disease control ("anti-rheumatic treatments have been shown to reduce CVD events"), screen for and manage traditional risk factors (HTN, smoking, diabetes, dyslipidemia), "1.5 multiplier should be applied to general risk for patients with RA", and exercise. A statin and cutting back NSAIDs and steroids are added by the session notes.

  • B The same slides tell you to apply the 1.5 multiplier to the general risk score in RA.
  • C The opposite: the slide says anti-rheumatic treatments reduce cardiovascular events.
  • D Slides (Malette, "Cardiovascular Risk in Rheumatic Disease"): "NSAIDs and selective COX-2 inhibitors can increase CVD risk."

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 58-year-old man with RA on infliximab presents with fever, cough and weight loss. Chest X-ray: upper lobe infiltrates and cavitation.

stem: What is the most likely working diagnosis? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Community-acquired pneumonia from the commonest bacteria
A cavitating squamous cell lung cancer

answer:
The correct answer is C. Slides (Malette, "Anti-TNF Inhibitors Infection Risk"): TNF inhibitors "can reactivate latent TB", with the "risk increased 10x", "typically in first 6-12 months of initiation". Slides (Boyd, Biologics): TNF inhibitor adverse effects include "risk of infections (including tuberculosis + opportunistic infections)". Constitutional symptoms with upper lobe cavitation is the classic picture; that TNF keeps granulomas intact is from the session notes.

  • A The same slide lists serious bacterial infection (pneumonia commonest in the first 6 months), but weight loss and upper lobe cavities point to mycobacteria.
  • B Pulmonary nodules are on the lecture's list of RA lung manifestations, but they do not cause fever and weight loss.
  • D Malignancy is on the session notes' differential of a cavity, but on infliximab with fever, TB comes first.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 58-year-old man with RA on infliximab has fever, cough, weight loss and upper lobe cavitation. You suspect reactivation tuberculosis.

stem: What should you do first? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: Order an interferon-gamma release assay, and exclude TB if it is negative
Isolate him with airborne precautions and send three sputum samples for AFB smear, culture and NAAT
Continue infliximab and start antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia
Order a CT of the chest, which can confirm tuberculosis on its own without any need for sputum microbiology

answer:
The correct answer is B. The slides do not cover the TB workup: the Case 4 slide only asks "What tests would you order?" The answer rests on the session notes: respiratory isolation (airborne precautions) immediately, then sputum ×3 for AFB smear, mycobacterial culture (the gold standard) and NAAT/PCR, with bronchoscopy if sputum is non-diagnostic. The session's summary table: "Sputum AFB / culture / NAAT". The slides do settle the drug: Slides (Boyd, Biologics, "When to Stop TNF Inhibitors"): stop "if you develop a fever" or "if you have an infection".

  • A The session notes: IGRA and TST can be falsely negative on immunosuppression and do not separate latent from active TB, so they cannot rule it out.
  • C Boyd's slide says to stop the TNF inhibitor with a fever or infection.
  • D The session notes use CT to define the cavities and nodes, but only microbiology confirms TB.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 58-year-old man with RA developed reactivation tuberculosis within months of starting infliximab.

stem: What should have been done before the biologic was started? (originally an open prompt; rewritten as MCQ)

options.html: A yearly chest X-ray once the biologic is running, to catch TB early
Infliximab chosen over etanercept, since the antibody carries the lower TB risk
No screening, since he had no history of tuberculosis
A TB skin test or IGRA with a chest X-ray, treating any latent TB first

answer:
The correct answer is D. Slides (Malette, "Prior to Starting Biologic"): screen for a "History of TB", and under "Tests before use" order a "TB skin test" and a "Chest x-ray", alongside CBC, creatinine, hepatic enzymes, lipids, CRP, hepatitis B and C serologies and HIV if there are risk factors. The slide names the skin test only; the IGRA alternative and treating latent TB first come from the session notes: "Screen before any biologic: IGRA or TST plus chest X-ray, and treat latent TB first".

  • A The slide puts screening before the drug; most reactivation happens in the first 6-12 months ("Anti-TNF Inhibitors Infection Risk").
  • B The slides do not compare the two drugs. The session notes put the risk the other way: infliximab carries a higher TB risk than etanercept.
  • C The slide lists both a TB history and a TB skin test, so a negative history does not replace testing.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding DMARD and biologic use for rheumatologic conditions is FALSE?

options.html: Biologics are very expensive treatment but have the potential to drive some rheumatologic conditions into remission
Methotrexate requires baseline and monthly bloodwork to monitor for adverse effects like hepatotoxicity
Hydroxychloroquine requires annual eye exams due to the risk of retinal toxicity
Biologics act by targeting TNF and other inflammatory molecules
DMARDs are 3rd line medications, after treatment failure with steroids and NSAIDs

answer: The correct answer is E. DMARDs are best used as early and aggressively as possible to prevent early joint damage. Most also take many weeks for their onset of action, so they ideally should be initiated within the first 3 months of symptom onset.

stem: Which of the following statements is true?

options.html: Repetitive strain injuries (RSI) are caused by maximal or over the maximal exertion
Around 5% of the Canadian General population experience chronic pain
Opioid analgesics can result in Respiratory depression, mental clouding, nausea/vomiting, constipation, drug tolerance
The majority of the chronic pain are caused through the nociceptive pathway whereas the acute pain are usually neuropathic

answer:
The correct answer is C. All of those are side effects of opioids. Each other option has a specific error:

  • A — RSI is caused by submaximal exertion over a period of time without recovery (sitting in a funny position for too long), not maximal exertion.
  • B — around 30%, not 5%, of the Canadian general population experience chronic pain.
  • D — backwards: chronic pain is more neuropathic, acute pain more nociceptive.

See 06 - Understanding and Managing Chronic Pain.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[03 - Body Pain]].
stem: What is the dose referred to as the 'watchful dose' in opioid management?
answer:
The correct answer is D. 90 mg/day of morphine or equivalent is the "watchful dose" — where significant increases in side effects such as constipation appear, and where the risk of drug diversion/sale rises.

To manage risk at this level, some suggest titrating opioids for a 30% increase in function or reduction in pain.

C is the old answer: in previous years 200 mg was the watchful dose; the updated guidelines moved it to 90 mg.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q41, Q43-Q45. Tests [[03 - Body Pain]].
stem: Which of the following is false about ASA?

options.html: Indication: pain, fever, anti-inflammatory in high doses, anti-thrombotic in low dose
Contraindications include hypersensitivity reactions to NSAIDs and children with fever (risks of Reyes syndrome)
Adverse drug reaction includes GI bleeding, tinnitus in high doses, hypersensitivities, prolonged bleeding
Aspirin has little to no toxicity and mortality risk

answer:
The correct answer is D. There is significant risk of overdose with aspirin, due to rapid saturation of the drug's conjugation system — once conjugation saturates, kinetics shift and levels climb disproportionately.

A-C are all accurate: dose-dependent indications, contraindication in children with fever because of Reye syndrome, and the ADR profile including tinnitus at high doses.

stem: Which of the following does not have anti-inflammatory effects?
answer: The correct answer is B. Acetaminophen has antipyretic and analgesic effects but essentially no anti-inflammatory effects — which is exactly what separates it from the NSAIDs. All the other listed drugs do have anti-inflammatory effects.

stem: You have a patient coming to you for corticosteroid and anesthetic injection for subacromial bursitis. The patient asks what the risks are for having the injection. What are the risks?

options.html: Failure to relieve pain or confirm diagnosis

answer: The correct answer is G — all of the above. All of these are possible. The consent principle: communicate risks that are frequent as well as those that are very serious — include everything any reasonable person would want to know. See bursitis and corticosteroids.

stem: You have a patient coming to you for corticosteroid and anesthetic injection for trochanteric bursitis. You have previously explained the risk associated with receiving the injection. You are now assessing if there are any contraindications to administering this treatment to the patient. What from this list is a contraindication/relative contraindication to administering the injection?

options.html: Infection on the skin over the trochanter
Inability to properly position the patient

answer: The correct answer is F — all of the above. In addition to those four, you must confirm that you have the patient's consent, the ability to manage an emergency situation, and adequate equipment, assistance and monitoring. See trochanteric bursitis.
