stem: Match the rheumatologic condition to its best corresponding investigation.
answer:
The pairings:

ConditionInvestigation
Systemic lupus erythematosusANA, then anti-DNA (if ANA is positive), anti-Smith
Inflammatory myositisCK, ESR, ANA
Sjogren’sCBC, ANA, ESR, RF, anti-Ro (aka SSA), anti-La (aka SSB)
SclerodermaANA nucleolar pattern, Scl70 (topoisomerase 1)
ANCA vasculitisANCA, PR3, MPO
Enthesitis-related arthritisHLA B27, ESR, CRP, CBC
  • Inflammatory myositis: anti-Jo1 and anti-PM-Scl can also be ordered to check for interstitial lung disease and scleroderma polymyositis respectively, which are disease correlations.
  • ANCA vasculitis: PR3 stands for anti-proteinase 3 aka c-ANCA; MPO stands for anti-myeloperoxidase aka p-ANCA.
  • Enthesitis-related arthritis: 30-50% of enthesitis-related arthritis have a positive HLA B27; CBC might show anemia and leukocytosis & thrombocytosis, ESR may be normal or elevated.

items.right: ANA, then anti-DNA (if ANA is positive), anti-Smith
CBC, ANA, ESR, RF, anti-Ro (aka SSA), anti-La (aka SSB)

stem: In which of the following cases is ordering an ANA indicated? Choose 1

options.html: A family doctor is unsure if a patient has an autoimmune disorder and the patient had a negative ANA result last year (no new symptoms).
A rheumatologist wants to follow a SLE patient’s progress/response to treatment.
A patient presents to the ER with delirium, acute pericarditis, fever, alopecia, and proteinuria.
A patient is presenting with swollen and achy knees that are stiff (<30 min every morning), prone to night pain, and have a reduced ROM.

answer: The correct answer is C. In answer C, the patient actually fulfills multiple clinical domains for SLE. Since an autoimmune CTD is suspected, ANA can be ordered. ANA is not ordered if there was a negative ANA in the past. It is also not ordered to follow a patient. Case D describes a patient with osteoarthritis (not inflammatory = no ANA needed).

preamble.title: The case - Marnie
preamble.html: The case. Over the phone, your friend Marnie tells you that she is sad because her manicurist made mean comments about her nails. Some insults include: “Your nails have pits and ridges, yellow dots and dark streaks, and are basically lifting right off. Your fingers also look like sausages.” Your friend is also stressed because she thinks she has relentless dandruff, pinkeye, and arthritis in her knees. You suspect your friend actually has a type of spondyloarthritis.

stem: Beside giving emotional support, you want to help Marnie in some way. You recommend all of the following csDMARDs (conventional synthetic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs) but tell her to avoid which one?
answer: The correct answer is C. hydroxychloroquine is often avoided due to case reports of severe psoriasis flares.

stem: You are meeting with your clerk friend Osler. For the past year, he has had unrelenting headaches, forgets things easily, and he never feels refreshed no matter how much he sleeps. You joke that he might be overworked and just needs a break, but he says that he also has severe chest pain, jaw pain, back pain, bilateral shoulder pain, leg pain, abdomen pain, AND hip pain. None of his doctors could explain his symptoms. You suspect he has a disorder relating to his descending (inhibitory) and ascending (facilitatory) pain pathways resulting in decreased serotonin and increased substance P and glutamate. This time you recommend all of the following treatments except which one?
answer: The correct answer is D. he likely has fibromyalgia. Prednisone shouldn’t be used for fibromyalgia.

stem: Which of the following cases likely has polymyalgia rheumatica?

options.html: A 64 y.o patient who has a history of giant cell arteritis presents with new weight loss and also pain in shoulder and hip.
A 43 y.o male presenting with pain and stiffness in the shoulder and hip girdles with profound morning stiffness and fatigue.
A 56 y.o febrile female presenting with pain in just her left shoulder, which is also warm and swollen.

A 73 y.o patient with long-standing pain in hip (which is not stiff), worse with activity. Her shoulder muscles has weakness but no pain. They sadly have not responded to prednisone that you previously prescribed.

answer: The correct answer is A. giant cell arteritis often occurs with polymyalgia rheumatica. B is not correct because polymyalgia rheumatica only affects people older than 50. C is likely septic arthritis (bacterial monoarthritis). D is likely hip osteoarthritis and shoulder myositis. Polymyalgia rheumatica won’t have muscle weakness and should respond dramatically to prednisone.

stem: Your 45 year old male patient comes in for regular blood work. Results show that he has elevated uric acid. What are your next steps? Choose the best answer.

options.html: Advise him to start eating more seafood

answer: The correct answer is C. Hyperuricemia does not necessarily mean gout. In this case, this patient does not have any symptoms of gout (i.e., swollen joint, red, painful). Therefore, doing further investigations and/or treatment is unnecessary. Furthermore, if you patient has gout, you should advise them to decrease the amount of seafood in their diet; and we typically do not prescribe allopurinol right away (unless it is debilitating to their life), and especially not during the gout attack. Lastly, gout is more commonly found on 1st MTP joint (big toe), not on the knee (CPPD more commonly found in knee).

stem: Which of the following - if found in your patient highly suspicious of pseudogout - does not necessarily support the diagnosis of CPPD? (Choose multiple answers)

options.html: Chondrocalcinosis (deposition of calcium pyrophosphate) on imaging

answer: The correct answer is C, E. these are characteristics that support Gout. Pseudogout typically lasts for a few days~ few weeks (takes longer to reach a peak compared to gout).

stem: True or False: X-ray is the best way to diagnose chronic osteoarthritis
answer: The correct answer is B. False - osteoarthritis is a clinical diagnosis (symptoms such as joint pain, stiffness, chronic >6weeks, and worse with activity; without other causes of arthritis). X-ray is used for staging OA.

stem: A 32 year-old woman presents with alopecia, malar rash, oral ulceration, pleurisy, and swollen MCP and PIP joints. Blood work comes back positive for ANA 1:640 with a speckled pattern, positive double-stranded DNA, and low complement. A diagnosis of systemic lupus erythematosus is made and you have decided to start prednisone and hydryoxychloroquine. You discuss potential benefits and adverse effects of the medication. Which of the following are not side effects of prednisone?

options.html: All of the above are side effects of prednisone

answer: The correct answer is D. Prednisone increases the risk of infection. All of the other answers are potential complications of prednisone. Prednisone is a good treatment option to treat acute inflammation, but is not good long-term due to potential complications.

stem: A 75 year-old gentleman presents with a 2-day history of a red, swollen, exquisitely tender 1st MTP joint. He has a medical history consisting of end-stage renal disease, congestive heart failure requiring diuretic use, and poorly controlled diabetes. He drinks approximately 20 beers per week. Blood work shows elevated inflammatory markers and a normal urate. Synovial fluid aspiration of the MTP joint shows intracellular monosodium urate crystals, a cell count of 17.1 x 109, and negative culture and Gram stain. Which of following is the best treatment option of acute gout in this patient?

options.html: Oral prednisone 30 mg daily x 3 days, followed by taper

answer: The correct answer is B. Given this patient’s comorbidities, the best treatment option for acute gout affecting one joint would be intra-articular steroids. Intra-articular steroids have minimal systemic absorption. Prednisone is relatively contraindicated due to his heart failure and diabetes, both of which can worsen with prednisone. NSAIDs should be avoided in patients with end-stage renal disease.

stem: A clinical clerk is rotating through an elective block in rheumatology and asked to obtain informed consent for joint aspiration for a 55 year-old gentleman presenting with acute monoarthritis of the right knee. After discussing potential benefits, the student then discusses potential complications of the procedure. Which of the following are not complications of arthrocentesis (joint aspiration)?

options.html: All of the above are complications of joint aspiration

answer: The correct answer is D. Post injection flare and minimal systemic absorption of prednisone that can worsen hyperglycemia are complications of steroid injection, not joint aspiration - which does not involve injection of cortisone. Infection, bleeding, and tendon rupture are potential complications of inserting the needle, but are rare in clinical practice.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[02 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 65 year-old woman with a history of gastritis presents to clinic for suggestions regarding pain control for her hand osteoarthritis. She has previously tried occupational therapy, topical NSAIDs, acetaminophen, and glucosamine chondroitin with limited improvement of her symptoms. She wonders about trying an anti-inflammatory but is concerned about potential worsening of her gastritis. Which of the following NSAIDs has the least risk of GI toxicity?
answer: The correct answer is B. Due to its selective inhibition of COX-2, celecoxib is associated with less GI toxicity than non-selective NSAIDs (i.e., all other available NSAIDs). Celecoxib can still result in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease and should be used with caution in this patient, possibly with a proton pump inhibitor.

stem: A 45 year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has recently been referred to your rheumatology clinic. She has been taking hydroxychloroquine 400 mg PO daily for twenty years since she was initially diagnosed with lupus. Her disease is currently under control. She has not had any recent eye exam. What is the retinal finding of hydroxychloroquine that you would be concerned about?
answer: The correct answer is D. Bull’s eye maculopathy is a toxic retinopathy caused by hydroxychloroquine. It is important to tell patients about the potential complication when starting this medication and ensure they are getting annual eye exams to monitor for this complication.

preamble.title: The case
preamble.html: A 45 year-old woman with systemic lupus erythematosus has recently been referred to your rheumatology clinic. She has been taking hydroxychloroquine 400 mg PO daily for twenty years since she was initially diagnosed with lupus. Her disease is currently under control. She has not had any recent eye exam.

stem: What is the most appropriate next investigation? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): C. Hydroxychloroquine's serious risk is retinal toxicity (bull's eye maculopathy), so it needs a baseline and yearly eye exam with visual acuity, colour vision and visual fields. It needs no laboratory monitoring and causes no myelosuppression 02 - Rheumatology Treatments.

  • A: Monthly CBC and ALT is the monitoring for methotrexate and sulfasalazine, not hydroxychloroquine.
  • B: G6PD screening and hepatitis serology are baseline checks before sulfasalazine.
  • D: A chest X-ray is part of the baseline workup for methotrexate, not hydroxychloroquine.

stem: A 45 year-old gentleman with psoriatic arthritis on sulfasalazine presents to your clinic after developing a new skin rash. He reports a itchy, red rash on his arms and torso that started 2 weeks ago. He has had some relief of the pruritis with anti-histamines. He continues to have a raised, erythematous, urticarial rash on exam. He asks if it is caused by his sulfasalazine. Which of the following are not potential side effects of sulfasalazine?
answer: The correct answer is F. Acute pneumonitis (shortness of breath, cough, fever) is not associated with sulfasalazine, but rather methotrexate and less commonly leflunomide. This patient has a pruritic, erythematous rash with an urticarial appearance that is consistent with a drug rash. Both sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine can cause drug rashes. This patient should avoid sulfa drugs in the future.

lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[02 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 45 year-old gentleman with psoriatic arthritis is about to start a TNF inhibitor for his skin and joint disease. Which of the following is not a contraindication to starting a TNF inhibitor.
answer: The correct answer is C. So long as patients do not have advance congestive heart failure, coronary artery disease is not a contraindication to starting biologic therapy with a TNF inhibitor. The rest of the conditions listed are relative or absolute contraindications to starting TNF inhibitors.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Source: Elentra Rise module knowledge checks (10 questions). Tests [[02 - Rheumatology Treatments]].
stem: A 24 year-old woman with rheumatoid arthritis is being worked up for biologic therapy after failing sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine. She wants to avoid using methotrexate and leflunomide because she wants to conceive in the near future. She has a family history of multiple sclerosis. Which class of biologic therapy should she avoid?
answer: The correct answer is B. Due to potential for demyelinating disease, TNF inhibitors are avoided in patients with a personal or family history of multiple sclerosis. The other classes of biologics do not cause this. There is limited data available for some of the newer biologic medications and pregnancy, so the patient should be made aware about this before trying to conceive.

stem: Which cells are most directly responsible for myelinating neurons in the CNS?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The full glial roster, all in one place:

CellRole
Oligodendrocytesmyelinate CNS neurons — hence the target in multiple sclerosis
Schwann cellsmyelinate PNS neurons
Microgliamacrophages of the CNS
Astrocytessupport neurons and vasculature (nutrients, etc.)

lectureMeta: Workbook Q2-Q4, Q121. Tests [[05 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy]], [[12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex]], [[09 - Introduction to Neurophysiology]].
stem: Which region of the brain is responsible for moving your right hand?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Two independent facts must both be right:

  • Precentral gyrus (the ridge in front of the central sulcus) = primary motor cortex, part of the frontal lobe. The postcentral gyrus (behind the sulcus) = primary sensory cortex, receiving touch, proprioception, vibration, pain and temperature, part of the parietal lobe.
  • The left motor cortex controls the right side of the body, and vice versa.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q2-Q4, Q121. Tests [[05 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy]], [[12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex]], [[09 - Introduction to Neurophysiology]].
stem: Which area of the brain is responsible for taste?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The insular cortex is responsible for taste.

  • Corpus callosum — connects the two hemispheres
  • Uncus — smell. The key's mnemonic: "you can smell your uncle, but you shouldn't taste him"
  • Cingulate gyrus — part of the limbic system (emotion and memory)
  • Broca's area — coordinates the motor movements involved in speech

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q2-Q4, Q121. Tests [[05 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy]], [[12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex]], [[09 - Introduction to Neurophysiology]].
stem: Which of the following is an inhibitory neurotransmitter?
answer: The correct answer is B — GABA. Glutamate is the principal excitatory CNS neurotransmitter; the amines listed are modulatory.

lecture: The cranial cavity, meninges & skull foramina
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q20, Q61. Tests [[08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity]].
stem: A large blood clot in the cavernous sinus compressed one of the nerves running through the lateral wall of the sinus resulting in numbness of the left upper eyelid, eyebrow, and forehead. Which nerve did it compress?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Two filters:

  1. What runs where — CN III, IV, V1 and V2 run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus; CN VI runs through the sinus; the optic nerve runs above it, carrying visual input from the retina to the LGN of the thalamus. That eliminates A and E.
  2. What is numb — CN III, IV and VI are motor to the eye, so they cannot cause numbness. V1 (ophthalmic) supplies the upper eyelid, eyebrow and forehead; V2 (maxillary) supplies the cheeks and maxillary teeth.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lecture: The cranial cavity, meninges & skull foramina
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q20, Q61. Tests [[08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity]].
stem: A 32-year-old man crashes his car into a pole. His head hits the steering wheel, fracturing his cribriform plate and severing the nerves that pass through it. Which of the following deficits will he have from this specific injury?
answer: The correct answer is B. Cranial nerve I (olfactory) passes through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone and is responsible for smell.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lecture: The cranial cavity, meninges & skull foramina
lectureMeta: Workbook Q19-Q20, Q61. Tests [[08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity]].
stem: Which of the following separates the two cerebral hemispheres?
answer: The correct answer is B — the longitudinal fissure. C is the trap: the corpus callosum connects the hemispheres, it does not separate them (compare Q4 and Q141).

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: A patient presents with unilateral facial paralysis and loss of taste sensation on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue. Imaging reveals a mass in the posterior fossa of the brainstem. Which cranial nerve is most likely affected by the mass?
answer: The correct answer is C. The facial nerve (CN VII). The loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is due to the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve — pair that with the facial paralysis and CN VII accounts for both findings at once. Contrast Q77, where taste to the posterior third is the discriminator.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: Which of the following cranial nerves is correctly matched with one of its targets?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The trigeminal nerve handles sensory perception of the face and controls the muscles of mastication (via V3).

Every distractor is a real pairing with the wrong nerve attached:

  • Lateral rectus → abducens (VI); abducens abducts
  • Parotid gland → glossopharyngeal (IX) — C is the best trap in the question, because the facial nerve does travel through the parotid gland without innervating it
  • Sternocleidomastoid → spinal accessory (XI)
  • Intrinsic tongue muscles → hypoglossal (XII)

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: Which of the following is consistent with a lesion of cranial nerve III?

options.html: Contralateral pupil is deviated superiorly and laterally
Ipsilateral pupil is deviated inferiorly and laterally

answer:
The correct answer is E. CN III (oculomotor) drives ipsilateral pupillary constriction and eyelid elevation, plus all ipsilateral extraocular muscles except lateral rectus and superior oblique — the mnemonic LR6, SO4.

So a CN III lesion gives: pupil dilation, ptosis, and deviation of the eye inferiorly (because the still-working superior oblique pulls it down) and laterally (because the still-working lateral rectus pulls it out) — the classic "down and out". All findings are ipsilateral, which kills B and D. C is CN VII, which closes the eye.

flags.title: Muscle slip in the key
flags.html: The key writes "superior rectus moves it inferiorly and slightly medially from the neutral position". It means superior oblique, which is the muscle spared by a CN III lesion and the reason the eye deviates down. Superior rectus is CN III-innervated and elevates the eye.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: A 36-year-old woman is taken to the emergency department for stitches of a laceration just above the right eyebrow. Branches of which of the following nerves must be anesthetized?
answer: The correct answer is A. The ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (V1) supplies the forehead, upper eyelid and most of the nose — that is what needs anesthetizing. Same territory as Q19. See 05 - cranial nerve V.

stem: Which of the following is not a function of the facial nerve and its branches?

options.html: Supplies taste to anterior 2/3 of tongue
Motor innervation to muscles of face
Parasympathetic innervation to submandibular and sublingual glands
Supplies taste to posterior 1/3 of tongue

answer: The correct answer is E. Taste to the posterior 1/3 of the tongue is supplied by the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). Everything else on the list is CN VII — the same functional roster used in Q26 and Q30.

stem: A 55-year-old male presents to your clinic with acute facial paralysis. He is able to raise his forehead normally and has left facial weakness. He has a history of hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia and smoking. What is the most likely cause of his facial weakness?

options.html: Right-sided stroke affecting right motor cortex
Left-sided stroke affecting left motor cortex

answer:
The correct answer is A. The forehead receives innervation from both the left and right motor cortices, so a right-sided stroke gives left facial weakness with normal forehead raising — forehead sparing is the hallmark of an upper motor neuron lesion.

Bell's palsy (B) is the trap, because it is the common cause of acute facial paralysis — but Bell's palsy is a lower motor neuron lesion and would not spare the forehead (see Q125). Also note the stroke risk factors stacked in the stem: hypertension, diabetes, hypercholesterolemia, smoking.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: Which of the following presenting features is not a prognostic variable for Bell's palsy?

options.html: Late onset of return of facial function
All of the above are prognostic variables

answer:
The correct answer is E. All of them are prognostic. The good prognostic variables for Bell's palsy:

  • Incomplete palsy — 94% of patients progress to full recovery
  • Early onset of return of function — return within 1 week → ~90% recover; 2nd week → 83%; 3rd week → 60%
  • Age < 60 years
  • Normal hearing and tearing
  • No diabetes and no hypertension

Note B is phrased as the bad version ("late onset of return") — it is still a prognostic variable, just an adverse one, which is exactly why E is correct.

lectureMeta: Workbook Q26, Q28-Q29, Q62, Q77-Q79, Q125. Tests [[06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function]], [[07 - Facial Anatomy]].
stem: A patient presents with left facial weakness with the left forehead being spared. These symptoms could be attributed to a:
answer:
The correct answer is D. The forehead is supplied by both motor cortices, so a right-sided stroke gives left facial weakness with the left forehead spared — the left forehead still has input from the left motor cortex.

The rule in one line: an UMN lesion is forehead-sparing; a LMN lesion affects the entire face, because the facial nerve itself is damaged and no signal gets through at all. Same principle as Q78, and the reason Bell's palsy involves the whole hemiface. See facial nerve palsy.

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: If a person has an eyeball that is too long or a lens that is too round, what is their diagnosis?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Myopia (near-sightedness) means you can only focus on close targets. The reason from the geometry: when objects are close they are larger, and their image can make it all the way to the back of a long eyeball; when far away they are too small to reach the retina of a long eye.

The four distractors are two matched pairs — eye vs. ear:

  • Hyperopia — far-sightedness; only distant objects focus
  • Presbyopia — age-related, a stiff lens that cannot adjust to close objects
  • Presbycusis — age-related hearing loss of high-pitched frequencies
  • Hyperacusis — over-sensitivity to certain noises

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: If a person has an eyeball that is too short or a lens that is too flat, what kind of lenses do they need in their glasses?
answer: The correct answer is A. Convex = convergent lenses help focus the light sooner, which is what a far-sighted person needs to see objects close to themselves. Concave = divergent lenses are for the near-sighted. Note that B and D name the same lens, as do A and "convergent".

lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Which of the following is true regarding rods?

options.html: They have higher visual acuity than cones
They are responsible for colour vision
They are found primarily in the fovea
They are more sensitive to light than cones
Their function is tested using a Snellen eye chart

answer:
The correct answer is D. Rods are more sensitive to light than cones, hence "night vision". Every other option is a cone property:

  • Cones have higher visual acuity, are responsible for colour vision, and are what the Snellen chart tests.
  • The fovea contains primarily cones; the peripheral retina contains primarily rods.

stem: If a patient cannot see objects in the bottom right side of their vision (from both eyes), what type of visual deficit would this be called?
answer: The correct answer is C — right homonymous inferior quadrantanopia. Build the name from the three descriptors in the stem: right side of vision, both eyes (= homonymous), and only the bottom quarter (= inferior quadrantanopia rather than a full hemianopia). See homonymous hemianopia.

stem: How would vision be affected if a pituitary tumor compressed the optic chiasm?

options.html: Loss of left visual field bilaterally
Loss of right visual field bilaterally
Loss of vision in left eye

answer:
The correct answer is D. Fibres from the nasal half of each retina — which see objects in the temporal visual fields — are the ones that cross at the optic chiasm. Disrupting them therefore produces bitemporal hemianopsia (loss of temporal vision bilaterally).

The nasal-retina/temporal-field inversion is the whole trick, and is why E is the trap.

lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Damage to the inferior temporal lobe is more likely to cause which of the following visual deficits?
answer:
The correct answer is D. This requires the dorsal and ventral streams of vision:

StreamRouteFunction
Dorsal — the "where" pathwayoccipital → posterior parietal cortexspatial location, and selecting an appropriate action
Ventral — the "what" pathwayoccipital → inferior temporal lobeperception and recognition of objects

Because the lesion is in the inferior temporal lobe, the ventral system is damaged, so both perception (A) and recognition (C) of objects are affected — but spatial location (B) is spared. Hence D, not E.

lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: Narrowing of which of the following could result in reduced vision in the left eye (from compression of the optic nerve)?
answer:
The correct answer is C. The left optic nerve carries visual input from the retina to the LGN of the thalamus and travels through the optic canal.

The foramen roster, which this question and Q19 between them cover:

  • Superior orbital fissure — CN III, IV, V1, VI
  • Supraorbital foramen — a branch of V1 continues through it
  • Foramen rotundum — V2
  • Foramen ovale — V3

weekLabel: Week 12 - Rheumatology Review, Body Pain, Neuroanatomy & the Cranial Nerves
lecture: Vision: refraction, the retina & visual fields
lectureMeta: Workbook Q6-Q7, Q10-Q12, Q14, Q21, Q103. Tests [[10 - Orbital Anatomy]], [[11 - Neurophysiology of Vision]].
stem: A 15-year-old patient is unable to read a book unless it is held at arm's length. His eyeballs are too __________ so you prescribe him __________ lenses as he has __________.
answer:
The correct answer is B. He can only see things far away, so he is far-sighted (hyperopia), which means the eyeball is too short and the rays converge beyond the retina. A converging lens makes the rays converge sooner, landing them on the retina.

E is excluded by age: presbyopia is the age-related stiff-lens problem (Q6), not a 15-year-old's. Same physics as Q7.

stem: What is your differential diagnosis for acute onset of aphasia? (Select all that apply.)
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D.

A,B,C,D; Differential diagnosis for acute onset of aphasia includes ischemic stroke, intracranial hemorrhage, migraine, post ictal todd’s paresis, metabolic derangement in the setting of underlying structural lesion and psychogenic.

stem: What body parts have the largest representations on the sensory homunculus?
answer:
The correct answer is C.

From 12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. The sensory homunculus gives cortex to body parts by receptor density, not size, so the densely innervated face (lips, tongue) and hands (fingertips) get the largest areas of the postcentral gyrus. The motor homunculus follows the same logic for fine movement, and the hands dominate there too.

  • A fails: the hands are large but the arms are not.
  • B fails: legs and feet sit on a small strip on the medial surface (ACA territory).
  • D fails: the trunk is tiny; the genitals are represented but small.

stem: What view of the brain is this?
answer:
The correct answer is B.

From 05 - Introduction to Neuroanatomy. The three planes: a coronal cut runs side to side, like a slice of bread, so both hemispheres, the ventricles and (further back) the hippocampi appear together, symmetric about the midline. An axial cut is parallel to the horizon. A sagittal cut runs front to back and shows one hemisphere in profile.

  • A would show a side-on profile with the corpus callosum as an arch.
  • C, D are the same plane (transverse is another name for axial), which is a hint that neither can be the single answer.

stem: Lou had a stroke 1 week ago. You are assessing him at your family clinic and find that he has poor fluency, poor repetition, and poor naming, but can follow commands. Which area of his brain did his stroke most likely affect?
answer: The correct answer is B. The findings of poor fluency, repetition, and naming, with preserved command following, would be seen in Broca’s aphasia. Broca’s area is found in the frontal lobe. It is most commonly found in the patient’s dominant hemisphere, which most often is their L hemisphere.

stem: Which of the following statements regarding cerebrum function is TRUE?

options.html: The parietal lobe comprises the primary motor cortex and the ventral stream of the visual system
Occipital seizures often begin with auditory hallucinations and can be triggered by repetitive sounds
The anterior multimodal association area helps integrate information from past experience with information received from other areas of the brain to appropriately respond to stimuli
The function of the neurons in the postcentral gyrus is to send impulses to the spinal cord for motor activity
The face is mapped most medially on the sensory and motor homunculi

answer: The correct answer is C. The description of the anterior multimodal association area is true. The parietal lobe comprises the somatosensory cortex and the dorsal stream of the visual system. Occipital seizures often begin with visual hallucinations and can be triggered by flashing lights or repeating patterns. The function of the neurons in the precentral gyrus is to send impulses to the spinal cord for motor activity, not the postcentral gyrus; the postcentral gyrus contains the primary somatosensory cortex. The face is mapped more laterally on the sensory and motor homunculi.

stem: 53-year-old man presents with a history of daily stabbing headache associated with dizziness, progressive blurred vision, right ocular pain, ptosis and ophthalmoplegia. Upon examination, he is found to have a CN III palsy and ipsilateral Horner syndrome. Brain MRI identified a lesion homogeneously enhanced after gadolinium administration on T1-weighted images. Findings were consistent with a meningioma. What is at the top of your differential diagnosis?

options.html: Third nerve compression via posterior communicating artery aneurysm

answer: The correct answer is B. Cavernous sinus syndrome (CSS) is a condition caused by any pathology involving the cavernous sinus which may present as a combination of unilateral ophthalmoplegia (cranial nerve (CN) III, IV, VI), autonomic dysfunction (Horner syndrome) or sensory CN V1- CN V2 loss. The common clinical findings of CSS are as follows: Total/partial ophthalmoplegia: CN III palsy, CN IV palsy, CN VI palsy, Facial sensory loss: CN V1 loss and CN V2 loss, Horner syndrome: loss of sympathetic tone due to damage of sympathetic plexus, and Proptosis and chemosis: due to increased pressure within cavernous sinus. A CSS is caused by any pathology or lesion present within the cavernous sinus that disrupts the function of other anatomical structures. The most common cause of CSS is mass effect from tumor. Other common causes of CSS include trauma and self-limited inflammatory disease. Less common causes are vascular etiologies and infections.

stem: Which of the following methods can be used to test the vestibulocochlear nerve (CN VIII)? (Select all that apply)
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D.

From 06 - Cranial Nerve Anatomy and Function. CN VIII carries two sensory functions, hearing and balance, and the note tests each: a hearing test, the Romberg sign, and assessment for nystagmus.

  • A, B are the hearing tests: 09 - Hearing Loss pairs Weber (lateralizes) with Rinne (separates conductive from sensorineural) and says to always do both.
  • C tests the vestibular half: an acute vestibular loss produces nystagmus.
  • D is listed for CN VIII too: with the eyes closed, balance rests on vestibular input plus proprioception, so a vestibular lesion can unmask a positive Romberg.

stem: 29-year-old male presents with a 1-year history of headaches, weight loss, decreased muscle strength, stamina, decreased libido and morning erections. He shaves every second day. Investigations showed decreased testosterone(nmol/L) but elevated prolactin (1257ug/l). MRI showed a pituitary mass. What is at the top of your differential diagnosis, and what cranial nerve should you test?

options.html: Diabetes Mellitus and Oculomotor Nerve (CN III)
Prader-Willi syndrome and Vestibulocochlear Nerve (CN VIII)
Kallmann syndrome and Olfactory Nerve (CN I)

answer: The correct answer is D. Macroprolactinoma can cause compression of the optic chiasm which disrupts the nasal fibers of the optic nerve leading to a bitemporal visual field defect. Refer to “Clinical Presentation and Evaluation of Pituitary Gland Disease” lecture, slide 7-9.

stem: 17-year-old male presents with absent pubertal development. He was born to consanguineous parents and had normal delivery. He has no siblings. He had normal developmental milestones. Bilateral cryptorchidism was discovered at age six years and surgically corrected. Physical examination showed that his secondary sexual characters were deficient (Tanner stage 1). He had micropenis (stretched phallus length 2.5 cm). The scrotal contents were barely palpated on both sides. Investigations showed low FSH/LH and normal prolactin. MRI showed agenesis of the olfactory bulb. What is at the top of your differential diagnosis and what cranial nerve should you test?

options.html: Diabetes Mellitus and Oculomotor Nerve (CN III)
Prader-Willi syndrome and Vestibulocochlear Nerve (CN VIII)
Kallmann syndrome and Olfactory Nerve (CN I)

answer: The correct answer is C. Kallmann syndrome (KS) is a genetic disorder that prevents a person from starting or fully completing puberty. Kallmann syndrome is classified under hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. To distinguish it from other forms of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, Kallmann syndrome has the additional symptom of a total lack of sense of smell (anosmia) or a reduced sense of smell. Refer to “Disorders of Puberty”, slide 31.

stem: What supplies sensation over the ear and the skin in the temporal region?
answer:
The correct answer is E.

From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The auriculotemporal nerve is a branch of V3 that runs with the superficial temporal artery and vein, supplying the skin in front of the ear, the temporal scalp and the TMJ.

  • A (frontal, V1) gives off the supraorbital nerve to the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) supplies the midface through the infraorbital foramen.
  • C (mental, V3) supplies the chin through the mental foramen.
  • D (great auricular, C2-C3) supplies the angle of the mandible and is the one facial territory outside the trigeminal nerve.

stem: What supplies sensation over the angle of the mandible?
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The great auricular nerve comes from the cervical plexus (ventral rami of C2 and C3) and supplies the skin over the angle of the mandible, the one patch of the face the trigeminal nerve does not cover.

  • A (frontal, V1) is the forehead.
  • B (infraorbital, V2) is the midface and upper lip.
  • C (mental, V3) is the chin and lower lip, anterior to the angle.
  • E (auriculotemporal, V3) is in front of the ear and the temporal scalp.

stem: Which of the following pairings are incorrect?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Orbicularis oris closes the mouth

From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The sphincters are named for the opening they surround: orbicularis oris surrounds the lips and closes the mouth; it is orbicularis oculi that closes the eye. That makes C the incorrect pairing.

  • A is correct: frontalis (occipitofrontalis over the frontal bone) raises the eyebrows.
  • B is correct: zygomaticus major pulls the corners of the mouth up into a smile.
  • D is correct as the lecture states it: platysma helps depress the mandible.
  • E is correct: occipitalis moves the scalp.

stem: What are the muscles of mastication?
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 07 - Facial Anatomy. The muscles of mastication act on the TMJ and are supplied by V3, not the facial nerve. The lecture names masseter (strongly closes and protrudes the jaw) and temporalis (closes and retracts it).

  • B fails: the orbicularis muscles are facial-expression sphincters of the mouth and eye (CN VII).
  • C fails: the zygomatici raise the corners of the mouth.
  • D fails: buccinator helps chewing by keeping food between the teeth but is a muscle of facial expression; platysma is too.

stem: Which of the following pairings are correct? (Select all that apply.)
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D, E.

From 07 - Facial Anatomy. CN VII splits in the parotid into five branches, each matched to the muscle it supplies, and every pairing here matches the lecture:

  • A Temporal → occipitofrontalis (frontalis), plus the upper orbicularis oculi.
  • B Zygomatic → zygomaticus major, plus the lower orbicularis oculi.
  • C Buccal → buccinator, plus part of orbicularis oris.
  • D Marginal mandibular → the inferior orbicularis oris.
  • E Cervical → platysma.

D is the one to hesitate on: orbicularis oris has two supplies (buccal above, marginal mandibular below), so both pairings are correct.

stem: 69-year-old woman presents with right-sided hemiparesis, right-sided hemisensory loss, right-sided homonymous hemianopia, and aphasia. Past medical history is significant for hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and diabetes mellitus. What vessel has been occluded?
answer: The correct answer is C. Complete MCA strokes will primarily cause a visual field loss or homonymous hemianopia to the opposite side because they affect the optic radiations projecting to the occipital cortex. MCA strokes on the left side can cause an aphasia, right sided hemiparesis, and right sided hemisensory loss.

stem: What would you be concerned about if the interventricular foramen become blocked?
answer: The correct answer is C. If an interventricular foramen became blocked, cerebrospinal fluid could not flow from the lateral ventricles into the third ventricle. Cerebrospinal fluid would continue to form within that ventricle, so the blocked ventricle would swell with fluid - a condition known as hydrocephalus.

stem: What would you expect to see on post-mortem examination of Parkinson’s disease brains?

options.html: Loss of neuromelanin pigmentation in the substantial nigra
Excess neuromelanin pigmentation in the substantia nigra

answer: The correct answer is C. Post-mortem examination of Parkinson’s disease brain at a macroscopic level shows no brain shrinkage; there is not significant difference between Parkinson’s disease brains and age-matched controls in the number of neurons. In the Parkinson’s disease brain, there is significant and specific degeneration of the dopaminergic neuron of the substantia nigra.

stem: 45-year-old man has been experiencing an increase in accidents at work over the last couple of months, such as accidentally cutting his fingers with his knife and dropping plates. In the emergency room, you (the physician) notice that he was stumbling often and had difficulty with his upper limb coordination. He told you that he has had a difficult time at work using his knife recently and mentioned that “it must be due to being tired”. You also noted that the man had a short temper and got angry with some of the other patients in the waiting room. MRI of the brain showed ventricular enlargement and degeneration of cortical layers. Genetic testing showed over 69 CAG repeats on the short arm of chromosome 4. What is at the top of your differential diagnosis?
answer: The correct answer is A. MRI findings and genetic testing are consistent with Huntington’s disease.

stem: Which of the following structures will be affected by a cavernous sinus thrombus (multiple correct answers)?
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, E, F.

From 08 - Anatomy of the Cranial Cavity, and the cavernous sinus note. The contents of the cavernous sinus are the internal carotid artery (with its sympathetic plexus) and CN III, IV, V1, V2 and VI. That is why compression, whether by thrombus, pituitary mass or carotid aneurysm, causes ophthalmoplegia, orbital and facial pain, chemosis and trigeminal sensory loss.

  • B (CN IV), E (CN V2), F (ICA): all run through the sinus, so all are affected.
  • A, optic chiasm: not a content of the sinus.
  • C, CN VIII: runs in the internal acoustic meatus of the posterior fossa.
  • D, CN V3: leaves through the foramen ovale and does not pass through the sinus.

stem: Which component of the eye is responsible for accommodation
answer:
The correct answer is A.

From 11 - Neurophysiology of Vision. Accommodation is the lens changing shape to keep the image focused on the retina. The ciliary muscles change its shape through the suspensory fibres. When they contract, the lens rounds up for near vision. When they relax, the lens flattens for distance.

  • B: the iris and pupil control how much light enters (the pupillary light reflex), not focus.
  • C: only half right. The pupil constricts along with accommodation (both are driven by CN III through the ciliary ganglion) but does no focusing itself.
  • D: light passes through the cornea first, but the lecture gives the focusing change to the lens.
  • E: the fovea receives the image, and the posterior chamber is a fluid space.

stem: Which of the following eye pathology is caused by increased intra-ocular pressure compressing axons of retinal ganglion cell
answer:
The correct answer is D.

From 11 - Neurophysiology of Vision. The lecture defines glaucoma as raised intraocular pressure compressing the axons of retinal ganglion cells, the axons that form the optic nerve. It takes peripheral vision first, giving "tunnel vision". (06 - Monocular Vision Impairment refines this: glaucoma is the optic neuropathy itself, and it can occur at normal pressure.)

  • A fails: cataract is clouding of the lens from misfolded proteins.
  • B fails: Horner syndrome is a sympathetic-chain lesion (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), not a pressure problem.
  • C fails: macular degeneration is deposits or new vessels under the fovea, distorting central vision.
  • E fails: myopia is a refractive error.

stem: Which of the following is involved in the formation of memory (multiple correct answers)
answer:
The correct answer is A, B, C, D.

From 12 - Neuroanatomy of the Cortex. Memory is distributed:

  • A The hippocampus forms new memories and converts short-term to long-term; bilateral loss (patient H.M.) causes anterograde amnesia.
  • D The amygdala, anteromedial to it, has an integral role in emotion, learning and memory.
  • B, C The prefrontal cortex is a multimodal association area responsible for working memory, and association cortex links new input to memories of past experience.

All four count.

answer: The correct answer is D. The deck's note: AComm and PComm completing the circuit. The circle of Willis (ACA, AComm, MCA, ICA, PCA, PComm) lets the left ACA (via the AComm) and the posterior circulation (via the PComm) refill the right anterior circulation distal to the ICA block.

stem: 45M brought presents to ER with sudden onset new R facial droop and slurred speech. They are unable to blink on the right side and have complete paralysis of facial muscles including on their forehead. They have had a recent viral infection. There is no rash. They deny any headache or symptoms in the limbs. Where does this localize and what is the likely cause?
answer: The correct answer is C. The deck's notes: complete paralysis of facial muscles (CN VII); Ramsay Hunt is more shingles/rash; Bell's palsy is more post-viral. Forehead involvement and an eye that cannot close mean a peripheral (LMN) lesion; a central lesion such as an MCA stroke spares the forehead.

stem: Mrs. Peterson was diagnosed with fibromyalgia by a rheumatologist and is seeing you today for ongoing care. She complains of pain throughout her body. The pain comes in spurts at times and interferes with activity. She is always tired and doesn’t feel like getting out of bed some mornings. You would like to try Mrs. Jones on a treatment for her fibromyalgia. Which is the following would NOT be an acceptable option for her condition?

options.html: Tylenol with codeine 3/300 three times a day as needed for pain

answer: The correct answer is C. Tylenol with codeine is not an acceptable option because it contains an opioid. Opioids have no role in the management of fibromyalgia and should be avoided. All the other options are accepted treatments for fibromyalgia.

stem: Jeannette is a 34 year old female who complaints of generalized achiness for the past 6 months. She complains that she has pain especially in her hands and feels like her joints are always swollen. She also complains of dry eyes and dry mouth. She can no longer work due to profound fatigue. She feels unrefreshed when she awakens in the morning. You review her chart and note a past history of irritable bowel syndrome and headaches which have been fully evaluated. You do some labs on her which reveal the following: Positive ANA 1:2560, positive rheumatoid factor 300, ENA positive for Ro Antibody. You do a fibromyalgia questionnaire and her Widespread Pain Index (WPI) is 8 and her Symptoms Severity Score (SS) is 6. Which of the following statements is TRUE?

options.html: Jeannette has an autoimmune disease that needs to be investigated and also has fibromyalgia.

answer: The correct answer is B. Jeannette laboratory workup suggests she has an autoimmune disease. Based on the information provided (which does not include a joint exam), the differential would include rheumatoid arthritis, or any of the connective tissue diseases. However, she also describes chronic widespread pain for > 3 months duration. She meets criteria for Fibromyalgia based on the results of her WPI and SS scores. The best available answer is b.

You do a fibromyalgia questionnaire and her Widespread Pain Index (WPI) is 8 and her Symptoms Severity Score (SS) is 6. stem: What is the most appropriate initial management of her fibromyalgia? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Low-dose opioid for her widespread pain

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): D. Fibromyalgia treatment starts with education and exercise, which has the best evidence, and non-drug therapy is as effective as drugs. Fibromyalgia often sits alongside another disease, and treating that disease alone will not fix the fibromyalgia 03 - Body Pain.

  • A: Opioids should not be used in fibromyalgia: they are no better for pain, and sleep, disability and pain interference are better without them.
  • B: The other disease should be treated too, but treating it alone won't fix the fibromyalgia.
  • C: Prednisone 15-20 mg daily is the treatment for polymyalgia rheumatica, not fibromyalgia.

stem: Maria is a 53 year old female who was previously healthy. She was in a motor vehicle accident 5 years ago. She injured both of her legs below her knees. She now suffers from pain that has gotten progressively worse through her entire body. She feels pain when she someone touches her even lightly. She denies any numbness or tingling. She takes Percocet for her pain which helps slightly. On exam, she is well appearing. She is overweight. Her joints do not reveal any swelling, redness, or warmth. Neurologic exam for sensation is normal in the hands and feet. Her muscle exam demonstrates to reproducible weakness however she flinches noticeably with even just a light touch. Which of the following descriptions of central pain is correct?

options.html: It responds to very well to opioids.
It is the result of damage to the peripheral nerves.
It is a disturbance of pain processing.

answer: The correct answer is D. Central pain is a disturbance in pain processing. It does not respond well to opioids. It is not related to direct damage of the peripheral nerves. Hence choice D is correct.

Later: her pain is central pain, a disturbance of pain processing.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)
answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): A. Central pain responds to drugs that change the neurotransmitters of pain; in central pain the descending norepinephrine and serotonin pathway is turned down, so a drug that raises both helps. Duloxetine is the SNRI with the best evidence in fibromyalgia, the lecture's central pain example, started as one drug at the lowest dose and titrated slowly 03 - Body Pain.

  • B: Opioids are not used in fibromyalgia: they are no better for pain, and sleep, disability and pain interference are better without them.
  • C: NSAIDs treat nociceptive pain from tissue inflammation, and her joints show no swelling, redness or warmth.
  • D: A stronger opioid has the same problem as a higher dose.

stem: Mrs. Cadillac is a very pleasant woman you are seeing in followup in the clinic today. One month ago, she came in complaining of body aches especially in her shoulders. She needed help to dress herself. She had lost 15 lbs due to lack of interest in food. She complained of stiffness lasting throughout the morning and alleviated some time in the middle of the afternoon. You had done some labs which revealed ESR 73 mm/hr and CRP 17.8mg/L. You suspected she had PMR and put her on prednisone 20mg daily. She called you a week later telling you that you are her favorite doctor. She felt better right away. She continues to feel quite well but is worried about what the prednisone could be doing to her body. Which of the following is NOT a steroid related side effect that she could be experiencing?
answer: The correct answer is D. All of the other listed side effects may be caused by steroids. Steroids may cause generalized swelling, but not of the joints.

stem: What is the most appropriate next step in management? (follow-up written for this bank; the source does not ask it)

options.html: Stop the prednisone now that she is well
Halve the dose to 10 mg daily now
Taper quickly by 5 mg every week

answer:
Reasoned answer (written for this bank): B. Polymyalgia rheumatica needs prednisone held until she is well and the markers are normal, then a slow taper, with an average of about 2 years on steroids. Anyone expected to take over 7.5 mg of prednisone for over 3 months needs bone protection: calcium 1500 mg a day, vitamin D 1000-2000 IU a day and an antiresorptive such as a bisphosphonate 03 - Body Pain.

  • A: Stopping now ignores the long course the lecture teaches, and relapses are common.
  • C: The dose is held until she is well and the markers are normal, then lowered slowly, not halved at once.
  • D: The lecture's taper is slow, for example 15 to 12.5 to 10 mg a month apart, then 1 mg a month.

stem: Mr. Jones is a 64 year old male who complains of pain in his back, thighs, without weakness for the past 3 months. He reports low grade fevers and has a weight loss of about 10 lbs. His ESR is elevated to 54 mm/hr and CRP is increased to 10.5mg/L. You suspect he has polymyalgia rheumatic and you initiate prednisone at a dose of 20mg/d. After one week, he returns to the clinic and reports that he is 10 percent better. Which of the following statements are true?

options.html: Mr. Jones’ response to prednisone confirms the diagnosis of PMR.
Mr. Jones has had an inadequate response to the prednisone dose prescribed and therefore, the prednisone dose should be increased to 40mg a day.
The diagnosis of PMR is incorrect and you should investigate Mr. Jones for other causes of his complaints.
Mr. Jones needs more time on his current regimen of prednisone to get 100% better.

answer: The correct answer is C. The patient has had an inadequate response to the prednisone trial after 1 week which suggests he may have a alternate diagnosis, not PMR. The patient should be reassessed for other causes of his complaints.

stem: Mrs. Abbey is a 74 year old female who has been complaining of pain and stiffness in her neck, shoulders, and back for the last three months. She reports her weight has dropped by about 5lbs because food no longer tastes good to her. She also has a hard time getting out of bed in the morning. She describes herself as a "TinMan that needs some oil." She finds she feels a bit "looser" around mid afternoon. You suspect she has PMR. You order some labs that reveal the following: WBC 10.4 (4.0-11.0) Hemoglobin 112 (normal 120-148) Platelets 79 (normal 150-400) ESR 103mm/hr (normal 0-30) CRP 78 (normal 0-7.5) Which of the following is NOT a feature of PMR?
answer: The correct answer is B. All of the choices are features of PMR except for thrombocytopenia. PMR can cause a reactive thrombocytosis but thrombocytopenia is not seen.

stem: A 24-year-old man is taken to the emergency department for treatment after he was assaulted during a robbery. In order to stitch the laceration above the eye in the patient shown below, branches of which of the following nerves must be anesthetized?
answer:
The correct answer is B. The ophthalmic division of Trigeminal nerve (V1) supplies the forehead, upper eyelid and most of the nose and would be implicated for this treatment.

  • A) C1 Ventral Ramus: Most cervical plexus nerves supply the neck and posterior aspect of the skull. The C1 ventral ramus does not carry any sensory neurons from the skin over the face.
  • C) CN V2: The maxillary division of Trigeminal nerve (V2) supplies the mid face, lower eyelid, upper lip, and lateral to the orbit and would not be implicated for this treatment.
  • D) CN V3: The mandibular division of Trigeminal nerve (V3) supplies most of the skin over the mandible, anterior to ear, and lateral scalp and would not be implicated for this treatment.
  • E) CN VII: The facial nerve (CN VII) provides motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department by her parents because they are scared that she has had a stroke. On physical exam she was asked to smile, an image of which is shown below. An MRI showed a 1cm bony mass on her skull that is compressing a nerve, which seems to be the cause of her symptoms. Which of the following nerves is being compressed?
answer:
The correct answer is D. Carries motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression, which are responsible for smiling. This girl's left facial nerve is being compressed and is responsible for her symptoms.

  • A) CN V1: Carries sensory innervation from the upper portion of the face
  • B) CN V2: Carries sensory innervation from the mid portion of the face and parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland
  • C) CN V3: Carries sensory innervation from the lower portion of the face, taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue, and motor to the muscles of mastication. The muscles of mastication are not involved in smiling.

stem: A 51-year-old woman sees a plastic surgeon for treatment options for minimizing or eliminating the wrinkles that have formed near the lateral corners of her eyes ("Crow’s feet"). The surgeon suggests Botox injections. Botox injections and subsequent paralysis to which of the following facial muscles will be most effective in reducing the appearance of these wrinkles?
answer:
The correct answer is B. Orbicularis oculi encircles the eye and is involved in the formation of crow's feet wrinkles.

  • A) Frontalis: Frontalis lies over the forehead and is involved in the formation of forehead lines.
  • C) Orbicularis Oris: Orbicularis oris encircles the mouth and is involved in the formation of lip wrinkles
  • D) Zygomaticus Major: Zygomaticus major is involved in smiling and is responsible for the formation of laugh lines.

stem: A 63-year old woman is seen for her annual physical exam. During her exam, she notes that she has experienced tingling and numbness along her jaw and has had difficulty chewing (mastication). Which of the following nerves is most likely compressed or injured?
answer:
The correct answer is C. Carries sensory innervation from the lower portion of the face, taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue, and motor to the muscles of mastication. This is the nerve that is likely affected in this case.

  • A) CN V1: Carries sensory innervation from the upper portion of the face and is not involved in motor to the muscles of mastication
  • B) CN V2: Carries sensory innervation from the mid portion of the face and parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland and is not involved in motor to the muscles of mastication
  • D) CN VII: Carries motor innervation to the muscles of facial expression and is not involved in sensory to the face or motor to the muscles of mastication.

stem: A 7-year-old boy contracts mumps, causing painful swelling of his right parotid gland. The physician assistant treating him is concerned about structures within the gland. Which of the following structures within the parotid gland would most likely be compressed?
answer:
The correct answer is E. Facial nerve (CN VII) is embedded within the parotid gland and due to the parotid fascia surrounding the gland, if the gland were to become inflamed the facial nerve would likely be compressed and result in paralysis to the muscles of fascial expression on that side.

  • A) Branch of V3: V3 arises deep to the ramus of the mandible and innervated the muscles of mastication from the deep aspect. The parotid gland is superficial to the ramus of the mandible and thus it is unlikely swelling of the gland would compress this structure.
  • B) Buccinator muscle: The buccinator muscle sits anterior to the parotid gland and is unlikely to be compressed from the swelling of this gland.
  • C) External Jugular Vein: The retromandibular vein, which drains into the external jugular vein, may be compressed by swelling of the parotid gland, but the external jugular vein itself begins inferior to the parotid gland with the junction of the retromandibular vein and the posterior auricular vein.
  • D) Facial Artery: Facial artery branches from the external carotid artery inferior to the parotid gland and then courses toward the midline and is unlikely to be compressed from the swelling of this gland.
